title: AI vs machine learning vs deep learning vs generative AI
text: Intuition Think of four boxes, one inside the other. The biggest box, AI, holds every way of making a computer act smart, including rules a programmer types in by hand. Inside it, machine learning is the part where the computer learns the rules from examples instead. Inside that, deep learning learns with large neural networks. And inside that, generative AI uses those networks to create new text, images or code. A cooking comparison: a recipe card is rules, a cook who learns by tasting many dishes is machine learning, and a cook who can invent a new dish in the same style is generative AI. Mechanism These four terms describe nested sets. Each inner one is a particular way of doing the outer one. Artificial intelligence (AI) : any technique that makes a computer perform a task we would call intelligent if a person did it, such as planning, recognising, deciding or conversing. Hand-written rules count. Machine learning (ML) : AI where behaviour is learned from data instead of written by hand. You supply examples; an algorithm fits a function to them. Deep learning (DL) : ML using neural networks with many layers. Layers learn their own intermediate features, so you do not hand-design them. Generative AI (GenAI) : models that produce new content (text, images, audio, code) by learning the distribution of their training data and sampling from it. Today almost all GenAI is deep learning. The practical difference is where the knowledge comes from . In rule-based AI it comes from the programmer. In classical ML it comes from labelled examples plus features the engineer chose. In deep learning it comes from large amounts of data, and the model chooses the features. In generative AI the model has learned enough about the data to create plausible new samples. A second difference is the output type . Classical ML typically outputs a number or a label from a fixed set ("fraud: 0.93"). Generative models output open-ended content ("Dear customer, we noticed…"). Open-ended output is more flexible and much harder to verify, which is why evaluation (chapter 8) is so central to GenAI work. AI search, planning, expert rules ML regression, trees, clustering Deep learning CNNs, RNNs, transformers Generative AI LLMs, diffusion Examples AI only: chess engine with hand-coded evaluation ML: credit-risk gradient boosting on 40 features DL: image classifier that learns its own features GenAI: LLM drafting a support reply Nested sets. Every LLM is generative, deep and machine-learned, so it inherits all the outer sets' concerns: it needs data, it can overfit, and its behaviour is statistical. Example: one business problem, four approaches Routing incoming support emails to the right team: Rules (AI): if "invoice" in subject → Billing . Transparent, brittle when wording changes. Classical ML: TF-IDF word features + logistic regression trained on 20,000 labelled emails. Cheap, fast, accurate on common categories. Deep learning: fine-tuned BERT-style encoder. Handles paraphrase and context better; needs more compute. Generative AI: prompt an LLM with the team descriptions and ask for a label plus a one-line reason. Zero training data needed to start; higher cost per email; must validate that the label is one of the allowed values. The numbers What each approach needs before it can start , for the email-routing example above. The prices and times are illustrative. Rules: no data, but someone must write and keep updating every keyword. Twenty rules might take a day to write. Classical ML: labelled examples. Labelling 20,000 emails at 30 seconds each is 20,000 × 30 = 600,000 seconds, about 167 hours of work. Generative AI: no labelled data to start, but every email costs money. With 500 tokens in and 20 tokens out, at $1 per million input tokens and $4 per million output tokens, one email costs 500 × 1 ÷ 1,000,000 + 20 × 4 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ $0.0006. A million emails a month is about $580. Running a trained classical model on the same million emails costs only a few dollars of computer time. That gap is why many teams start with an LLM to learn the task and later switch high-volume, stable tasks to a cheaper model. Code The program sorts your example project’s labelled text twice: first with a short list of hand-written keyword rules, then with a classifier that learns which words go with which label. It tests both on rows the classifier has not seen. Add a keyword to a rule, run it again, and see the rules’ score change. Rules against learning, in real Python. It runs in your browser after you opt in to the Python download. The data is synthetic, so the scores are not what you would get on real text. Primary sources Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach The standard textbook; chapter 1 defines AI and its approaches. Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville (2016), Deep Learning, chapter 1 How deep learning relates to machine learning and AI, with the same nested-sets picture. Bommasani et al. (2021), On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models Where generative models sit today and why they changed how AI is built. scikit-learn: Naive Bayes The classifier used in the code, in a production library.

title: Evolution: from rules to foundation models and agents
text: Intuition Each era of AI fixed the biggest problem of the one before. First people wrote rules by hand, which broke on anything unexpected. Then computers learned weights from data, but people still had to choose what to look at. Then neural networks learned what to look at too. Then attention let a model look at a whole sentence at once instead of word by word, which made training fast on GPUs and opened the way to today's large models. It is like the history of maps: hand-drawn sketches, then surveyed maps, then satellite photos, then live maps that update themselves. Each step kept what worked and removed one big limit. Mechanism Each era of AI solved the main limitation of the previous one, and introduced a new one. Knowing this chain tells you why transformers look the way they do. Rule-based 1950s–80s Statistical ML 1990s–2000s Neural nets 1986 → 2012 RNNs / LSTMs 1997 → 2015 Attention 2014 Transformers 2017 Foundation models 2018 → Agents 2023 → Rule-based / expert systems. Knowledge engineers wrote IF–THEN rules (MYCIN for infections, 1970s). Worked in narrow domains; broke on anything the rules did not anticipate, and thousands of rules became unmaintainable. Statistical ML. Instead of writing rules, learn weights from data: naive Bayes spam filters, support vector machines, decision trees. Robust to noise, but engineers still hand-designed the features (e.g. "count of exclamation marks"). Neural networks. Backpropagation (popularised 1986) trains multi-layer networks that learn features themselves. The breakthrough came when GPUs and large datasets arrived: AlexNet won ImageNet in 2012 by a wide margin. RNNs and LSTMs. Language is a sequence, so recurrent networks read one token at a time and carry a hidden state. LSTMs (1997) added gates to remember longer. Limits: they process tokens strictly in order (slow to train in parallel) and still forget over long distances. Attention. For translation (2014), a decoder learned to "look back" at every encoder position and weight the relevant ones. Long-range dependencies became direct lookups instead of a chain of hidden states. Transformers. "Attention Is All You Need" (2017) removed recurrence entirely. Every token attends to every other token in parallel, which suits GPUs and scales to huge datasets. Foundation models . Pretrain one large transformer on broad data, then adapt it to many tasks: BERT (2018), GPT-2 (2019), GPT-3 (2020) showed abilities improve with scale. Instruction tuning and RLHF (2022) made them follow instructions, producing chat assistants. Agents . LLMs that call tools, observe results and decide next steps in a loop. Reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks (2024–25) produced "reasoning" models that think longer before answering. Protocols like MCP (2024) standardised tool access. Step through the eras. The recurring theme: hand-made knowledge was replaced by learned knowledge, and sequential computation was replaced by parallel computation that scales with hardware. Example: the same sentence across eras Task: decide whether "The movie was not bad at all" is positive. A rule-based system that flags "bad" says negative. A bag-of-words classifier may also say negative because "bad" has a negative weight. An LSTM can learn that "not … at all" flips meaning. A transformer attends from "bad" to "not" directly, and a foundation model has seen millions of similar phrases during pretraining, so it gets it right with no task-specific training. The numbers How the models grew. Parameter counts of some milestone models: Model Year Parameters AlexNet (images) 2012 about 60 million BERT large 2018 340 million GPT-2 2019 1.5 billion GPT-3 2020 175 billion From 2012 to 2020 that is about 175,000,000,000 ÷ 60,000,000 ≈ 2,900 times bigger. Training text grew too: GPT-3 was trained on about 300 billion tokens, and Llama 3 (2024) on about 15 trillion, 50 times more. Why transformers won. An RNN reads a 1,000-word text in 1,000 steps, one after another, because each step needs the one before. A transformer handles all 1,000 positions of a training text in one parallel pass, which is exactly the kind of work a GPU with thousands of cores is good at. Code The program classifies the same three sentences in three ways: counting good and bad words (rules), learning a weight for each single word, and learning weights for pairs of neighbouring words too. Add your own sentence to TESTS , or a new review to TRAIN , and run it again. One sentence, three eras, in real Python. Fourteen invented reviews are far too few for a real model; compare the three columns, not their accuracy. Primary sources Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (1986), Learning representations by back-propagating errors The paper that made multi-layer neural networks trainable. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014), Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate The first attention mechanism. Vaswani et al. (2017), Attention Is All You Need The transformer, which removed recurrence. Brown et al. (2020), Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3) Showed that a large pretrained model can do new tasks from a few examples. Ouyang et al. (2022), Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback The instruction tuning and RLHF behind chat assistants. Model Context Protocol documentation The open standard for connecting agents to tools (11.8).

title: What language models predict, and what makes a model an LLM
text: Intuition A language model is a very well-read autocomplete. Give it the start of some text and it tells you, for every word piece it knows, how likely that piece is to come next. To write an answer, it picks one, adds it to the text, and asks itself the same question again, hundreds of times. It never looks anything up. "Canberra" comes after "the capital of Australia is" because that pattern was common in what it read, not because it checked a fact. That is why it can sound sure and still be wrong. Mechanism A language model assigns probabilities to sequences of text. Modern ones do this one step at a time: given all the text so far, output a probability for every possible next token . Generating text means repeatedly picking a token from that distribution and appending it. That is the whole core mechanism. Answering a question, writing code and summarising a document are all the same operation: continue the text in a way that is likely given everything before it. Instruction-tuned models have been trained so that the likely continuation of "a user question" is "a helpful answer", but they are still predicting continuations. A model is called a large language model (LLM) when it combines three things: a transformer architecture; a large number of learned parameters (there is no agreed cut-off; today the term usually means billions, and frontier models are far larger, but parameter count alone does not measure quality: data, training objectives, adaptation and the task matter as much); and pretraining on a very large, broad text corpus (trillions of tokens). The "large" matters because many abilities, such as following instructions in a new format or translating between rare language pairs, only become reliable above a certain scale. Context: "The invoice is due on the 15th of" → next-token distribution ␣March ␣each ␣every ␣next ␣the ␣April … 100,000+ other tokens Illustrative distribution. The model outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary; these sum to 100%. Note that "March" wins because it is common, not because the model knows which invoice you mean. That gap between "likely" and "true" is the root of hallucination (1.5). Example: a "question" is just a prefix Input: Q: What is the capital of Australia?\nA: . The model computes that "␣Canberra" is the most likely next token, then that "." is likely after it, then an end-of-answer token. Nothing in the model is a database row labelled "capital of Australia"; the association is spread across billions of weights. The numbers One answer is many small guesses. If the model gives "␣Canberra" a chance of 0.92 and then "." a chance of 0.80, the two-step answer "Canberra." has a chance of 0.92 × 0.80 ≈ 0.74. Every token of an answer is one more step, and at each step the model scores its whole vocabulary: a 500-token answer is 500 choices, each among about 128,000 tokens. How large is large. An 8-billion-parameter model stored at 2 bytes per parameter needs 8 × 2 = 16 GB of memory just for its weights. Llama 3 was trained on about 15 trillion tokens. At about 0.75 words per token that is roughly 11 trillion words. A person reading 250 words a minute for 8 hours a day reads 120,000 words a day, so it would take them about 11,000,000,000,000 ÷ 120,000 ≈ 92 million days: around 250,000 years. Code The program builds the simplest language model: a table of which word followed each pair of words in your example project’s messages. It prints the chances for one context, checks they add up to 1, and generates three messages by picking word after word. Change random.seed(1) to another number to get different messages. Next-word prediction from counts, in real Python. A count table sees only two words back; an LLM uses a neural network and the whole context. Primary sources Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd edition draft) The chapter on n-gram language models builds the same count table as the code. Bengio et al. (2003), A Neural Probabilistic Language Model The first neural network language model. Kaplan et al. (2020), Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models How quality improves with parameters, data and compute. Wei et al. (2022), Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models Abilities that appear only above a certain scale. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo (2023), Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? The counter-argument: some "emergence" comes from how it is measured.

title: Tokens, parameters, embeddings, context windows, training and inference
text: Intuition A model reads text the way a shop till reads a barcode: as numbers. The text is cut into pieces called tokens, each piece is swapped for its id number, and each id is swapped again for a list of numbers the model has learned. Everything the model knows lives in its parameters, billions of numbers set during training. Training is like writing a textbook: slow, expensive, done once. Inference is like a student using the book in an exam: fast, done every day, and the book does not change while it is being used. Chatting with a model never rewrites its book. Mechanism Token : the unit of text a model reads and writes. Usually a word or a piece of a word ("unbeliev" + "ably"). In English prose, 1 token is roughly 4 characters or 0.75 words on average; other languages, code, numbers and identifiers differ widely, so always count with the model's own tokenizer rather than converting from words. Prices, speed and limits are all counted in tokens. Vocabulary : the fixed list of tokens a model knows, typically 32,000–260,000 entries. Each has an integer ID. Parameter (weight) : one learned number inside the model. An "8B model" has about 8 billion of them. Parameters store everything the model learned. Embedding : a list of numbers (a vector) that represents a token or a piece of text. Similar meanings get nearby vectors. An embedding is not a compressed copy of the text: you cannot reliably decode the original document from it. Context window : the maximum number of tokens (input plus output) the model can consider at once, for example 128,000. Anything outside it is invisible to the model. Training : adjusting parameters so predictions improve. Expensive, done rarely. Inference : using fixed parameters to produce outputs. Cheap per call, done millions of times. Prompting and chatting change only the input, never the weights: a conversation does not retrain the model, and "memory" in chat products is application storage (7.5). Text "Refund my order" Tokens Ref · und · ␣my · ␣order Token IDs [4032, 1263, 856, 2015] Embeddings 4 × 4096 numbers Transformer layers billions of parameters Logits → probabilities one per vocab entry Next token "␣please" Your application sends text. Everything that will influence the answer (system instructions, history, retrieved documents) must be in this text, because the model has no other input. A tokenizer splits the text into tokens using rules learned before model training (chapter 5.1). The same text can be a different number of tokens for different models. Each token is replaced by its integer ID in the vocabulary. This list of IDs, plus the room for the output, must fit in the context window. Each ID selects a row from an embedding table (itself part of the parameters), giving one vector per token. The vectors flow through dozens of transformer layers. Each layer mixes information between positions (attention) and transforms each position (feed-forward). This is where almost all parameters and computation live. The final vector at the last position is turned into one score ( logit ) per vocabulary token, then into probabilities with softmax. A decoding rule picks one token (chapter 5.6). It is appended to the input and the loop repeats until a stop condition. That loop is inference . One pass through a model. Token IDs shown are illustrative. During training the same forward pass runs, then the error against the real next token is pushed backward to adjust the parameters. Training weeks · thousands of GPUs parameters change Inference milliseconds–seconds per call parameters frozen Batch of text Forward pass Loss vs truth Update weights User prompt Forward pass Pick token Append & repeat Same forward pass, different purpose. Training loops over data to change weights. Inference loops over output tokens with weights fixed. Most engineers only ever run inference, but understanding training explains model behaviour. Token, cost and latency estimator. The text estimate is a rough heuristic (about 4 characters per token for English prose, fewer for code, digits and non-Latin scripts); always confirm with the model's real tokenizer. Latency assumes prefill at 10,000 tokens/s and the decode speed you set. Prices are illustrative inputs. Example: estimating cost before writing code A summariser receives 3,000-word documents (≈ 4,000 tokens) and writes 200-word summaries (≈ 270 tokens). At an illustrative price of $1 per million input tokens and $4 per million output tokens, one summary costs 4,000 × 1/10⁶ + 270 × 4/10⁶ ≈ $0.005 . 100,000 documents a month ≈ $500. Output tokens are usually priced higher and generated much more slowly than input tokens are read, which is why output length dominates latency. The numbers Fitting a request into the context window. A support assistant with a 128,000-token window sends, with every question: Part Tokens Instructions 2,000 8 retrieved passages of 800 tokens 6,400 20 earlier turns of 150 tokens 3,000 Room for the answer 1,000 Total 12,400 That fits easily, but the window is not the only limit: every one of those 12,400 tokens is paid for on every question, and more input means a slower first token. Parameters take memory. An 8-billion-parameter model at 2 bytes per parameter is 16 GB. Its embedding table alone, 128,256 tokens × 4,096 numbers, is about 525 million parameters. Code The program estimates tokens per message for each language in your example project’s messages using the two English rules of thumb, shows the byte count that limits a byte-level tokenizer, then works out a monthly cost and the size of an embedding table. Change the prices, PROMPT_TOKENS or MESSAGES_PER_MONTH and run it again. Tokens, cost and parameters, in real Python. The prices are illustrative, and the token counts are estimates, not a real tokenizer’s. Laptop lab: see tokens Laptop · CPU from transformers import AutoTokenizer tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2") # small download, no model weights for s in ["Refund my order", "Unbelievably", "Rückerstattung", "退款", " def f(x):"]: ids = tok.encode(s) print(f"{s!r:22} {len(ids):2} tokens {tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids)}") Notice that non-English text and code whitespace take more tokens per character. Try a different tokenizer (for example "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B" ) and compare counts for the same strings. Primary sources Hugging Face: Summary of the tokenizers How BPE, WordPiece and SentencePiece split text. Hugging Face: Generation with LLMs The inference loop from token ids to generated text, in code. Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd edition draft) The chapters on embeddings and transformers explain each step of the flow above. Llama Team (2024), The Llama 3 Herd of Models Real figures for vocabulary size, parameters, context length and training tokens.

title: Capabilities and limitations: hallucination, stale knowledge, bias and unreliable confidence
text: Intuition An LLM is like a very confident friend who has read a lot but cannot check anything. Ask about something they half remember and they will still give a smooth, sure answer, because sounding right is what they learned. They also stopped reading on a certain date, and they have never seen your company's private documents. The fix is not to trust the friend more, but to hand them the right page and ask them to answer from it, quoting where the answer came from, and to say "I don't know" when the page does not have it. Mechanism LLMs are strong at language transformation (summarise, rewrite, translate, extract), at pattern-following from a few examples, at writing and explaining code, and at broad general knowledge. Their weaknesses follow directly from "predict the likely next token from frozen weights": Hallucination : fluent, confident output that is false. The model produces what is plausible ; when it lacks the fact, a plausible-sounding fabrication is still the likely continuation. Invented citations, API methods and policy clauses are typical. Outdated knowledge : weights reflect data up to a training cutoff . The model does not know about your product release last week, or your internal documents at all, unless you put them in the context (that is RAG, chapter 9). Bias : training data reflects the world's skews. Models can associate professions with genders, rate dialects as less formal, or default to US conventions. In hiring, lending or moderation this becomes a legal and ethical problem. Unreliable confidence : tone does not track correctness. "I'm certain" carries no information. Even token probabilities are only loosely related to factual accuracy after instruction tuning. Do not use the model's self-reported confidence as a control signal without measuring it (3.5, 8.3). Other practical limits : arithmetic and exact counting errors (tokens are not characters), sensitivity to prompt wording, non-determinism, and vulnerability to instructions hidden in input text (prompt injection, chapter 16). "What is our refund window?" Weights only generic e-commerce patterns "30 days with receipt." fluent, possibly wrong ✕ unverifiable no source to check "What is our refund window?" Retrieve policy doc Rule: cite or abstain Model reads context "14 days [policy §3]" checkable ✓ grounded citation verifiable Design around the limitation. You cannot remove hallucination from the model, but you can supply the facts (retrieval), constrain behaviour (cite or say "I don't know"), and verify outputs (evaluation). Example: a real failure pattern An internal assistant is asked "Which config flag enables audit logging in our gateway?" It answers --enable-audit-log=true . That flag does not exist; the real one is audit.sink in a YAML file. The model generated the most typical shape of such a flag. Mitigation: retrieve the gateway's documentation, require answers to quote the doc, and add this question to the evaluation set. Giving the model the facts in its input and asking it to answer from them, with citations, is called grounding . The numbers Small error rates add up. Suppose a model gets each fact right 95% of the time. An answer that depends on 10 separate facts is fully right only if all 10 are, which happens about 0.95 multiplied by itself 10 times ≈ 60% of the time. Four answers in ten have at least one mistake. Confidence that does not match accuracy. Collect 100 answers where the model said it was "90% sure" and check them. If only 70 are correct, the model is overconfident by 20 points, and "90% sure" cannot be used to decide what to show a customer without measuring it first (3.5). Stale knowledge. If a refund policy changed from 30 days to 14 days after the training cutoff, a model answering from memory will keep saying 30 days, every time, with full confidence, until the new policy is put into its input. Code The program answers four questions from your example project’s documents. For each, it finds the document that shares the most words with the question, quotes its best sentence with the document id, and declines when no document shares enough words. Add a question of your own to QUESTIONS , or change MIN_OVERLAP , and run it again. Answer from a source, or say so, in real Python. Word overlap is a crude way to find sources; chapter 9 builds real retrieval. Primary sources Ji et al. (2022), Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation Types and causes of hallucination, and how it is measured. Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks The original RAG paper: answering from retrieved documents. Kadavath et al. (2022), Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know How well a model’s confidence matches its accuracy, and where it does not. Bender et al. (2021), On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots Bias and other risks that come from the training data. OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications Prompt injection and the other security risks listed above (chapter 16).

title: AI problem selection: rules, search, traditional ML or an LLM
text: Intuition Pick the simplest tool that does the job. You would not hire a novelist to add up a bill, and you would not use a calculator to write a thank-you letter. Rules and code are the calculator: exact, free and easy to check. An LLM is the novelist: great with messy language, but slower, more expensive and sometimes wrong. Most good systems mix them: code for anything that must be exact, search to find the facts, and an LLM only for the parts that really need language. Mechanism The most expensive mistake in enterprise AI is using an LLM where a simpler tool is more accurate, cheaper and easier to audit. Choose by asking what the task really is. Approach Fits when Strengths Weaknesses Rules / code The logic can be written down and must be exact: tax calculation, eligibility, validation, permissions. Deterministic, auditable, free to run. Brittle with messy language; costly to maintain if rules explode. Search The answer exists in a document and users need to find it: policy lookup, product catalog. Shows sources; fast; no fabrication. Users must read and synthesise; poor with vague queries. Traditional ML Structured or tabular data, a fixed set of outputs, plenty of labels: churn, fraud, demand forecasts. Cheap at scale, measurable, calibrated scores. Needs labelled data and feature work; does not generate text. LLM Open-ended language in or out: drafting, summarising, extracting from free text, conversational help, code. No training data to start, handles variety. Cost, latency, non-determinism, hallucination, injection risk. Combination Most real systems: search to find facts, LLM to phrase, rules to enforce limits. Each part does what it is good at. More components to build and monitor. Interactive decision guide. Answer the questions for a problem you are considering. The guide reflects the table above; real decisions also weigh data access, risk and team skills. Example: an insurance claims intake "Is the policy active on the incident date?" is a database query and a date comparison: rules. "Which clause covers water damage?" is search. "Is this claim likely fraudulent?" is traditional ML on claim history. "Turn the customer's long email into the structured claim form" is an LLM job, with schema validation (7.4) and rules checking the extracted amounts. One product, four techniques. The numbers The same task, a million requests a month (illustrative prices). An LLM call with 1,500 tokens in and 200 out, at $1 and $4 per million tokens, costs 1,500 × 1 ÷ 1,000,000 + 200 × 4 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.0023. A million calls is $2,300 a month, and each takes about a second and a half. A rule that does the same job runs in about a millisecond and costs almost nothing. If rules can answer 70% of requests and only 30% go to the LLM, the LLM bill falls to 30% of $2,300 = $690, and 7 in 10 users get an instant, exact answer. Accuracy is a cost too. If an LLM is right 97% of the time on a task a rule gets 100% right, then on a million requests that is 30,000 wrong answers a month to find, explain and fix. Code The program compares the monthly cost and the wait of rules, search, traditional ML and an LLM for a million requests, then a combination where rules answer first. Change SHARE_FOR_LLM , the token counts or the prices and run it again. What each approach costs, in real Python. Every price and wait here is illustrative. Primary sources Google: Rules of Machine Learning Rule 1: do not be afraid to launch a product without machine learning. Sculley et al. (2015), Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems The long-term cost of adding ML to a system. Anthropic: Building effective agents Start with the simplest solution and add LLM steps only when they are needed.

title: Linear algebra: vectors, matrices, dot products, norms, projections and similarity
text: Intuition A vector is a list of numbers, and you can picture it as an arrow. AI turns words, sentences and images into these arrows so that things with similar meaning point in similar directions. "Invoice" and "bill" point almost the same way; "giraffe" points somewhere else. To compare two arrows, you check how much they point the same way, like two people pointing at the same building from different distances. Searching for similar documents then becomes "find the arrows pointing closest to my question's arrow". Mechanism Vector : an ordered list of numbers, e.g. [0.2, −1.3, 0.7]. Geometrically, an arrow in space. An embedding is a vector with hundreds or thousands of entries (its dimensions ). Matrix : a grid of numbers with rows and columns. Multiplying a vector by a matrix transforms it (rotates, stretches, projects). A neural network layer is mostly a matrix multiplication. Dot product a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ. Large when vectors point the same way. Norm ‖a‖ = √(a·a), the vector's length. Cosine similarity = a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖), the cosine of the angle between them: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated (perpendicular), −1 = opposite. Projection of a onto b: the shadow of a along b's direction, (a·b/‖b‖²)·b. It answers "how much of a points along b?" Why this matters: an embedding model maps text to vectors so that related meanings point in similar directions. Retrieval then becomes "find the stored vectors with the highest cosine similarity to the query vector". If vectors are normalised (scaled to length 1), cosine similarity equals the dot product, which is cheaper to compute, so vector databases usually normalise. A matrix multiply y = W·x computes many dot products at once: each output entry is the dot product of one row of W with x. A transformer layer with a 4096×4096 weight matrix does 16.7 million multiply-adds per token for that one matrix. This is why AI hardware is designed around fast matrix multiplication. Angle of a Angle of b Length of a Length of b Drag the sliders. The orange segment is the projection of a onto b. Cosine similarity ignores length; the dot product does not. Doubling the length of a doubles the dot product but leaves cosine unchanged, which is why cosine is used to compare meaning. Example: three tiny "embeddings" Suppose "invoice" = [0.9, 0.1, 0.2], "bill" = [0.8, 0.2, 0.3], "giraffe" = [0.1, 0.9, 0.1]. cos(invoice, bill) = (0.72+0.02+0.06)/(0.93·0.88) ≈ 0.98; cos(invoice, giraffe) = (0.09+0.09+0.02)/(0.93·0.91) ≈ 0.24. A search for "bill" therefore retrieves documents about invoices even though the word differs. Lab, in real Python if you opt in: cosine similarity with NumPy. Pyodide runs Python and NumPy in a worker on your device, over your example project's documents. The checks recompute each answer themselves and tell you which part is off. The numbers Same direction, different length. Take a = [3, 4] and b = [6, 8]. b is a twice as long. Dot product: multiply matching numbers and add them up: 3 × 6 + 4 × 8 = 18 + 32 = 50. Lengths: a is 5 long (a 3-4-5 triangle) and b is 10. Cosine similarity: 50 ÷ (5 × 10) = 1. The arrows point exactly the same way. Now c = [4, −3]: 3 × 4 + 4 × (−3) = 12 − 12 = 0, so a and c are at a right angle: unrelated. Why GPUs matter. One 4,096 × 4,096 weight matrix applied to one token is 4,096 × 4,096 ≈ 16.8 million multiply-and-add steps. An 8-billion-parameter model does about 2 × 8 billion = 16 billion operations for every token it reads or writes. Code The program turns your example project’s English messages into word-count vectors, then finds the three messages closest to one of them: first by dot product, then by cosine similarity. Change QUERY to another message number and run it again. Dot product and cosine similarity, in real Python. Word counts do not capture meaning; embeddings (9.3) do. Laptop lab Laptop · CPU import numpy as np E = np.array([[0.9,0.1,0.2],[0.8,0.2,0.3],[0.1,0.9,0.1]]) # rows = vectors E = E / np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True) # normalise print(np.round(E @ E.T, 3)) # all pairwise cosine similarities in one matrix multiply q = np.array([0.85,0.15,0.25]); q /= np.linalg.norm(q) print(np.argsort(-(E @ q))) # brute-force "vector search": rank rows by similarity Primary sources Strang, MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra (OpenCourseWare) Free lectures on vectors, matrices and projections. Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning, chapter 2 The linear algebra deep learning uses, and no more. NumPy: linear algebra The functions used in the code: dot products, norms and matrix products. 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra Short animated videos on what vectors and matrices do.

title: Probability and statistics: distributions, conditional probability, Bayes, sampling and confidence intervals
text: Intuition Probability is about counting what usually happens. The trap is forgetting how rare something is to begin with. If one transaction in two hundred is fraud, then even a very good fraud alarm will ring mostly for honest customers, simply because there are so many more of them. The second trap is trusting small tests. Toss a coin ten times and you might get seven heads; that does not make it unfair. A score measured on a hundred test cases wobbles the same way, so two prompts that score 82% and 86% might be equally good. Mechanism Probability distribution : how likely each possible outcome is; the probabilities sum to 1. An LLM's output at each step is a distribution over its vocabulary. Conditional probability P(A | B): probability of A given that B is true. Language modelling is P(next token | previous tokens). Bayes' theorem : P(A | B) = P(B | A)·P(A) / P(B). It flips a conditional around and forces you to account for the base rate P(A). Sampling : drawing outcomes at random according to a distribution. Generation samples tokens; evaluation samples test cases from all possible inputs. Confidence interval (CI) : a range that, under the method's assumptions, would contain the true value in (say) 95% of repeated experiments. It expresses how much your measurement could be off because you only tested a sample. Two places this bites engineers. First, base rates : a fraud model with 95% recall and a 2% false positive rate sounds excellent, but if only 0.5% of transactions are fraudulent, most flagged transactions are still legitimate. Second, small evaluation sets : "our new prompt scores 86% vs 82%" on 100 test cases is within noise. The 95% CI for 86/100 is roughly 78%–91%. Base rate (fraud) Recall (true positive rate) False positive rate Bayes as counting. 1,000 transactions, one square each. Red = fraud caught, outlined red = fraud missed, amber = legitimate but flagged. P(fraud | flagged) is red ÷ (red + amber). Lower the base rate and watch precision collapse even though the model did not change. Test cases Observed pass rate Wilson 95% confidence interval for a pass rate. Halving the interval width needs about four times as many test cases. Use this before claiming one prompt or model is better than another. Example: is the new model better? Model A passes 412/500 cases (82.4%), model B 431/500 (86.2%). Their 95% intervals are about 78.8–85.5% and 82.9–88.9%, which overlap. Because both models ran on the same cases, a paired test (count cases where only A passed vs only B passed, then a sign/McNemar test) is more powerful and is the right next step (8.3). The numbers Bayes by counting. 10,000 transactions, 0.5% of them fraud, and a detector that catches 95% of fraud and wrongly flags 2% of honest transactions: Fraud: 10,000 × 0.5% = 50 transactions. Caught: 50 × 95% ≈ 48. Honest: 9,950 transactions. Wrongly flagged: 9,950 × 2% = 199. Flagged in total: 48 + 199 = 247, and only 48 of them are fraud: 48 ÷ 247 ≈ 19%. Four out of five alarms are false, even though the detector sounds excellent. How much a score wobbles. A prompt passes 86 of 100 test cases. The 95% confidence interval is roughly 78% to 91%: the true pass rate could be anywhere in there. With 400 cases and the same 86%, it narrows to about 82% to 89%. Four times the cases halves the width. Code The program measures how often an event happens in your example project’s data, counts how many alarms from a 95%-recall detector would be real at that rate, and then measures the rate on 100 random rows a thousand times to show how much it wobbles. Change RECALL , FALSE_ALARMS or SAMPLE and run it again. Base rates and sampling, in real Python. The detector is imaginary: its recall and false-alarm rate are set by hand. Primary sources Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning, chapter 3 Probability, conditional probability and Bayes’ rule for machine learning. OpenIntro Statistics (free textbook) Sampling, confidence intervals and tests, explained for beginners. Miller (2024), Adding Error Bars to Evals How to put confidence intervals on LLM evaluation scores.

title: Calculus and optimisation: derivatives, gradients, chain rule and gradient descent
text: Intuition Imagine standing on a foggy hillside, trying to reach the valley floor. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a step downhill, feel again, and take another step. That is gradient descent, and it is how every neural network learns. The height of the hill is the loss: how wrong the model is. The direction you feel is the gradient. The size of your step is the learning rate: tiny steps take forever, and giant leaps jump right over the valley. Mechanism Derivative f′(x): how fast f changes when x changes a little; the slope. Gradient ∇f: the vector of partial derivatives, one per parameter. It points in the direction of steepest increase . Loss function : a single number that measures how wrong the model is. Training minimises it. Gradient descent : repeat θ ← θ − η·∇L(θ). Step against the gradient by a learning rate η. Chain rule : if y = f(g(x)) then dy/dx = f′(g(x))·g′(x). Backpropagation is the chain rule applied through every layer. A model with 8 billion parameters has a loss landscape in 8 billion dimensions. You cannot see it, but the gradient still tells each parameter which direction lowers the loss locally. Training is millions of small downhill steps. The learning rate is the most important setting: too small and training crawls; too large and the steps overshoot, the loss oscillates or explodes (often showing up as NaN ). Gradient descent on a real function , L(x) = 0.1x² + sin(x) + 3, which has a local and a global minimum. Try η ≈ 0.2 (smooth), η ≈ 1.0 (oscillates), η ≈ 1.9 (bounces between valleys) and different starts (lands in different valleys). Real optimisers (4.2) add momentum and per-parameter step sizes. From one parameter to two, in 3D. Real models have millions of parameters, but two are enough to see what an optimiser does. Below, three update rules start from the same point on the same surface. Momentum keeps a running velocity, so it speeds up on long slopes and can roll through small dips. Adam divides each step by a running estimate of the gradient's size, so every parameter moves at a similar pace however steep its direction is. Chapter 4.2 covers how they are used in training. x = 2 u = 3x = 6 du/dx = 3 y = u² = 36 dy/du = 2u = 12 dy/dx = 12 × 3 = 36 Input value x = 2. Forward: first function u = 3x. Record its local derivative du/dx = 3. Forward: second function y = u². Local derivative dy/du = 2u = 12. Backward: multiply local derivatives along the path. This product rule, applied across millions of operations, is backpropagation (4.1). Chain rule, step by step. Each operation only needs its own local derivative; the framework multiplies them on the way back. Example: one manual step Fit y = w·x to the single point (x=2, y=6). Loss L = (w·2 − 6)². Gradient dL/dw = 2·(2w − 6)·2. At w = 1: gradient = −16. With η = 0.05: w ← 1 − 0.05·(−16) = 1.8. Next step: gradient = 2·(3.6−6)·2 = −9.6, w ← 2.28. It converges toward w = 3. The numbers The step size decides everything. In the example above, at w = 1 the slope is −16 (the loss falls as w grows): Learning rate Step: rate × 16 New w Result 0.005 0.08 1.08 Right direction, very slow 0.05 0.8 1.8 Reaches 3 in a few steps 0.25 4 5 Jumps past 3, then swings back and forth The chain rule, in numbers. Suppose a model has three stages in a row. Nudge the input by a little, and the first stage’s output moves 2 times as much; that moves the second stage’s output 3 times as much again, and the third 2 times as much again. The input moves the final output 2 × 3 × 2 = 12 times as much. Backpropagation does that multiplication for every one of a model’s billions of parameters, at every training step. Code The program fits one number to four points by stepping downhill, at three learning rates, and measures the slope by nudging the number a tiny bit each way. Change the learning rates (try 0.14) or the points and run it again. Gradient descent by hand, in real Python. Real training computes slopes with backpropagation instead of nudging each parameter. Primary sources Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning, chapter 4 Gradient-based optimisation, and why learning rates matter. Ruder (2016), An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms Plain-language tour of momentum, Adam and the others. Kingma and Ba (2014), Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization The optimiser most models train with (4.2). PyTorch: A Gentle Introduction to torch.autograd How a framework applies the chain rule for you.

title: Information theory: entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
text: Intuition Information theory measures surprise. If your friend is always late, "they were late again" tells you almost nothing; "they came early" is a big surprise. Entropy is the average surprise of something: a fair coin is surprising every time, a coin that always lands heads never is. A language model is trained to be as little surprised as possible by the real next word. If it gave the right word a high chance, there is little surprise and a small loss; if it gave it a tiny chance, the surprise and the loss are big. That loss is called cross-entropy. Mechanism Entropy H(p) = −Σ p(x) log p(x): the average "surprise" of outcomes drawn from p. A fair coin has 1 bit; a coin that always lands heads has 0. Cross-entropy H(p, q) = −Σ p(x) log q(x): the average surprise when outcomes come from the true distribution p but you predicted q. It is the loss used to train language models : p puts all mass on the real next token, so the loss is simply −log q(real token). KL divergence KL(p‖q) = H(p,q) − H(p): the extra surprise caused by using q instead of p. Always ≥ 0; zero only when q = p. Used in RLHF and DPO to keep a tuned model close to its original (6.5), and in distillation. Perplexity = e cross-entropy (natural log): roughly "how many tokens the model is choosing between". Lower is better. True distribution p (what actually happens) vs the model's prediction q over three next tokens. p (truth) "yes" "no" "maybe" q (model) "yes" "no" "maybe" Live calculator (natural log, so units are nats). With p = 100% "yes", cross-entropy is −ln q(yes). Raise q(yes) toward 100% and the loss falls toward 0. Being confidently wrong (q(yes) near 1%) costs about 4.6 nats. Example: reading a training log A training log shows loss 2.30 at step 0 for a 10-class classifier. ln(10) = 2.30, which is exactly the loss of a uniform guess, so the model starts knowing nothing, as expected. For an LLM with a 50,000-token vocabulary, the initial loss should be near ln(50,000) ≈ 10.8. A first-step loss far from that suggests a bug in initialisation or labels. The numbers Surprise in bits. An outcome that had a 50% chance carries 1 bit of surprise; 25% carries 2 bits; 12.5% carries 3. Each halving of the chance adds one bit. A fair coin: every toss is a 50% outcome, so its entropy is 1 bit. A coin that lands heads 90% of the time: heads surprises you by about 0.15 bits, tails by about 3.3 bits. On average, 0.9 × 0.15 + 0.1 × 3.3 ≈ 0.47 bits. It is more predictable, so it has less entropy. The training loss. If the model gave the real next token a 90% chance, the loss for that token is small (about 0.1). At 1%, it is about 4.6. A model whose average loss corresponds to a perplexity of 10 is as unsure as if it were picking between 10 equally likely tokens at every step. Code The program measures how mixed your example project’s labels are, then how surprised two guessers are by the real labels: one that thinks every label is equally likely, and one that knows the real mix. Remove the rarest label from the data, or change the 0.9 and 0.01 at the end, and run it again. Entropy and cross-entropy of your labels, in real Python. Guessing from the label mix ignores the text, so these are baselines, not a model’s results. Primary sources MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (free book) Entropy and its links to learning, with many worked examples. Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning, section 3.13 Entropy, cross-entropy and KL as deep learning uses them. PyTorch: KLDivLoss KL divergence as a training loss, used in distillation and RLHF.

title: Python for AI: NumPy, pandas, visualisation, notebooks and reproducible experiments
text: Intuition Python itself is slow, but the libraries AI uses are fast because they hand whole arrays to compiled code. The trick is to ask for one big operation ("square every number and add them up") instead of looping over a million numbers yourself, like ordering a whole crate instead of buying one item at a time. The other habit is reproducibility: writing down everything that affected a result, the code, data, settings and random seeds, so you or anyone else can get the same answer next month. Mechanism Python is the working language of AI because its libraries wrap fast C, C++ and CUDA code. The core habit is vectorisation : express computation as whole-array operations instead of Python loops. A NumPy dot product over a million numbers runs in about a millisecond; a Python loop takes hundreds of times longer. NumPy : n-dimensional arrays ( ndarray ), broadcasting (combining arrays of different shapes by stretching size-1 axes), linear algebra, random numbers. pandas : tables ( DataFrame ) with named columns for loading, cleaning, joining and grouping data. Use it for evaluation results and datasets. Matplotlib / seaborn / Plotly : charts. Always plot loss curves, metric distributions and error breakdowns; numbers alone hide problems. Jupyter notebooks : interactive cells for exploration. Move code into modules once it stabilises, because notebooks hide execution order. Reproducibility means another person (or you next month) gets the same result from the same inputs. In AI that requires pinning more than code: random seeds, library versions, data snapshots, model versions, prompt versions and hardware notes. GPU kernels are not always bit-for-bit deterministic, so record tolerance as well. Pin environment lockfile Snapshot data hash / version Fix seeds numpy, torch, random Config file all hyperparameters Run & log metrics + artefacts Compare runs tracked, not remembered Lock exact package versions ( uv lock , pip freeze , or a container image). A minor library update can change tokenisation or numerics. Store the dataset with a content hash or a version tool (DVC, Hugging Face dataset revisions). "data.csv" is not a version. Set seeds for every random source. Record that GPU results may still vary slightly. Put every setting in a config file that is committed, never only in a notebook cell. Log metrics, the config, the git commit and output artefacts to an experiment tracker (MLflow, 13.7). Compare runs side by side. A decision should cite run IDs, not memory. Reproducible experiment workflow. The same discipline later becomes LLMOps versioning (18.1). Lab, in real Python if you opt in: summarise a column. Mean, median, a percentile and group means with NumPy , over your example project's data. Its long right tail is why the mean and the median disagree. The numbers Loop against vectorised. Summing the squares of a million numbers takes about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds with a Python loop and about 1 millisecond with NumPy on a laptop: a hundred or more times faster. On a training job that repeats the operation a billion times, that is the difference between hours and months. Why seeds matter. Draw 100 random test cases from a set of 2,000 and you get one pass rate; draw a different 100 and you get another, often a few points apart (2.2). With the seed written down, the same 100 come back every time, so a change in the score is caused by your change, not by the draw. Code The program sums the squares of a million values from your example project’s data with a Python loop and with one NumPy operation, checks both give the same answer, then draws a seeded sample and fingerprints the settings. Run it twice: the sample and fingerprint stay the same until you change SEED . Vectorised Python and a reproducible run, in real Python. Browser timings are slower than native Python and vary; read the ratio, not the seconds. Laptop lab: vectorisation and a reproducible run Laptop · CPU import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time, json, hashlib rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42) # explicit, seeded generator x = rng.standard_normal(1_000_000) t = time.perf_counter(); s = sum(v*v for v in x); loop = time.perf_counter() - t t = time.perf_counter(); s2 = x @ x; vec = time.perf_counter() - t print(f"loop {loop:.3f}s vectorised {vec:.5f}s speedup {loop/vec:.0f}x") df = pd.DataFrame({"case": range(5), "passed": [1,0,1,1,1], "latency_ms": [820,1400,760,990,1010]}) print(df.describe()) cfg = {"seed": 42, "model": "llama3.2:1b", "prompt_version": "v3"} print("config hash", hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(cfg, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]) Primary sources NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners Arrays, shapes and vectorised operations. pandas: Getting started Loading, cleaning and grouping tables. NumPy: random Generator Seeded random numbers, as used in the code. PyTorch: Reproducibility What can and cannot be made deterministic on GPUs.

title: Hardware basics: CPU vs GPU, tensors, numerical precision, memory and compute
text: Intuition A CPU is like a few brilliant chefs who can cook anything; a GPU is like thousands of kitchen helpers who can each only chop, but all at the same time. AI is mostly the same simple arithmetic repeated on huge tables of numbers, so the thousands of helpers win. The catch is feeding them. Every time a model writes a token, it has to read all of its weights from memory. So the size of the model in bytes, and how fast memory can deliver those bytes, often decide the speed. Storing each number in fewer bytes makes the model smaller and faster, at some cost in precision. Mechanism Tensor : an n-dimensional array (a scalar is 0-D, a vector 1-D, a matrix 2-D; a batch of token embeddings is 3-D: batch × sequence × dimension). Frameworks run tensor operations on CPU or GPU. CPU : a few to a few dozen powerful cores, optimised for branching, sequential logic. GPU : thousands of simpler cores plus specialised matrix units (Tensor Cores), optimised for doing the same arithmetic on huge arrays. FLOPs : floating-point operations; a measure of compute. Memory bandwidth : bytes per second that can be read from memory. Many AI workloads are limited by bandwidth, not FLOPs. Precision : bits per number. FP32 (4 bytes), FP16/BF16 (2 bytes), FP8 and INT8 (1 byte), INT4 (0.5 byte). Fewer bits = less memory and faster, with some accuracy loss. A rule of thumb you will use constantly: model memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter . An 8B model needs about 16 GB in BF16, 8 GB in INT8 and 4–5 GB in 4-bit. Your laptop's RAM bounds which models you can run; a GPU's VRAM bounds what it can serve, and inference needs extra memory for the KV cache (14.1). Why GPUs are faster for AI: generating one token from an 8B model needs ~16 GB of weights read from memory. A laptop with ~60–100 GB/s memory bandwidth can do that at most ~4–6 times a second at BF16; a datacentre GPU with several TB/s of HBM bandwidth can do it hundreds of times a second. Quantising to 4-bit reads a quarter of the bytes, which is why quantised models run usefully on laptops. FP16 vs BF16. Both use 2 bytes. FP16 has more precision (10-bit mantissa) but a small range (largest value ≈ 65,504), so large activations overflow and training needs loss scaling. BF16 keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent, so it has the same range as FP32 with less precision (7-bit mantissa). That is why most LLM training and serving use BF16 . Units: this manual writes GB = 10⁹ bytes and GiB = 2³⁰ bytes (≈ 1.074 GB); per-token KV sizes are given in KiB (1,024 bytes). Mixing the two silently introduces a 7% error at GB scale. CPU 8–24 complex cores · large caches Cache + control logic System RAM · ~50–120 GB/s GPU thousands of simple cores + matrix units HBM VRAM · ~1–8 TB/s Different designs for different work. The GPU core grid pulses to suggest many identical operations in parallel. Bandwidth figures are typical ranges for current laptops and datacentre GPUs, not specific products. Memory to hold the weights of an 8-billion-parameter model FP32 · 4 bytes BF16 / FP16 · 2 bytes INT8 / FP8 · 1 byte 4-bit (incl. scales) · ~0.56 byte Weights only. Training needs far more: gradients and optimizer state bring mixed-precision Adam to roughly 16 bytes per parameter (6.6). Model 0.5B (24 layers, 2 KV heads × 64) 1B (16 layers, 8 KV heads × 64) 3B (28 layers, 8 KV heads × 128) 8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads × 128) 14B (48 layers, 8 KV heads × 128) 70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads × 128) Weights format FP16 / BF16 Q8_0 (≈ 8.5 bits) Q5_K_M (≈ 5.5 bits) Q4_K_M (≈ 4.5 bits) Laptop RAM 8 16 32 64 GB Used by OS + apps (GB) Context (tokens) Memory bandwidth (GB/s) Will it fit on my laptop? Weights = parameters × bytes per parameter (quantised formats include their scales). KV cache assumes FP16 cache values, as llama.cpp uses by default. The speed ceiling is bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token; real speeds are lower. Apple-silicon and recent laptops reach 100–400 GB/s; typical x86 laptops 50–100 GB/s. Example: will it run on my laptop? A 16 GB laptop. Operating system and apps use ~5 GB, leaving ~11 GB. A 3B model at 4-bit ≈ 2 GB: comfortable. An 8B model at 4-bit ≈ 5 GB: works, a few tokens per second. A 70B model at 4-bit ≈ 40 GB: does not fit. Use a hosted API or rented GPU for that. The numbers Memory = parameters × bytes per parameter. For an 8-billion-parameter model: Format Bytes per parameter Weights FP32 4 32 GB BF16 2 16 GB INT8 1 8 GB 4-bit 0.5 (a little more with scales) 4 to 4.5 GB Training needs about 16 bytes per parameter for the weights, gradients and optimiser state together: 8 × 16 = 128 GB, far more than one consumer GPU has. Speed limit from bandwidth. Each new token reads all 16 GB of a BF16 8B model. A laptop reading 100 GB per second can do that at most 100 ÷ 16 ≈ 6 times a second. A datacentre GPU reading about 3,350 GB per second can do it about 210 times a second. At 4-bit, the laptop’s limit rises to about 100 ÷ 4.5 ≈ 22 tokens per second. Code The program stores the same numbers as float32, float16 and bfloat16 to show what each format keeps and loses, then prints the memory of 1B, 8B and 70B models in each format and the speed limit of an 8B model. Change BANDWIDTH to your own machine’s figure and run it again. Number formats and model memory, in real Python. The memory figures are weights only, and the speed is a ceiling, not a measurement. Laptop lab: measure your bandwidth ceiling Laptop · CPU import numpy as np, time a = np.ones(500_000_000 // 8) # ~500 MB of float64 t = time.perf_counter(); s = a.sum(); dt = time.perf_counter() - t print(f"~{a.nbytes/dt/1e9:.1f} GB/s effective read bandwidth") # tokens/sec upper bound for a model of size M GB ≈ bandwidth / M for m in (0.8, 2.0, 4.5): print(f"{m} GB model → ≤ {a.nbytes/dt/1e9/m:.0f} tok/s") This single-threaded NumPy read underestimates true bandwidth, but it shows why model size in bytes, not parameter count alone, sets your CPU generation speed. Primary sources NVIDIA: Train With Mixed Precision FP16, BF16 and loss scaling in practice. Micikevicius et al. (2017), Mixed Precision Training Why training in 16-bit works, and where it fails. Kalamkar et al. (2019), A Study of BFLOAT16 for Deep Learning Training Why BF16’s wide range made it the default. NVIDIA H100 product page Memory and bandwidth figures for a current datacentre GPU. llama.cpp Runs quantised models on laptops; its documentation lists memory per format.

title: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning
text: Intuition There are three ways to learn, and they differ in the feedback you get. With a teacher who marks every answer, you learn from right answers: that is supervised learning. With a pile of photos and no captions, you can still sort them into groups that look alike: that is unsupervised learning. And like learning to ride a bike, you can try things and learn from how well they went: that is reinforcement learning. LLMs use a clever fourth trick. They hide the next word of real text and try to guess it, so every sentence on the internet becomes a free lesson with its own answer. Mechanism Supervised learning : learn from input–output pairs ( labels ). "Email → spam/not spam", "house features → price". Unsupervised learning : find structure in inputs without labels: groups (clustering), compressed representations, anomalies. Self-supervised learning : create labels from the data itself, e.g. hide the next word and predict it. LLM pretraining is self-supervised, which is why it can use trillions of tokens without human labelling. Reinforcement learning (RL) : an agent takes actions in an environment , receives rewards , and learns a policy that maximises total reward. Used in RLHF and reasoning-model training (6.5). Supervised email text label: spam Model minimise error vs. known answers e.g. classifier, regressor Unsupervised no labels: discover groups/structure Reinforcement Agent Environment action state + reward learn by trial, maximise reward Three ways to learn. The difference is the feedback signal: correct answers, no answers, or a score for actions taken. Example: one company, three paradigms An e-commerce site trains a supervised model to predict return probability from order data, uses unsupervised clustering to discover customer segments for marketing, and uses RL-style bandit algorithms to choose which recommendation layout to show, rewarded by clicks. The numbers Why labels are the bottleneck. 10,000 labelled examples at 30 seconds each is 300,000 seconds: about 83 hours of someone’s time, before any checking. Why self-supervision scales. Every token in a text is a question with a known answer: "what comes next?". A 1,000-token page gives 1,000 lessons for free. A model trained on 15 trillion tokens gets 15 trillion lessons, with no one labelling anything. Reinforcement by trial. A learner choosing between three reply styles that succeed 5%, 12% and 8% of the time tries each one, keeps a running score, and picks its best so far 9 times in 10. After a few thousand tries it is choosing the 12% style most of the time, without ever being told which was best. Code The program runs a tiny example of each kind on your example project’s data: it predicts a number from a group average learned from labelled rows, groups the same numbers into three clusters with no labels, and lets a learner find the best of three options by trial and reward. Change TRUE_RATES , or the 0.1 that sets how often it explores, and run it again. Three kinds of learning, in real Python. The reinforcement part is simulated with made-up success rates. Primary sources Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning, chapter 5 Machine-learning basics, including the kinds of learning. scikit-learn: Supervised learning The standard library’s guide to supervised methods. scikit-learn: Unsupervised learning Clustering and other methods without labels. Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (free book) The standard text; chapter 2 covers the trial-and-reward example in the code.

title: Regression, classification, clustering, trees, ensembles and baseline models
text: Intuition Most prediction tasks are one of three shapes: guess a number (how long will delivery take?), pick a category (is this fraud?), or find groups nobody labelled (which customers behave alike?). Each shape has simple, well-tested tools. Before trusting any of them, ask "compared with what?". A weather forecaster who always says "same as today" is right surprisingly often. That lazy answer is the baseline, and a model is only worth what it adds on top of it. Mechanism Regression predicts a number (delivery time, price). Linear regression fits y = w·x + b by minimising squared error. Classification predicts a category. Logistic regression outputs a probability via the sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1+e −z ); a threshold turns it into a decision. Clustering groups similar points. k-means alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points. Decision trees split data with yes/no questions on features ("amount > 500?"). Easy to read, but a single deep tree overfits. Ensembles combine many models. Random forests average many trees trained on random subsets. Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) adds trees one at a time, each correcting the previous errors. For tabular data, gradient boosting is usually the strongest practical choice. Baselines are the simplest reasonable models: always predict the most common class, predict the mean, a keyword rule. If your sophisticated model barely beats the baseline, it is not adding value. Always report the baseline next to your result, including for LLM systems. Next step New data k 2 3 4 5 step 0 k-means, one step at a time. Odd steps assign each point to the nearest centre (colour); even steps move each centre (ring) to the mean of its points. It stops when assignments stop changing. Try k that does not match the true number of groups. debt/income > 0.45? late payments ≥ 2? tenure < 1 year? default 38% default 12% default 7% default 2% yes no yes no yes no A small decision tree (illustrative numbers). A random forest averages hundreds of trees like this; gradient boosting stacks them so each fixes the residual errors of the ones before. Example: baselines keep you honest A ticket classifier reports 91% accuracy. But 88% of tickets are "general", so always predicting "general" scores 88%. The real gain is 3 points, and recall on the rare "security incident" class might be terrible. Report per-class metrics (3.5) and the baseline. A small classifier, trained on your device if you opt in. Your example project's labelled text goes through a small open embedding model , then a softmax layer learns from a seeded, stratified split and is scored on the rows it never saw, beside the majority-class baseline. The text is synthetic and comes from a few templates, so this shows the method and how to read its results, not what the method would score on real messages. The numbers A baseline in numbers. 1,000 tickets, 880 of them "general". Always answering "general" is right 880 times: 88% accuracy. A model scoring 91% is only 3 points better. If 10 tickets are security incidents and the model catches 2, its recall on the class that matters most is 2 ÷ 10 = 20%. k-means by hand. Four values, 1, 2, 10 and 11, and two centres that start at 1 and 2: Each value joins its nearest centre: {1} and {2, 10, 11}. Each centre moves to the middle of its group: 1 and (2 + 10 + 11) ÷ 3 ≈ 7.7. Regroup: 2 is now nearer 1 than 7.7, so the groups become {1, 2} and {10, 11}. Move again: 1.5 and 10.5. Nothing changes after that, so it stops. Code The program predicts a rare yes/no outcome in your example project’s table, first with a baseline that always gives the most common answer, then with a logistic regression trained on a few columns, and prints the weight it learned for each column. Remove a column from the data, or change the 0.5 threshold, and run it again. A model against its baseline, in real Python. The data is synthetic and the features are few, so the numbers do not predict real performance. Laptop lab: baseline vs model Laptop · CPU from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True) Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0) for name, m in [("baseline", DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")), ("logistic", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))), ("boosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))]: print(f"{name:9} accuracy = {m.fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte):.3f}") Primary sources scikit-learn: DummyClassifier Ready-made baselines to report next to every model. Chen and Guestrin (2016), XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System The gradient-boosting library that dominated tabular competitions. Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux (2022), Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data? Evidence for choosing trees over neural networks for tables. scikit-learn: k-means The algorithm in the figure, with its options and pitfalls.

title: Data cleaning, labelling, feature engineering and class imbalance
text: Intuition A model can only be as good as the examples it learns from. If the labels are inconsistent, it learns the inconsistency; if the same row appears twice, it may simply memorise it. So most of the work in a real project is cleaning data and writing clear labelling rules, not choosing models. Rare events need special care. If only 3 transactions in 1,000 are fraud, a lazy model can say "not fraud" every time and be right 99.7% of the time while catching nothing. You have to tell it that missing a fraud matters more. Mechanism Data quality usually matters more than model choice. Most of a real ML project is spent here. Cleaning : remove duplicates, fix inconsistent formats ("NY", "New York"), handle missing values (drop, fill, or add a "missing" indicator), cap impossible values (age 210). Labelling : humans (or rules, or models) attach the correct output. Write a labelling guideline with definitions and edge cases, have two people label a sample, and measure inter-annotator agreement (e.g. Cohen's κ). Low agreement means the task is ambiguous, and no model can beat that ceiling. Feature engineering : turn raw data into model inputs: dates into "day of week", text into word counts, amounts into log scale, transactions into "count in last 24h". Deep learning learns features itself; tabular ML still benefits enormously from good features. Class imbalance : when one class is rare (fraud 0.3%), a model can ignore it and still score high accuracy. Remedies: use precision/recall instead of accuracy, class weights (penalise mistakes on the rare class more), resampling (oversample rare or undersample common), and tuning the decision threshold. Raw records 1.2M rows Deduplicate −4% Normalise & fix formats, units Handle missing fill + flag Label guideline + κ check Features derived columns Training table Raw data from operational databases and logs. Never edit it in place; keep it immutable so you can rebuild. Remove exact and near-duplicates. Duplicates split across train and test inflate scores (leakage, 3.4). Standardise categories, units, time zones and encodings. Decide per column: drop rows, impute a value, or add an is_missing flag (missingness is often informative). Labels from humans or outcomes (e.g. a chargeback 60 days later). Check agreement on a double-labelled sample. Compute features using only information available at prediction time . A versioned training table with a documented schema. A typical preparation pipeline. Each step is code, versioned and re-runnable, so the table can be rebuilt when raw data changes. Unweighted model on 0.5% fraud Accuracy Fraud recall Fraud precision Class-weighted + tuned threshold Accuracy Fraud recall Fraud precision Illustrative tradeoff. Accuracy barely moves, but the business outcome changes completely. Which side is better depends on the cost of a missed fraud versus a blocked legitimate customer. Class imbalance, trained live. Logistic regression is trained by gradient descent in your browser on 800 synthetic points, at a positive rate you choose; the first option is the real rate of your example project's rare class. Without weights the model mostly predicts the majority class: high accuracy, low recall. Turn on class weights (positives weighted by negatives ÷ positives) or lower the threshold and watch recall rise while precision falls. This shows the mechanism on simple synthetic data, not how a model would score on the project's real features. Example: a labelling guideline excerpt Label "urgent" if the customer reports service unavailable, data loss, or a security concern. Do not label urgent for angry tone alone. Edge case: "I can't log in" is urgent only if it affects more than one user or the account owner. Two annotators label 200 tickets; κ = 0.58 reveals disagreement on "can't log in", so the guideline is revised before labelling 10,000 more. The numbers Accuracy that means nothing. 10,000 transactions, 30 of them fraud. A model that never says fraud is right 9,970 times: 99.7% accuracy, 0% recall. Class weights. There are 9,970 ÷ 30 ≈ 332 normal transactions for every fraud. Giving each fraud 332 times the weight in training makes the two classes count equally, so missing one fraud costs the model as much as wrongly flagging 332 normal transactions. Agreement beyond chance. Two people label 200 tickets and agree on 170: 85%. But with these labels they would agree 70% of the time just by chance. The possible improvement over chance was 30 points (from 70% to 100%), and they achieved 15 of them: a Cohen’s kappa of 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5, which says the guideline needs work. Code The program counts repeated and broken rows in your example project’s table, then trains the same model twice: once treating every row alike, and once giving the rare outcome extra weight. Change WEIGHT to 1, 3 or 20 and run it again to watch precision and recall trade places. Cleaning and class weights, in real Python. The right balance depends on what each mistake costs; the synthetic data makes both numbers rosier than real ones. Primary sources scikit-learn: LogisticRegression (class_weight) Class weights in a production library. imbalanced-learn documentation Resampling methods for rare classes. scikit-learn: cohen_kappa_score Measuring agreement between two labellers. Sambasivan et al. (2021), "Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work" How data problems cascade into failed AI projects.

title: Train/validation/test splits, leakage, overfitting, regularisation and generalisation
text: Intuition A student who memorises last year’s exam answers will ace last year’s exam and fail this year’s. A model can do the same: learn its training examples so exactly that it fails on anything new. That is overfitting, and the only way to catch it is to test on data the model has never seen. Leakage is the sneakier version: the exam answers slipped into the study notes. A column that is only known after the event, or the same customer in both training and test data, makes the score look great until the model meets real life. Mechanism Training set : data the model learns from. Validation set : data used to choose settings and compare variants. Test set : held back until the end, used once to estimate real-world performance. Generalisation : performing well on new data, not just training data. It is the only thing that matters. Overfitting : memorising training noise, so training error is low but new-data error is high. Underfitting : too simple to capture the pattern. Regularisation : techniques that discourage overly complex fits: penalties on weight size (L2/ridge, L1/lasso), limiting tree depth, dropout (4.3), early stopping. Leakage : information in training or features that would not be available at prediction time, making results look better than they will be in production. Common leakage patterns: a feature computed from the future ("total refunds this month" used to predict a refund on day 3); the same customer in both train and test; duplicate or near-duplicate documents across splits; normalising with statistics computed over the full dataset; and, for LLMs, benchmark questions that appeared in pretraining data ( contamination , 8.6). For time-dependent data, split by time: train on the past, test on the future. Polynomial degree Regularisation λ (log) Overfitting, computed live. 14 noisy training points (filled) from a smooth curve; 40 validation points (hollow). Raise the degree and training error keeps falling while validation error rises. Then raise λ (ridge penalty) at a high degree and watch the curve smooth out and validation error recover. Random split (fine for i.i.d. data) Time-based split (required when the future must be predicted) train: Jan–Aug val: Sep–Oct test: Nov–Dec time → Choose the split that matches deployment. A random split on time-series or user-level data leaks the future or the same user into training. Example: a leak that reached production A churn model used days_since_last_login computed at data-extraction time. For churned customers this was always large because they had already left. Offline AUC was 0.97; in production, scored on active customers before they churned, it was 0.68. Fix: compute features "as of" the prediction date (a point-in-time join ). The numbers A typical split. 10,000 rows split 70/15/15: 7,000 to learn from, 1,500 to compare settings, 1,500 kept back for one final check. For data that changes over time, the split follows the calendar: January to August for training, September and October for validation, November and December for the test. Spotting overfitting. A model that gets 2% wrong on its training rows and 18% wrong on validation rows has learned the training rows, not the pattern. If both were 10%, it would be a simpler model that generalises; if both were 25%, it would be too simple. A leak, in numbers. The churn model in the example below scored 0.97 offline and 0.68 in use. The gap, 0.29, is the size of the leak: everything the model learned from a column it would not have when making a real prediction. Code The program splits your example project’s table by month, trains on the past and tests on the future, then adds one column that is only known after the outcome. Compare the two blocks of results, then move the cut-off date (the 0.75 ) earlier or later and run it again. A leak, caught, in real Python. The code cannot tell which columns leak; that depends on when each value becomes known. Primary sources scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and recommended practices Data leakage, with examples of how it creeps in. Kaufman et al. (2012), Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance The standard paper on leakage and how to find it. scikit-learn: Cross-validation Splitting data fairly when it is small. scikit-learn: TimeSeriesSplit Splitting by time so the test always comes after the training data.

title: Metrics: precision, recall, F1, ROC/PR curves and probability calibration
text: Intuition Imagine a smoke alarm. Precision asks: when it beeps, how often is there really a fire? Recall asks: when there is a fire, how often does it beep? Make it more sensitive and it catches every fire but also beeps at toast; make it less sensitive and it stays quiet at breakfast but may miss a real fire. The sensitivity knob is the threshold, and no setting is right for everyone. The best setting depends on what a missed fire costs compared with a false alarm. Mechanism Confusion matrix : counts of true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), false negatives (FN). Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of everything flagged, how much was right. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): of everything that should be flagged, how much we caught. F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R): harmonic mean, high only if both are high. ROC curve : true positive rate vs false positive rate across all thresholds; AUC summarises it (0.5 = random, 1 = perfect).
