PR curve : precision vs recall across thresholds; more informative when positives are rare. Calibration : a model is calibrated if, among cases it scores 0.8, about 80% are positive. Shown with a reliability diagram; summarised by expected calibration error (ECE). Move the threshold. 400 synthetic cases (80 positive) with overlapping score distributions. The dot on each curve is your current threshold. Lowering it raises recall and lowers precision. The curves are computed from the same scores. Reliability diagrams (illustrative). Bars below the diagonal mean the model claims more confidence than it earns. Platt scaling or isotonic regression, fitted on validation data, fixes this for classical models. LLM-generated confidence statements need the same measurement before you use them. Example: choosing the threshold from costs A missed fraud costs $400; a false alarm costs $5 of analyst time. Expected cost = 400·FN + 5·FP. Sweep thresholds on validation data and pick the minimum; with these costs it will sit at a low threshold (high recall). If false alarms instead block customers' cards (cost $60 in churn), the optimum moves up. Metrics serve a business cost function, not the other way round. Lab, in real Python if you opt in: precision and recall by hand. Score a simple rule over your example project's data, with the zero cases handled, then compare its accuracy with always answering no. The numbers Precision and recall from counts. 1,000 cases, 50 really positive. The model flags 60, and 40 of those are really positive. Precision: 40 right out of 60 flagged = 67%. Recall: 40 caught out of 50 real = 80%. Why F1 is not a plain average. A model with 90% precision and 30% recall averages 60%, but its F1 is only 45%: F1 stays close to the weaker of the two, so a model cannot hide a bad recall behind a good precision. Choosing the threshold by cost. A missed fraud costs $400 and a false alarm $5. Threshold A misses 10 frauds and raises 40 false alarms: 10 × 400 + 40 × 5 = $4,200. Threshold B misses 4 and raises 150 false alarms: 4 × 400 + 150 × 5 = $2,350. B is cheaper, even though it is wrong more often. Code The program scores the test rows of your example project’s table and shows precision, recall and F1 at five thresholds, picks the cheapest threshold for a given cost of misses and false alarms, and checks whether the scores behave like real chances. Change MISS_COST and ALARM_COST and see the best threshold move. Thresholds, costs and calibration, in real Python. The costs are illustrative, and this model’s scores are not calibrated chances. Primary sources scikit-learn: Metrics and scoring Every metric on this page, with definitions and code. Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015), The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets Why PR curves matter when positives are rare. Guo et al. (2017), On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks Modern models are often overconfident, and how to fix it. scikit-learn: Probability calibration Reliability diagrams, Platt scaling and isotonic regression.

title: Error analysis, hyperparameter tuning, distribution shift and reproducibility
text: Intuition When a model makes mistakes, read them before changing anything. Like a teacher marking a stack of tests, sort the wrong answers into piles: "misread the question", "never learned this topic", "answer key was wrong". The biggest pile tells you what to fix first. The world also moves on. New customers, new products and new tricks mean the data a model sees next month is not quite the data it learned from. That is distribution shift, and the only defence is to keep watching the data and the results. Mechanism Error analysis means reading failures and grouping them. Pull 100 errors, tag each with a cause ("short text", "non-English", "label wrong", "new product"), and count. The biggest bucket tells you what to fix next. Also compute metrics per slice (segment of the data); an average can hide a group where the model fails badly. Hyperparameters are settings chosen before training (learning rate, tree depth, regularisation strength). Tune them on the validation set only, using grid search, random search (usually better per trial), or Bayesian optimisation (Optuna). Use cross-validation when data is small. Touch the test set once. Distribution shift is when production data differs from training data. Covariate shift : inputs change (new customer region). Label/prior shift : class balance changes (fraud spikes). Concept drift : the relationship itself changes (new fraud tactics). Detect it by monitoring input statistics and, when labels arrive, performance (17.7). Accuracy by slice (illustrative) English, long English, short Spanish Mixed-language New product line training production message length (tokens) Two diagnostics. Left: slices reveal where the model fails, which the overall 89% average hides. Right: covariate shift in input length after a product change; the model sees a range it was rarely trained on. Sample errors Tag causes Count buckets Fix biggest data, features, model Re-evaluate same test set + slices Pull a random sample of failures from validation (not hand-picked ones). Write one cause per failure. Invent categories as you go, then merge. Rank buckets by count × business impact. The fix is often data (labels, coverage), not a bigger model. Check the fix did not break other slices. This loop is exactly how LLM prompts and RAG systems are improved too (8, 17.9). The error-analysis loop. Example A document classifier drops from 92% to 84% in March. Input monitoring shows the share of scanned PDFs rose from 5% to 30% after a new client onboarded; OCR text is noisy. Error analysis confirms 70% of new errors are scanned documents. Fix: improve OCR and add scanned samples to training, then add a "scanned" slice to the dashboard. The numbers Counting causes. 100 wrong answers, each tagged with one cause: Cause Errors Scanned PDFs with noisy text 45 Not in English 25 The label itself was wrong 20 Other 10 Fixing scanned PDFs could remove up to 45% of the errors; a bigger model might remove a few of each. Grid against random search. Trying 5 learning rates × 5 tree depths is 25 training runs, but tests only 5 different values of each setting. 25 random combinations test 25 different values of each, which is why random search usually finds a better setting for the same cost. Shift, in numbers. In the example below, scanned PDFs went from 5% to 30% of incoming documents. If the model is 92% right on clean documents and 65% right on scanned ones, its overall accuracy falls from about 91% to about 84% without anything in the model changing. Code The program breaks the results on your example project’s table down by one column, to find where the model is weakest, then compares the first and last three months of data to look for drift. Change which months are compared ( order[:3] and order[-3:] ) and run it again. Slices and drift, in real Python. The synthetic data has little real drift, so small changes here do not prove a real dataset is stable. Laptop lab: tuning with Optuna Laptop · CPU # pip install optuna import optuna from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True) def objective(t): m = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(learning_rate=t.suggest_float("lr", 0.01, 0.5, log=True), max_depth=t.suggest_int("depth", 2, 8), random_state=0) return cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=5, scoring="f1").mean() study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize", sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0)) study.optimize(objective, n_trials=30); print(study.best_params, round(study.best_value, 4)) Primary sources Bergstra and Bengio (2012), Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization Why random search beats grid search. Optuna documentation The tuning library used in the laptop lab. Rabanser, Günnemann and Lipton (2019), Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift Ways to detect that incoming data has changed. Google: Rules of Machine Learning Practical advice on monitoring, slices and fixing what the errors show.

title: Neurons, layers, activations, loss functions and backpropagation
text: Intuition A neuron is a tiny voting machine. It looks at its inputs, gives each one a weight for how much it matters, adds them up, and then decides how strongly to "fire". A network is many of these in layers, each layer building on what the one below noticed. Learning means fixing the weights after every mistake. Backpropagation is the blame game run backwards: start at the wrong answer and work back through the layers, telling each weight how much it contributed to the error and which way to move. Mechanism Neuron : computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, z = w·x + b, then applies an activation function a = f(z). Activation : a non-linear function. Without it, stacking layers would collapse into one linear function. Common: ReLU max(0,z); GELU and SiLU (smooth ReLU variants used in transformers); sigmoid and tanh (older, saturate). Layer : many neurons in parallel, computed as one matrix multiply. A network stacks layers: input → hidden layers → output. Loss function : mean squared error for regression; cross-entropy for classification and language modelling. Backpropagation : computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backward through the layers, reusing intermediate results. Logits in, softmax inside. Classification losses such as PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss expect raw logits and apply (log-)softmax internally in a numerically stable way. Applying softmax yourself first is a common bug: training still runs, but gradients shrink and the model learns slowly. w₁ w₂ bias b activation ReLU GELU sigmoid tanh none (linear) One neuron with inputs x₁ = 1.0, x₂ = 0.5. Left: the computation. Right: the activation curve with the current z marked. Note that ReLU outputs exactly 0 for negative z, so its gradient is 0 there too. x = 1.0 z = w₁x = 0.5 w₁ = 0.5 h = ReLU(z) = 0.5 ŷ = w₂h = 1.0 w₂ = 2.0 L = (ŷ − 2)² = 1.0 Forward pass. Compute and store each intermediate value. Target y = 2, prediction 1.0, loss 1.0. ∂L/∂ŷ = 2(ŷ − y) = −2. The prediction is too low, so the gradient is negative. ∂L/∂w₂ = ∂L/∂ŷ · h = −2 × 0.5 = −1.0. And pass back ∂L/∂h = ∂L/∂ŷ · w₂ = −4. ReLU's derivative is 1 because z > 0, so ∂L/∂z = −4. ∂L/∂w₁ = ∂L/∂z · x = −4. Update with η = 0.1: w₁ ← 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9, w₂ ← 2.0 + 0.1 = 2.1. New prediction 0.9 × 2.1 = 1.89, loss drops from 1.0 to 0.012. Backpropagation with real numbers on a two-weight network. Frameworks do exactly this, but for billions of weights and with tensors instead of scalars. Dataset circles XOR quadrants two moons spiral (hard) Hidden units per layer Activation tanh ReLU linear (no activation) Learning rate Train Reset weights Neural-network playground, trained live. A 2-layer network (2 → H → H → 1) learns by real backpropagation with momentum, full batch, in your browser. The background shows the predicted probability; points are the training data. Try "linear (no activation)" on circles: it can only draw a straight line, which is the non-linearity argument from this section made visible. Example: why non-linearity matters Two linear layers W₂(W₁x) equal one layer (W₂W₁)x. No matter how deep, a purely linear network can only draw straight decision boundaries. Insert ReLU between them and the network can bend boundaries, which is how it separates, say, a spiral of fraudulent transactions from normal ones. The numbers One neuron, by hand. Inputs 1.0 and 0.5, weights 0.8 and −0.5, bias 0.1: Weighted sum: 1.0 × 0.8 + 0.5 × (−0.5) + 0.1 = 0.8 − 0.25 + 0.1 = 0.65. ReLU keeps positive numbers and turns negatives into 0, so the output is 0.65. If the sum had been −0.3, the output would be 0, and so would the gradient: that neuron learns nothing from this example. Counting weights. A layer from 784 inputs to 128 neurons has 784 × 128 = 100,352 weights plus 128 biases: 100,480 parameters in one small layer. What a training step costs. The backward pass does about twice the work of the forward pass, so one training step costs about three times as much as just running the model. Code The program trains a two-layer network on XOR, the classic problem no straight line can solve, with every step of backpropagation written out. It runs once without an activation and once with tanh. Change HIDDEN to 2 or 8, or the learning rate, and run it again. A neural network with backpropagation by hand, in real Python. Four data points are a toy; frameworks do the same steps at scale. Primary sources Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning, chapter 6 Feed-forward networks, activations, losses and backpropagation. Stanford CS231n: Backpropagation, Intuitions Backprop worked through on small examples, like the figure above. Karpathy, micrograd A complete autograd engine in about 100 lines of Python. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (1986), Learning representations by back-propagating errors The paper that made backpropagation the standard.

title: Optimisers, learning rates, batch sizes, epochs and learning-rate schedules
text: Intuition Training is walking downhill in the dark, and the optimiser is your walking style. Plain gradient descent takes each step based only on the slope under your feet. Momentum is like a rolling ball: it builds up speed in a steady direction and is not thrown off by small bumps. Adam adjusts the step size for every direction separately, so it takes careful steps where the ground is steep and bigger ones where it is flat. The schedule is the pace: start gently while you get your bearings (warm-up), walk briskly, then slow down as you get close so you do not overshoot the bottom. Mechanism Batch : the group of examples used for one gradient estimate. Step (iteration): one weight update. Epoch : one full pass over the training data. SGD : plain stochastic gradient descent on mini-batches. Momentum : keep a running average of gradients so steps accelerate in consistent directions. Adam / AdamW : adapts the step size per parameter using running averages of the gradient (first moment) and squared gradient (second moment). AdamW decouples weight decay. It is the default for transformers. It stores two extra numbers per parameter, which matters for memory (6.6). Schedule : changing the learning rate over training. Standard for LLMs: linear warm-up from near zero for the first few hundred or thousand steps, then cosine decay to a small final value. Batch size trades noise for cost. Small batches give noisy gradients (which can help escape poor regions) but use hardware poorly. Large batches give smoother gradients and better throughput but may need a larger learning rate and warm-up. When memory limits the batch, gradient accumulation sums gradients over several small batches before one update, simulating a larger batch. Peak LR (×10⁻⁴) Warm-up % Decay cosine linear constant step Learning-rate schedule over 10,000 steps. Warm-up avoids huge early updates while Adam's statistics are still unreliable; decay lets the model settle into a minimum at the end. 10,000 examples · batch 1,000 → 10 steps per epoch · 3 epochs = 30 updates. Highlighted batch = the one being processed. Steps, batches and epochs. The highlight walks through batches; each completed batch is one optimiser step. Example: LoRA fine-tuning settings A typical small fine-tuning run: AdamW, peak learning rate 2×10⁻⁴, 3% warm-up, cosine decay, effective batch 32 (batch 4 × 8 accumulation steps), 2–3 epochs over 5,000 examples. If validation loss starts rising in epoch 3 while training loss keeps falling, stop at epoch 2 (early stopping). The numbers Steps per epoch. 10,000 examples in batches of 32 is 10,000 ÷ 32 ≈ 313 steps per epoch. Three epochs is about 940 updates. Gradient accumulation. If only 4 examples fit on the GPU, adding up the gradients of 8 small batches before each update acts like one batch of 4 × 8 = 32. Adam’s memory. Adam keeps two extra numbers for every parameter. For an 8-billion-parameter model stored in 4-byte numbers, that is 8 billion × 2 × 4 bytes = 64 GB, on top of the weights and gradients. Warm-up, in numbers. With a peak learning rate of 0.0003 and 100 warm-up steps, step 50 uses half the peak (0.00015), step 100 reaches the peak, and from there a cosine curve slowly lowers it towards a small final value. Code The program runs plain gradient descent, momentum and Adam for 60 steps down a long, narrow valley and prints how close each one gets to the bottom, then prints the learning rate of a warm-up and cosine schedule. Try a plain SGD learning rate of 0.08, or change WARMUP , and run it again. Optimisers and a schedule, in real Python. A two-number valley is not a real model’s loss surface, so the ranking may differ in practice. Primary sources Kingma and Ba (2014), Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization The Adam optimiser. Loshchilov and Hutter (2017), Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization AdamW, the version transformers use. Goyal et al. (2017), Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour Warm-up and scaling the learning rate with the batch size. Loshchilov and Hutter (2016), SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts The cosine schedule. PyTorch: torch.optim Optimisers and learning-rate schedulers in code.

title: Initialisation, normalisation, dropout and gradient stability
text: Intuition A deep network is like a long chain of people passing a message by whisper. If everyone speaks a little too quietly, the message fades to nothing by the end; a little too loudly, and it becomes a shout. Gradients passing back through dozens of layers have the same problem. The fixes are simple habits: start the weights at the right size, re-level the volume at every layer (normalisation), give the message a direct line around each person (residual connections), and cap any sudden shout (gradient clipping). Dropout is a different trick: randomly silencing some people during practice, so the team does not depend on any one of them. Mechanism Initialisation : weights start as small random numbers with a variance scaled to layer width (Xavier/Glorot, He/Kaiming). Too large and activations explode through the layers; too small and they shrink to zero. All-zero initialisation makes every neuron identical, so they never learn different things. Vanishing / exploding gradients : backprop multiplies many factors. If they are mostly below 1, gradients vanish in early layers (they stop learning); above 1, they explode. Deep networks stay trainable thanks to residual connections (5.3), normalisation and careful initialisation. Normalisation : rescale activations to a stable range. BatchNorm normalises each feature across the batch (common in CNNs). LayerNorm normalises across features within one example (used in transformers because it does not depend on batch size). RMSNorm is a cheaper LayerNorm variant used by many current LLMs. Dropout : during training, randomly zero a fraction of activations (e.g. 10%) so the network cannot rely on any single path. It is turned off at inference. Gradient clipping : if the gradient norm exceeds a limit (often 1.0), scale it down. A cheap guard against loss spikes. Gradient size reaching each layer (illustrative) Layer 1 · plain deep net Layer 10 Layer 20 Layer 30 (output) Layer 1 · with residuals + norm training: a new random 30% dropped each step Two stability tools. Left: without residual paths, the gradient shrinks layer by layer and early layers barely learn. Right: dropout disables different neurons at each training step (animated). Example: reading a loss spike Training loss falls smoothly to 2.1, then jumps to 7.8 at step 14,200 and goes NaN. Likely causes: learning rate too high for this phase, a corrupted batch (e.g. extremely long or garbage sequence), or FP16 overflow. Remedies: gradient clipping, lower peak LR, BF16 instead of FP16, skip or inspect the offending batch, resume from the last checkpoint. The numbers How fast it fades or explodes. If each of 30 layers shrinks the gradient to 0.7 of its size, the first layer receives 0.7 multiplied by itself 30 times: about 0.00002 of the original. If each layer grows it to 1.3, it arrives about 2,600 times bigger. Small differences per layer become huge over depth. The right starting size. He initialisation for ReLU layers 256 wide draws weights with a spread of about 0.09 (the square root of 2 ÷ 256). That keeps the signal roughly the same size from layer to layer. Dropout keeps the average. Dropping 10% of values and multiplying the other 90% by 1 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 1.11 leaves the average unchanged, so nothing needs adjusting when dropout is turned off for real use. Clipping. If the gradient’s overall size is 5.0 and the limit is 1.0, every number in it is multiplied by 1.0 ÷ 5.0 = 0.2. The direction stays the same; only the step gets smaller. Code The program sends a batch of data through 50 random ReLU layers with weights that are too small, too big and correctly scaled, then through too-big layers with residual connections and normalisation, and checks that dropout keeps the average. Change DEPTH or the scales and run it again. Signals through 50 layers, in real Python. The layers are random and untrained, so this shows the forward signal only. Primary sources Glorot and Bengio (2010), Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks Why initial weight scale matters, and Xavier initialisation. He et al. (2015), Delving Deep into Rectifiers He initialisation for ReLU networks. Ba, Kiros and Hinton (2016), Layer Normalization The normalisation transformers use. Srivastava et al. (2014), Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting The dropout paper. Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio (2013), On the difficulty of training Recurrent Neural Networks Exploding gradients and gradient clipping.

title: Embeddings and representation learning
text: Intuition An embedding gives every piece of text an address in a "meaning space", so that texts about the same thing live in the same neighbourhood. "My bill is wrong" and "invoice error" end up next door, even though they share no words; "giraffe" lives far away. Nobody draws this map by hand. A network learns it as a side effect of doing some other task well, like predicting missing words or matching questions to their answers. You are known by the company you keep, and so are words. Mechanism A representation is the internal vector a network builds for an input. Representation learning means the network learns useful representations as a by-product of its training task. If a model must predict the next word, it is forced to encode meaning, syntax and facts in its vectors. An embedding is a representation designed to be used directly. Word embeddings (word2vec, 2013) showed that vector arithmetic can capture relations: vec("Paris") − vec("France") + vec("Italy") ≈ vec("Rome"). Today's text embedding models map whole sentences or passages to one vector, trained with contrastive learning : pull matching pairs (question, answering passage) together and push non-matching pairs apart. Two kinds of embedding are easy to confuse. Token embeddings are the input lookup table inside an LLM (one vector per vocabulary entry). Sentence/document embeddings come from a separate embedding model and are what you store in a vector database for RAG (chapter 9). invoice bill payment due refund password reset login failed 2FA code shipping delay package lost tracking number giraffe Each dot = one text, projected from 384 dimensions to 2 for display. Billing cluster Account access cluster Delivery cluster Unrelated outlier Distances in a 2-D projection are approximate; similarity search uses the full-dimensional vectors. Illustrative embedding space. Texts with similar meaning land near each other regardless of wording ("bill" next to "invoice"). Retrieval, clustering, deduplication and routing all exploit this. Query "reset my 2FA" Positive passage 2FA reset guide Negatives other passages in batch Encode all Similarities Contrastive loss positive should win Take a query from training pairs. Its matching passage is the positive. The other passages in the same batch serve as negatives ("in-batch negatives"); hard negatives (similar but wrong) help most. The same encoder turns each text into a vector. Compute cosine similarity of the query with every passage. Treat it as classification: softmax over similarities, cross-entropy with the positive as the correct class (InfoNCE loss). Training moves vectors so positives score highest. How embedding models are trained. You will reuse this when adapting embeddings to your domain (13.5). The numbers Storage. One million passages, each embedded as 384 numbers of 4 bytes, take 1,000,000 × 384 × 4 = about 1.5 GB. At 1,024 numbers each, it is about 4.1 GB, which is why embedding size matters for a vector database (9.4). Free negatives. In contrastive training with a batch of 256 question–passage pairs, each question has 1 right passage and 255 wrong ones already in the batch, so every step teaches 256 small "pick the right one out of 256" lessons at no extra cost. Reading a similarity. If "invoice" and "bill" score 0.82 and "invoice" and "giraffe" score 0.05 (illustrative), a search for "invoice" will rank bill-related passages first. The exact values depend on the model, so compare scores within one model, never across models. Code The program learns word vectors from your example project’s English messages: it counts which words appear near each other, squashes the counts into 16 numbers per word, and lists each word’s nearest neighbours. Change DIM to 4 or 32, or the window of 3 words, and run it again. Word vectors from your messages, in real Python. A few hundred synthetic messages give rough neighbours; real embedding models learn from billions of sentences. Laptop lab: embed and cluster Laptop · CPU from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer from sklearn.cluster import KMeans texts = ["invoice overdue", "my bill is wrong", "refund please", "can't log in", "reset password", "2FA code not arriving", "package lost", "where is my parcel", "shipping delayed"] m = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") # ~90 MB, fast on CPU E = m.encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True) print(E.shape) # (9, 384) for t, c in zip(texts, KMeans(3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(E)): print(c, t) Primary sources Mikolov et al. (2013), Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (word2vec) Word vectors and their arithmetic. Reimers and Gurevych (2019), Sentence-BERT Sentence embeddings trained to be compared with cosine similarity. van den Oord, Li and Vinyals (2018), Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding The contrastive (InfoNCE) loss behind most embedding training. Sentence Transformers documentation The library used in the laptop lab, with model choices and training guides. Muennighoff et al. (2022), MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark How embedding models are compared across tasks.

title: CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs and sequence-to-sequence models (conceptual)
text: Intuition Before transformers, two designs did most of the work. A CNN looks at an image through a small window that it slides everywhere, like scanning a page with a magnifying glass: the same "edge detector" works in every corner. An RNN reads a sentence one word at a time and keeps a running summary in its head, like listening to a long story and trying to remember the beginning. The magnifying glass is efficient but only sees a little at once. The running summary forgets the start of long stories, and it cannot be hurried, because each word has to wait for the one before. Attention fixed both problems, but these designs still turn up in vision, OCR and small time-series models. Mechanism Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) slide small learned filters (kernels) across an image, detecting local patterns (edges → textures → parts → objects). Weight sharing makes them efficient. Still used for vision and OCR components in document pipelines. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) process a sequence one element at a time, updating a hidden state h t = f(W·x t + U·h t−1 ). The same weights are applied at each step. Information from early tokens must survive many multiplications, so it fades. LSTMs add a cell state and gates (forget, input, output) that learn what to keep, write and expose, which preserves information over longer spans. GRUs are a simpler variant. Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) : an encoder RNN reads the input into a vector; a decoder RNN generates the output from it. The single fixed vector is a bottleneck for long inputs, which is exactly what attention was invented to fix (1.2, 5.2). Convolution: a 3×3 filter sliding over an image RNN unrolled over 4 tokens h₁ h₂ h₃ h₄ the cat sat down same weights at each step; h₄ must carry "the" through 3 updates Two pre-transformer architectures. The CNN filter (animated) computes one output per position. The RNN must pass information strictly left to right, so it cannot be parallelised across time during training. Je suis étudiant vec I am student one vector for the whole input Je suis étudiant student attention: look at every input position directly The bottleneck and its fix. With attention, generating "student" can weight "étudiant" most heavily, regardless of input length. Example: where these still appear A document-ingestion pipeline (10.3) may use a CNN-based layout detector and a CNN/transformer OCR model before any LLM sees the text. Time-series anomaly detectors on GPU telemetry sometimes use LSTMs because they are small and fast. The numbers Why sharing weights is cheap. A 3 × 3 filter has 9 weights, and the same 9 are reused at every one of the roughly 50,000 positions in a 224 × 224 image. A fully connected layer linking all 50,176 pixels to 50,176 outputs would need 50,176 × 50,176 ≈ 2.5 billion weights. How fast an RNN forgets. If each step keeps half of the old state, the first word’s share after 20 steps is 0.5 multiplied by itself 20 times: about one millionth. LSTM gates learn to keep more, but very long inputs still fade. Why RNNs train slowly. A 1,000-word input takes 1,000 steps one after another, because each step needs the result of the one before. A transformer processes all 1,000 positions of a training example at once. Code The program counts your example project’s records per day, slides two hand-made filters along the series (a 7-day average and a change detector), and then shows how fast a plain RNN’s memory of its first input fades. Change the EDGE filter or KEEP and run it again. Convolution and a fading memory, in real Python. The filters here are written by hand; a CNN learns its own. Primary sources Stanford CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks How convolution layers, filters and pooling work. Olah (2015), Understanding LSTM Networks The clearest picture of LSTM gates. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997), Long Short-Term Memory The LSTM paper. Sutskever, Vinyals and Le (2014), Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks The encoder–decoder RNN with its single-vector bottleneck. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014), Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate Attention, added to fix that bottleneck.

title: PyTorch: tensors, automatic differentiation, training loops, checkpoints and debugging
text: Intuition PyTorch is a calculator that remembers how it got every answer. You write the forward calculation, and because it kept notes, it can work out all the gradients for you when you ask. That frees you to think about the model and the data instead of the calculus. Every training loop, however fancy the library wrapped around it, is the same short routine: get a batch, make predictions, measure the loss, clear the old gradients, work out new ones, take a step, and now and then check progress and save your work. Mechanism PyTorch gives you tensors that can live on CPU or GPU and autograd : every operation on a tensor with requires_grad=True is recorded in a computation graph, and loss.backward() runs backpropagation through it, filling each parameter's .grad . You write the forward computation; PyTorch derives the backward pass. Load batch DataLoader Forward model(x) Loss loss_fn(ŷ, y) Zero grads opt.zero_grad() Backward loss.backward() Clip & step opt.step() Schedule sched.step() Eval & checkpoint every N steps Fetch the next mini-batch, move it to the device (CPU here). Run the model to get predictions; the autograd graph is recorded. Compute a scalar loss. Clear gradients from the previous step, because PyTorch accumulates them by default (forgetting this is a classic bug). Backpropagate: every parameter's .grad is filled. Optionally clip gradient norm, then let the optimiser update weights. Advance the learning-rate schedule. Periodically switch to model.eval() with torch.no_grad() , compute validation loss, and save a checkpoint containing model and optimiser state so training can resume exactly. The training loop. Libraries like Hugging Face Trainer and TRL wrap this loop, but it is always these steps underneath. Debugging checklist Overfit one batch first. If the model cannot drive loss near zero on 8 examples, there is a bug (wrong labels, wrong loss, frozen weights). Check the initial loss against ln(number of classes) (2.4). Shapes : print tensor shapes at each step; silent broadcasting causes wrong but runnable code. Train/eval mode : dropout and normalisation behave differently; forgetting model.eval() gives noisy validation numbers. NaN : enable torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) briefly to find the operation; lower LR; clip gradients. no_grad is not eval mode : torch.no_grad() stops gradient recording but does not disable dropout or switch normalisation to inference behaviour; call model.eval() as well, and model.train() before resuming training. Watch gradient norms per layer; zeros mean a disconnected graph or dead ReLUs. A checkpoint saves the weights, the optimiser state and the step number together, so a run can resume exactly where it stopped. The numbers The laptop lab, in numbers. Parameters: 64 × 128 + 128 for the first layer and 128 × 10 + 10 for the second, 9,610 in total. Steps: 80% of 1,797 images is about 1,437; in batches of 64 that is 23 steps per epoch, and 40 epochs is 920 steps. Starting loss: with 10 classes and random guesses, it should be close to the natural log of 10, about 2.30. A starting loss of 15 means something is wrong before training begins. Checkpoint size: 9,610 parameters × 4 bytes is about 38 KB; AdamW’s two extra numbers per parameter bring the saved file to about 115 KB. Code The program writes out the training loop in NumPy so nothing is hidden. It first overfits 8 rows to prove the code can learn, then trains a small network on your example project’s table in mini-batches, with gradient clipping, a validation check every epoch and the best checkpoint saved and reloaded. Change the learning rate 0.1 or the number of epochs and run it again. A training loop with checkpoints, in real Python. It mirrors what PyTorch does; it does not show GPUs or automatic gradients. Laptop lab: a complete training loop Laptop · CPU · ~1 minute import torch, torch.nn as nn from sklearn.datasets import load_digits from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split torch.manual_seed(0) X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True) # 8x8 images of digits, 1,797 samples Xtr, Xva, ytr, yva = train_test_split(X / 16.0, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0) Xtr, Xva = map(lambda a: torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32), (Xtr, Xva)) ytr, yva = torch.tensor(ytr), torch.tensor(yva) model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.1), nn.Linear(128, 10)) opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3, weight_decay=0.01) sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=40) loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss() for epoch in range(40): model.train() for i in torch.randperm(len(Xtr)).split(64): # mini-batches of 64 loss = loss_fn(model(Xtr[i]), ytr[i]) opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step() sched.step() model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): acc = (model(Xva).argmax(1) == yva).float().mean() if epoch % 10 == 9: print(f"epoch {epoch+1} loss {loss.item():.3f} val_acc {acc:.3f}") torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(), "opt": opt.state_dict(), "epoch": epoch}, "ckpt.pt") Primary sources PyTorch: Learn the Basics Tensors, datasets, models, autograd and the training loop, step by step. PyTorch: Autograd mechanics How the computation graph is recorded and used. PyTorch: Saving and Loading Models Checkpoints that can resume training. Karpathy (2019), A Recipe for Training Neural Networks The debugging habits in the checklist above, explained.

title: Tokenisation: subwords, BPE, vocabulary and multilingual implications
text: Intuition A model cannot read letters or words directly; it reads numbers from a fixed list. If the list held every word, it would never be finished: typos, new product names and other languages keep arriving. If it held only single characters, every sentence would be very long and slow to process. Subword tokenisation sits in between: common words get one entry each, and rare words are spelled out from smaller pieces that are in the list. Think of it as a shorthand learned from one stack of documents. The shorthand is excellent for text like that stack and clumsy for anything else, which is why the same message can cost very different amounts in different languages. Mechanism Byte-pair encoding (BPE) learns the vocabulary from a corpus: start with individual characters (or bytes), count every adjacent pair, merge the most frequent pair into a new token , and repeat until the vocabulary reaches its target size. At tokenisation time, the learned merges are applied in the same order. Byte-level BPE starts from the 256 byte values, so any text, including emoji and unseen scripts, can be encoded with no "unknown" token. Other algorithms (WordPiece, Unigram/SentencePiece) differ in how they choose merges but have the same effect. Real BPE, running in your browser. "▁" marks the start of a word. Each click finds the most frequent adjacent pair and merges it everywhere. In the classic example, frequent endings like "est" and "er" become tokens quickly and rare words stay split. Train it on your example project's text, or your own, to see which pieces its vocabulary forms. Multilingual implications. Tokenisers are trained mostly on English-heavy data, so other languages often need more tokens for the same meaning. More tokens means higher cost, slower responses, and less content fitting in the context window. Some scripts (e.g. Thai, Amharic, Burmese) can need several times more tokens than English on older tokenisers. Newer models with larger vocabularies (100k–260k tokens) reduce but do not eliminate the gap. Always measure token counts on your real languages before estimating cost. Relative token count for the same sentence (illustrative, varies by tokeniser) English Spanish German Hindi Japanese Tamil Burmese The " token tax ". A multilingual support bot with a fixed per-conversation token budget gives non-English users less history and less retrieved context. Treat this as a fairness and cost issue. Measure it, if you opt in. Three real tokenizers ( GPT-2 , BERT multilingual and XLM-R ) run on your device over your example project's messages, so the chart above stops being only an illustration. The counts are exact for these three tokenizers. They are not what a hosted model will bill, so measure with its own tokenizer before you estimate cost. Example: why models miscount letters "How many r's in strawberry?" The model may see tokens like str · aw · berry , never individual letters. Counting requires knowledge it learned indirectly about spelling. Tasks that depend on characters (counting, reversing, exact string edits) should be done in code, with the LLM calling a tool (7.4). The numbers One BPE step. Look at every pair of neighbouring pieces in every word, and count how often each pair appears. A word that appears 10 times in the text counts 10 times. The pair with the highest count is merged into one new piece, and that piece is added to the vocabulary. Vocabulary size. Every merge adds exactly one token. Byte-level BPE starts with 256 tokens (one per byte), so 50,000 merges give 50,256 tokens. GPT-2 did exactly this and added one special end-of-text token: 50,257 in total. The token tax. Take the same message in two languages and count the tokens in each. Divide the other language's count by the English count: English: 100 tokens. Tamil: 240 tokens. The tax is 240 ÷ 100 = 2.4. The Tamil conversation costs about 2.4 times as much. It also fits only 100 ÷ 240 ≈ 42% as much text into the same context window . Code The program trains BPE on your example project's English messages only, shows the first merges it learns, and then measures tokens per character for every language in the dataset. Change N_MERGES and run it again: more merges shorten English further, while the other scripts barely move. BPE from scratch, in real Python. It runs in your browser after you opt in to the Python download. The tokenizer is tiny and word-level, so the ratios are not a production tokenizer's; the direction of the gap is the point. Primary sources Sennrich, Haddow and Birch (2016), Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units The paper that brought BPE to language models; its algorithm is the one above. Radford et al. (2019), Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2) Section 2.2 introduces byte-level BPE. Kudo and Richardson (2018), SentencePiece Language-independent subword tokenisation, used by many multilingual models. Petrov et al. (2023), Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages Measures the token tax across many languages and tokenizers. Hugging Face Tokenizers documentation How to train and run BPE, WordPiece and Unigram tokenizers in practice.

title: Self-attention, cross-attention, multi-head attention and causal masking
text: Intuition To understand a word you look at the words around it, and some neighbours matter much more than others. In "The server that crashed restarted", the word "restarted" needs to find its subject, "server", and can mostly ignore "that". Attention is how a transformer does this: every token asks a question, every token advertises what it holds, and each token collects a blend of the others, weighted by how well they answered its question. It works like a soft lookup in a dictionary. A normal lookup returns the one entry whose key matches exactly; attention returns a weighted mix of all entries, with the closest matches weighted most. Mechanism Query (Q), Key (K), Value (V) : three vectors computed from each token's representation by learned matrices W Q , W K , W V . Intuition: the query says "what I am looking for", the key says "what I contain", the value is "what I will pass on". Attention : each token's output is a weighted average of all values, weighted by how well its query matches each key. The numbers part below works through an example. Self-attention : Q, K and V all come from the same sequence. Cross-attention : Q comes from one sequence (the decoder) and K, V from another (the encoder's output), as in translation. Multi-head attention : run several attentions in parallel with different learned projections (e.g. 32 heads of dimension 128), then concatenate. Different heads learn different relations (syntax, coreference, position). Causal mask : in a generator, token i may only attend to tokens ≤ i. Scores for future positions are set to −∞ before softmax, so their weight is exactly 0. Token vectors X n × d Q = XW Q , K = XW K , V = XW V Scores QKᵀ/√d n × n Mask future −∞ above diagonal Softmax per row weights sum to 1 Weighted sum of V n × d Concat heads → W O Input: one vector per token (embedding plus position information). Three matrix multiplies produce queries, keys and values for every token at once. Every query is compared with every key by dot product: an n × n score matrix. This is the quadratic cost (5.7). For generation, future positions are masked so a token cannot peek ahead. Softmax turns each row of scores into attention weights. Each token's output is the weighted sum of value vectors: it has "gathered" information from relevant tokens. Outputs of all heads are concatenated and mixed by one more matrix. Attention as a pipeline of matrix operations. Everything happens for all tokens in parallel during prefill. Attention weights for "The server that crashed restarted". Rows are the attending token (query), columns the attended token (key). The weights are computed live with real softmax over hand-designed scores that mimic patterns observed in trained models; they are not from a real model. Select a row to see its weights in words. Raising the score scale makes attention sharper. Multi-head attention as tensors, in 3D. Step through the pipeline above with real numbers: the token matrix X, the projections to Q, K and V, the split into 3 heads laid one behind another (the third axis is the head), each head's causal attention weights, the weighted sum of values, and the concatenation mixed by W O . The arithmetic is real, computed in your browser, but X and the weights are random, so the attention patterns mean nothing: the figure above shows hand-designed heads with recognisable patterns. Drag or use the arrow keys to turn the view, or switch to the 2D view; the text under the figure describes each step. Example: what attention resolves In "The server that crashed restarted", the verb "restarted" needs its subject. A trained head may put high weight from "restarted" onto "server", skipping "crashed". The output vector for "restarted" then contains information about the server, which later layers use to predict the next token (e.g. "at", "after"). The numbers A small worked example. Take the token "restarted". Its query is compared with the key of every earlier token, giving one score each. The scores here are illustrative: Token Score After softmax (weight) server 4 0.84 that 1 0.04 crashed 2 0.11 Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1 (5.5 shows how). The output for "restarted" is then 84% of the value of "server", 4% of "that" and 11% of "crashed", added together. So it mostly carries information about the server. Why scores are divided by the square root of the width. A score is the sum of one multiplication per dimension, so wider vectors give bigger scores. With very big scores, softmax gives almost all the weight to one token and learning stalls. Dividing by the square root of the width brings scores back to a normal size: for 128 dimensions that is about 11.3, so a raw score of 45 becomes about 4. The cost. Every token is compared with every token, so each head builds a table of tokens × tokens scores: 1,000 tokens: 1,000 × 1,000 = 1 million scores. 2,000 tokens: 4 million scores. Double the text, four times the work (5.7). Code The whole of attention fits in a few lines of NumPy. The program takes the first words of one of your example project's messages, computes causal attention, checks that each row of weights sums to 1 and that nothing above the diagonal is attended to, then splits the work into two heads. Try deleting the / np.sqrt(K.shape[1]) and multiplying X by 10 to see softmax saturate. Scaled dot-product attention, in real Python. The operations are exact; the embeddings and weights are random, so the pattern of weights carries no meaning. Primary sources Vaswani et al. (2017), Attention Is All You Need Defines scaled dot-product and multi-head attention (section 3.2), including the √d scaling argument. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014), Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate The first attention mechanism, as cross-attention in a translation model. Ainslie et al. (2023), GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models Grouped-query attention, which most current LLMs use to shrink the KV cache. PyTorch: scaled_dot_product_attention The production function, with its reference implementation, masking and scaling options.

title: Positional representations, residual connections, normalisation and feed-forward layers
text: Intuition Attention on its own has no sense of order: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" contain the same tokens, and attention would treat them the same. So each token is also given its position, in a way that lets the model tell how far apart two tokens are. A transformer is then a tall stack of identical blocks. Think of a shared notebook, one page per token, passed up through the stack: each block reads the page, writes a short note, and adds it to what is already there instead of rewriting the page. Normalising before each block keeps the handwriting a readable size, so a hundred blocks can be stacked without the numbers exploding or fading away. Mechanism Attention by itself treats its input as a set: shuffling tokens shuffles outputs identically. Word order must be injected as positional information . Absolute positional embeddings (original transformer, BERT, GPT-2): add a learned or sinusoidal vector for position 1, 2, 3… to each token embedding. RoPE (rotary position embedding) , used by most current LLMs: rotate each query and key vector by an angle proportional to its position. The dot product between a query at position m and a key at position n then depends on m − n, i.e. relative distance. RoPE scaling methods are part of how context windows are extended after training. ALiBi and similar methods add a distance-based penalty directly to attention scores. A transformer block (layer) has two sub-layers, each wrapped in a residual connection (output = input + sublayer(input)) and normalisation. Residuals give gradients a direct path through all layers, which is what lets models stack 30–100+ blocks. Modern LLMs use pre-norm : normalise before each sub-layer ( RMSNorm is common). The feed-forward network (FFN / MLP) is applied to each position independently: expand the vector (often ~3.5–4× wider), apply a non-linearity (commonly SwiGLU ), project back. About two-thirds of a dense model's parameters sit in FFNs, and they are thought to store much of the model's factual associations. x (residual stream) RMSNorm Multi-head attention + RoPE on Q, K Add: x + attn RMSNorm FFN expand → SwiGLU → project Add: x + ffn Next block The residual stream : one vector per token that each block reads from and writes back into. Normalise so values have a stable scale. Attention mixes information between positions. Rotary position encoding is applied to queries and keys here. Add the result to the stream instead of replacing it. Normalise again. FFN transforms each position independently : where much of the "knowledge" lives. Add back to the stream. Repeat for all L layers (e.g. 32 for an 8B model, 80 for a 70B model). A final norm and the output projection (the "LM head") produce logits. One pre-norm decoder block. A whole LLM is: embedding lookup → L identical blocks → final norm → LM head. The same block, exploded into floors. Each floor is one stage's output, lying flat (tokens towards you, features across), stacked in the order the block computes them, so the third axis is the order of operations and each floor's width is its tensor's width. The numbers are a real forward pass of a tiny block (8 features, 2 heads, a 24-wide SwiGLU FFN) computed in your browser with random weights, so they show the shapes, the normalisation and the residual adds, not what a trained model computes. The parameter counts in the text compare it with an 8B-like model. q @ pos 2 k @ pos 5 Δ = 3 steps q @ pos 102 k @ pos 105 Δ = 3 steps Both pairs are rotated by different absolute amounts, but the angle between q and k is the same, so their dot product depends only on relative distance. Rotary position embedding, one 2-D slice. Real RoPE rotates many 2-D slices of each vector at different frequencies. Preset Llama-3-8B-like 3B-like 70B-like GPT-2 small d_model heads KV heads layers FFN width vocab FFN type SwiGLU (3 matrices) GELU (2 matrices) tied input/output embeddings sequence batch Transformer shape and parameter tracer. Exact arithmetic for one pre-norm block with grouped-query attention, ignoring biases (most current LLMs have none) and small norm weights. Choose a preset or edit any field. The 8B preset reproduces the ≈ 8.0B count worked out in the example below; GPT-2 small (with learned position embeddings, 1,024 positions) gives ≈ 124M. Example: counting an 8B model's parameters Llama-3-8B-style shape: d = 4096, 32 layers, FFN width 14,336, vocabulary 128,256, grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads (each key and value head is shared by 4 query heads). Per layer: attention ≈ 4096×4096 (Q) + 2×4096×1024 (K,V) + 4096×4096 (O) ≈ 42M; FFN (SwiGLU has 3 matrices) ≈ 3×4096×14,336 ≈ 176M. 32 layers × 218M ≈ 7.0B, plus input and output embeddings 2×128,256×4096 ≈ 1.05B → ≈ 8.0B. The numbers RoPE, like the hand of a clock. Each position turns the query or key vector by a fixed step, the way a clock hand moves a fixed amount every minute. A query at position 5 is turned 5 steps and a key at position 2 is turned 2 steps, so the angle between them is 3 steps. At positions 105 and 102 both are turned much further, but the angle between them is still 3 steps. The attention score depends on that angle, so it depends only on how far apart the two tokens are. Real RoPE does this with many clock hands turning at different speeds. RMSNorm on a tiny vector. Take the vector [3, 4]: Square each number and take the average: (9 + 16) ÷ 2 = 12.5. Take the square root: about 3.54. This is the vector's typical size. Divide each number by it: [0.85, 1.13]. Multiply by learned gains, which the model tunes during training. A vector ten times bigger, [30, 40], gives the same [0.85, 1.13], so every token reaches the next layer at a similar scale. The residual add. Each sub-layer's output is added to its input: new value = old value + what the sub-layer adds. If a sub-layer learns nothing useful, it can add almost nothing and the signal passes through unchanged, which is why 100 layers can be stacked. The FFN's size. A SwiGLU FFN has three matrices of 4,096 × 14,336 numbers each. That is 3 × 4,096 × 14,336 ≈ 176 million parameters in every layer of the 8B model above. Code The program checks the RoPE property numerically (the same score at positions 5, 105 and 1005 when the distance is 3), then shows RMSNorm putting four tokens at very different scales onto the same scale, and a pre-norm residual add. Change the distance from 3 to 4 at one of the three positions and the scores stop matching. RoPE, RMSNorm and the residual add, in real Python. These are exact properties of the formulas, shown on random vectors. Primary sources Su et al. (2021), RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding Defines RoPE and proves the relative-position property used above. Zhang and Sennrich (2019), Root Mean Square Layer Normalization RMSNorm and why dropping the mean costs little. Xiong et al. (2020), On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture Why pre-norm trains more stably than the original post-norm block. Shazeer (2020), GLU Variants Improve Transformer SwiGLU and the other gated feed-forward layers. He et al. (2015), Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition Residual connections, introduced for very deep image networks. Press, Smith and Lewis (2021), Train Short, Test Long (ALiBi) The distance-penalty alternative to RoPE.

title: Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder–decoder architectures
text: Intuition The same transformer block can be wired three ways, and the wiring decides what the model is good at. A reader that sees the whole page at once is best at understanding it. A writer that can only see what it has written so far is built for producing text. A translator first reads a whole sentence with one part of itself and then writes with another, looking back at what it read. The only difference between these three is who may look at whom: the attention mask. Mechanism Family Attention Trained to Good for Examples Encoder-only Bidirectional: every token sees every token Fill in masked tokens Understanding: classification, NER, embeddings, rerankers BERT, RoBERTa, ModernBERT, most embedding models Decoder-only Causal: only earlier tokens Predict the next token Generation, chat, code, agents; everything via prompting GPT family, Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, Claude Encoder–decoder Encoder bidirectional; decoder causal + cross-attention to encoder Map input sequence to output sequence Translation, summarisation, speech recognition T5, BART, Whisper Who can attend to whom. Filled cell = row token may attend to column token. Decoder-only won for general-purpose models because one simple objective scales on any text and every task can be phrased as continuation. Example: picking architectures in one RAG system A bi-encoder (encoder-only) embeds documents and queries for fast vector search; a cross-encoder reranker (encoder-only, reading query and passage together) re-scores the top 50; a decoder-only LLM writes the answer. Three transformers, three architectures, each matched to its job. The numbers Who can see whom. Count the allowed pairs with 4 output tokens and 5 input tokens: Encoder-only, with 4 tokens: every token sees all 4, so 4 × 4 = 16 pairs. Decoder-only, with 4 tokens: the first sees 1, the second 2, the third 3, the fourth 4, so 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 pairs. Cross-attention: each of the 4 output tokens sees all 5 input tokens, so 4 × 5 = 20 pairs. How much each text teaches. A decoder-only model gets a lesson at every position: a 1,000-token text gives 1,000 "what comes next?" questions. BERT hides about 15% of the tokens and learns only from those, so the same text gives about 150 questions. Why the decoder can reuse work. In a decoder-only model, an earlier token never sees later tokens, so its keys and values do not change when a new token is added. They can be saved and reused (the KV cache ). In an encoder, adding a token changes what every earlier token sees, so everything would have to be computed again. Code The program builds the three masks as matrices of ones and zeros and counts what each token can see. Change n_src and n_tgt to see how the causal triangle and the cross-attention rectangle grow. The three attention patterns, in real Python. The masks are the whole difference between the families' attention; the rest of a real model is not shown. Primary sources Devlin et al. (2018), BERT The encoder-only model and its masked-language-model objective. Brown et al. (2020), Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3) A decoder-only model doing many tasks by continuation alone. Raffel et al. (2019), Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (T5) Compares the three families and their objectives under one setup. Radford et al. (2022), Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision (Whisper) An encoder–decoder model for speech, in production use.

title: Next-token prediction, autoregressive generation, logits and softmax
text: Intuition An LLM does one thing over and over: given the text so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary for how well it would fit next. The scores become probabilities, one token is chosen, it is appended to the text, and the whole step repeats. A long answer is thousands of these small guesses in a row, like predictive text on a phone, run with a far better model. Training uses the same step in reverse: show the model real text, and nudge it to give more probability to the token that really came next. Mechanism Logits : raw, unbounded scores the LM head outputs, one per vocabulary token. Higher = more likely. Softmax : converts logits to probabilities that are positive and sum to 1. Adding a constant to all logits changes nothing; only differences matter. Autoregressive : each output token becomes part of the input for the next step. Generation is inherently sequential: token 50 cannot be computed before token 49. Two phases matter for performance. Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass (fast per token). Decode then produces one token per forward pass (slow per token). To avoid recomputing keys and values for earlier tokens at each step, engines store them in the KV cache (14.1). Autoregressive generation, animated. Each step shows the top candidates and their probabilities (illustrative), the chosen token is appended, and the loop repeats until an end-of-sequence token. The numbers The probability of a whole sentence is the probabilities of its tokens multiplied together. If the model gives "The" 0.2, then "cat" 0.1, then "sat" 0.3, the whole phrase gets 0.2 × 0.1 × 0.3 = 0.006. Softmax in three steps. Raise the number e (about 2.718) to the power of each score, add the results, and divide each by the total. The example below does this by hand. Adding the same number to every score changes nothing: the scores [12, 11, 10.1] give the same probabilities as [2, 1, 0.1]. Example: softmax by hand Logits for three tokens: [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]. e 2 = 7.39, e 1 = 2.72, e 0.1 = 1.11, total 11.22. Probabilities: 0.66, 0.24, 0.10. If the true next token is the second one, its cross-entropy loss is −ln(0.24) = 1.42. The training loss. For each position, take the probability the model gave to the token that really came next, and take minus its natural log (the cross-entropy , 2.4). A confident right answer costs little and a confident wrong one costs a lot: Probability given to the right token Loss 0.9 0.11 0.24 1.42 0.01 4.61 A model that guesses evenly across a 128,000-token vocabulary scores a loss of about 11.8, so training starts near there and goes down. Code The program builds the smallest possible language model from your example project's English messages: a bigram model whose logit for the next word is the log of how often it followed the current word. It prints the top candidates with their probabilities, generates greedily, and measures its loss on messages it did not train on, next to the loss of an even guess. Change the smoothing value 0.1 to 1.0 and watch the held-out loss and the probabilities change. From logits to a generated sentence, in real Python. The operations are the ones an LLM uses; the model sees one word of context, so its output and loss are not comparable to an LLM's. Laptop lab: look at real logits Laptop · CPU import torch from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM name = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M" # 135M params, ~270 MB, fast on CPU tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name); model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name) ids = tok("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt").input_ids with torch.no_grad(): logits = model(ids).logits[0, -1] # scores for the next token probs = torch.softmax(logits, -1); top = torch.topk(probs, 8) for p, i in zip(top.values, top.indices): print(f"{p:.3f} {tok.decode(i)!r}") out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=12, do_sample=False) # greedy autoregressive loop print(tok.decode(out[0])) Primary sources Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville (2016), Deep Learning, chapter 6 Section 6.2.2.3 derives softmax outputs, their cross-entropy loss and its gradient. Radford et al. (2019), Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2) Language modelling as next-token prediction, with the factorisation above. PyTorch: CrossEntropyLoss The loss as implemented, taking raw logits rather than probabilities. Hugging Face Transformers: generation strategies How generate runs the autoregressive loop, with greedy and sampling options.

title: Decoding: temperature, top-k, top-p, stop conditions and reproducibility limits
text: Intuition The model gives you a probability for every possible next token; it does not tell you which one to pick. Decoding is that choice. Always taking the favourite is safe but dull and can loop. Drawing at random from the whole list is varied but occasionally picks something absurd from the long tail. The usual controls sit between the two: they reshape the probabilities or cut off the tail, and then draw. It is like asking a room for suggestions: you can take only the loudest answer, listen to everyone, or listen only to the few people who clearly know the topic. Mechanism Greedy : always take the most probable token. Deterministic in principle; can be repetitive. Temperature T : divide logits by T before softmax. T < 1 sharpens the distribution (more predictable), T > 1 flattens it (more varied, more errors). T → 0 approaches greedy. Top-k : keep only the k most probable tokens, renormalise, sample. Top-p (nucleus) : keep the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p (e.g. 0.9), renormalise, sample. Adapts to how confident the model is. Stop conditions : end-of-sequence token, a maximum number of new tokens, or stop strings (e.g. "\n\nUser:" ). Always set a max token limit; it bounds cost and latency. Other controls: repetition/frequency penalties, min-p, and constrained decoding to force valid JSON (7.4). Filter order varies by engine. Engines differ in the order they apply temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p and penalties, and in whether they renormalise between steps, so identical settings can give different distributions on different engines. The demo below applies temperature first, then top-k and top-p together. Check your engine's documentation before comparing settings across providers. Temperature Top-k Top-p Prompt: "Our quarterly results were ___" Sample 20 times Decoding controls, computed live on a fixed set of 10 illustrative logits. Greyed tokens are excluded by top-k or top-p. Sampling uses real random draws from the resulting distribution. Reproducibility limits. Even with temperature 0 and a fixed seed, outputs can differ between runs. Causes include floating-point non-associativity on GPUs (summing in a different order gives slightly different results), batching with other requests changing kernel choices, different hardware or library versions, and silent model updates by providers. Tiny numeric differences can flip a near-tie between two tokens, and the texts then diverge. Design tests to check properties ("valid JSON", "mentions clause 4.2") rather than exact strings, and pin model versions. Example: settings per use case Data extraction into JSON: temperature 0, constrained schema, max 500 tokens. Customer reply drafting: temperature 0.5–0.7, top-p 0.9, stop at signature. Brainstorming product names: temperature 1.0, sample several candidates and rank them. Reasoning models often recommend specific settings; check the provider documentation, as some ignore or restrict these parameters. The numbers Temperature. Divide every score by the temperature, then apply softmax. With two tokens scored 2 and 1: Temperature Scores after dividing Chance of the first token 0.5 4 and 2 88% 1 2 and 1 73% 2 1 and 0.5 62% A low temperature makes the favourite even more likely; a high one evens things out. Top-k, top-p and min-p on five tokens with probabilities 0.50, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10 and 0.05: Top-k = 2 keeps the two biggest, 0.50 and 0.20. They add to 0.70, so after renormalising (dividing each by 0.70) they become 0.71 and 0.29. Top-p = 0.8 adds from the top until the total reaches 0.8: 0.50 + 0.20 = 0.70 is not enough, + 0.15 = 0.85 is. It keeps three tokens, which become 0.59, 0.24 and 0.18. Min-p = 0.25 keeps tokens with at least a quarter of the top token's probability: 0.25 × 0.50 = 0.125, so it keeps 0.50, 0.20 and 0.15. If the top token had 0.95, top-p 0.8 would keep only that one: top-p keeps fewer tokens when the model is sure and more when it is not. Code The program takes the word in your example project's messages with the most varied next words, turns their counts into logits, and shows what temperature, top-k and top-p do to them, then samples with a fixed seed. Change TOP_P , k and the temperatures, or the seed, and run it again. Temperature, top-k and top-p, in real Python. The rules are the real ones; the candidates come from word counts in a small dataset, not from a language model. Try decoding on a real model, on a GPU in Google Colab . Colab · GPU The figure above uses illustrative logits. This guide takes you from a new notebook to a real model on a free GPU, one step at a time, using your example project's question and document. The code runs on Google's machines, not on this site, and free GPU access is limited and not guaranteed . Primary sources Holtzman et al. (2019), The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration Introduces nucleus (top-p) sampling and shows why greedy and pure sampling both fail. Fan, Lewis and Dauphin (2018), Hierarchical Neural Story Generation Top-k sampling for open-ended generation. Nguyen et al. (2024), Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs The min-p rule above. Hugging Face Transformers: generation strategies The decoding parameters as one widely used library implements them.

title: Dense vs mixture-of-experts models, context length and attention costs
text: Intuition A dense model is a generalist who reads every request in full with everything they know. A mixture-of-experts model is a firm of specialists with a receptionist: each token is handed to the two or three specialists who suit it best, so the firm knows a lot but only a small part of it works on any one token. You still have to pay rent for the whole office, though: every expert must be in memory. Context length has a cost of its own. With attention, every token looks at every other token, so a text twice as long means four times as many comparisons, and every token kept in context also takes memory. Mechanism In a dense model, every parameter is used for every token. In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, each FFN is replaced by many "expert" FFNs plus a small router that picks the top few experts (e.g. 2 of 8, or 8 of 128) per token. Total parameters grow, but active parameters per token stay small. Mixtral 8x7B, for example, has ~47B total parameters and ~13B active per token. Tradeoff: MoE gives near-large-model quality at small-model compute per token, but all experts must sit in memory, so it needs as much memory as a dense model of its total size. Serving also needs good load balancing across experts (expert parallelism, 14.5). MoE routing, animated. Each incoming token is scored by the router and sent to its top-2 experts (highlighted); their outputs are combined by the router weights. Different tokens use different experts. Attention cost. Self-attention compares every token with every other, so compute and the score matrix grow with n² (sequence length squared). Doubling context quadruples attention compute. Optimised kernels such as FlashAttention avoid storing the full n × n matrix, but the compute is still quadratic. The KV cache grows linearly with n and is often the real memory limit in serving (14.1). Long contexts also have a quality cost: models use information in the middle of long contexts less reliably than at the start or end, so "fits in the window" does not mean "used well". Measure it on your task (9.5). Context length How costs scale with context for an 8B-class model (32 layers, 8 KV heads × 128 dims, BF16). Attention work grows with the square of the context length, and the KV cache grows in a straight line with it (the numbers part below works through both). Computed exactly, not simulated. Example: stuffing the context vs retrieving You could put a 400-page manual (≈ 250k tokens) in every prompt. Each request would pay for 250k input tokens, wait seconds for prefill, and need ~33 GB (≈ 31 GiB) of KV cache for an 8B model. Retrieving the 5 most relevant chunks (≈ 3k tokens) is roughly 80× cheaper in tokens and usually more accurate. Prompt caching (14.3) reduces the cost of repeated long prefixes, but not the quality issue. The numbers MoE: stored versus used. Mixtral 8x7B has 8 experts in each layer and uses 2 of them for each token: Stored: about 47 billion parameters. All of them must fit in memory. Used for each token: about 13 billion, so each token costs about as much compute as a 13B dense model. A rule of thumb is about 2 calculations per used parameter per token: 2 × 13 billion ≈ 26 billion calculations for each token. Attention grows with the square of the length. Going from 1,000 to 8,000 tokens makes the text 8 times longer and the attention work 8 × 8 = 64 times bigger. The KV cache. For each token, an 8B-class model keeps a key and a value (2) in each of 32 layers, for 8 key-value heads of 128 numbers, at 2 bytes per number: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, which is 128 KiB per token. For the 250,000-token manual in the example above: 128 KiB × 250,000 ≈ 31 GiB, just for one request's cache. Code The program counts stored and active parameters for a dense and an 8-expert configuration, then prints attention cost next to the rest of a layer's cost for contexts from 1k to 128k tokens, and the KV cache per token. Change experts and active_experts , or the context lengths, and find where attention starts to dominate. What MoE and long contexts cost, in real Python. The formulas are the standard estimates and the configurations are illustrative; measured speed also depends on kernels and hardware. Primary sources Shazeer et al. (2017), Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer The top-k router and load-balancing loss. Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer (2021), Switch Transformers Top-1 routing at scale, with the simplified balancing loss. Jiang et al. (2024), Mixtral of Experts The 8-expert, top-2 model whose total and active counts are quoted above. Dao et al. (2022), FlashAttention Exact attention without storing the n × n matrix; the compute stays quadratic. Liu et al. (2023), Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts The quality cost of long contexts described in the Mechanism. Kaplan et al. (2020), Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models Section 2.1 derives the 2N FLOPs-per-token estimate.

title: Pretraining, continued pretraining, supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation
text: Intuition Making an assistant happens in stages, like training a doctor. First comes years of general reading (pretraining): the model reads a huge slice of the internet and learns language, facts and patterns, but it only knows how to continue text. Then comes residency (supervised fine-tuning): it studies thousands of example conversations and learns to answer like an assistant. Last comes feedback from supervisors (preference tuning): it learns which of its own answers people prefer. The first stage takes almost all the effort. Everything after it is small by comparison, which is why companies can adapt an existing model instead of building one. Mechanism Pretraining : next-token prediction on a huge general corpus. Produces a base model that continues text but does not reliably follow instructions. This stage uses >95% of total compute. Continued pretraining (domain-adaptive pretraining): more next-token training on domain text (legal, medical, code, a new language) to shift knowledge and vocabulary use. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) / instruction tuning: train on curated (instruction, response) conversations so the model learns to act as an assistant. Preference optimisation : train on comparisons ("response A is better than B") via RLHF or DPO, and increasingly on verifiable rewards (tests pass, maths answer correct) to improve helpfulness, safety and reasoning. Random weights Pretraining 10T+ tokens Base model completes text Continued pretraining optional, domain SFT 10k–1M conversations Preference / RL comparisons, rewards Assistant model instruct / chat Weights start random; the model outputs gibberish (loss ≈ ln(vocab size)). Months on thousands of GPUs predicting the next token of web pages, books, code and papers. The model absorbs grammar, facts, reasoning patterns. A base model asked "What is the capital of France?" may continue with more quiz questions instead of answering. Optional: extend with domain or recent data; risk of forgetting general skills if the mix is not balanced. SFT teaches the conversation format and helpful behaviour from examples of ideal answers. Preference and RL stages shape tone, refusal behaviour, honesty and multi-step reasoning beyond what demonstrations can teach. The released "instruct" or "chat" model. Most applications use this, not the base model. The training pipeline. Each stage starts from the previous checkpoint. Compute drops by orders of magnitude after pretraining, which is why customisation (chapter 13) is affordable. Example: base vs instruct Prompt "Write a haiku about Kubernetes". A base model may continue: "Write a haiku about Docker. Write a haiku about…" because lists of prompts are common online. The instruct model writes the haiku. Fine-tuning for a narrow format usually starts from the instruct model; continued pretraining usually starts from the base model. The numbers How lopsided the stages are for an 8-billion-parameter model (illustrative token counts): Stage Training tokens Pretraining 15 trillion Supervised fine-tuning: 100,000 conversations × 600 tokens 60 million Preference tuning: 50,000 pairs a few hundred million, counting the extra passes 15 trillion ÷ 60 million = 250,000: pretraining reads a quarter of a million times more text than fine-tuning. At about 500,000 GPU-hours, pretraining costs millions of dollars; fine-tuning the same model can take a few GPU-hours. Code The program works out the GPU-hours of each training stage for an 8B model and each stage’s share of the total compute. Change the token counts in STAGES , for example a much bigger fine-tuning set, and run it again. Where the training compute goes, in real Python. The token counts and GPU speed are illustrative. Primary sources Ouyang et al. (2022), Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback The SFT then preference-tuning recipe behind chat assistants. Gururangan et al. (2020), Don’t Stop Pretraining Continued pretraining on domain text, and when it helps. Llama Team (2024), The Llama 3 Herd of Models A full account of every stage for a modern open model. Lambert et al. (2024), Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training An open, reproducible post-training recipe with its data.

title: Training corpora: collection, licensing, filtering, deduplication, quality and contamination
text: Intuition A model is mostly what it reads. Training data starts as an enormous, messy pile, much of the web, and is then cleaned like gold panning: wash away spam and junk, keep the language you want, score the rest for quality, and throw out the copies. Most of the pile is discarded. Two things need special care. Duplicates waste money and make the model memorise. And if test questions leak into the training pile, the model can ace the test without having learned anything, like a student who saw the exam paper in advance. Mechanism Collection : web crawls (Common Crawl is the common starting point), code repositories, books, academic papers, encyclopedias, forums, licensed datasets, and synthetic data generated by other models. Licensing and consent : copyright, terms of service, robots.txt preferences, personal data laws, and open-data licences constrain what may be used.
