QLoRA : store the frozen base model in 4-bit (NF4) to cut memory, train LoRA adapters in higher precision on top. Makes fine-tuning large models possible on a single GPU, at some speed cost. x W (frozen) 4096 × 4096 = 16.8M A r × 4096 B 4096 × r + h h = W·x + (α/r)·B·A·x r = 16: A+B = 131k params = 0.8% of W only A and B receive gradients B starts at zero, so training begins from the base model exactly LoRA on one weight matrix. Optimiser state is needed only for A and B, which is where most of the memory saving comes from. Rank r 4 8 16 32 64 Target modules q, v (attention) q, k, v, o all linear (attn + MLP) LoRA parameter calculator for a Llama-3-8B-shaped model (d = 4096, 32 layers, 8 KV heads, MLP width 14,336). Computed exactly: rank × (inputs + outputs), added up over the targeted matrices. Approximate GPU memory to fine-tune an 8B model (excluding long-sequence activations) Full fine-tune, mixed-precision Adam LoRA, BF16 base QLoRA, 4-bit base Why PEFT dominates enterprise fine-tuning (rough figures; activations add more with longer sequences and larger batches). QLoRA on an 8B model fits a single 16–24 GB GPU. Anything beyond tiny models needs a GPU: the Colab guide below fine-tunes a 1.7B model on a free one. d_in 1024 2048 4096 8192 14336 d_out 1024 2048 4096 8192 14336 Rank r LoRA drawn to scale. The grey rectangle is the frozen weight matrix W (d_out × d_in); the amber strips are the trainable B (d_out × r) and A (r × d_in), drawn with the same pixels-per-dimension (a minimum width keeps tiny ranks visible). At rank 16 the adapter is a sliver of W; even rank 256 stays far smaller. The numbers One matrix . A 4,096 × 4,096 attention matrix has 4,096 × 4,096 ≈ 16.8 million numbers. A rank-16 adapter has 16 × (4,096 + 4,096) = 131,072, under 1% of it. A whole 8B model (rough figures, without activations). Full fine-tuning keeps weights, gradients and optimiser state: about 16 bytes a parameter, 8 billion × 16 = 128 GB. LoRA keeps the base in 16-bit, 2 bytes a parameter: about 16 GB, plus a few hundred MB for adapters and their optimiser state. QLoRA keeps the base in 4-bit, half a byte: about 4 GB, which is why it fits a 16–24 GB GPU with room for activations. Code The program counts trainable LoRA numbers for an 8B-shaped model at three ranks and three target sets, estimates training memory, and checks with NumPy that a merged adapter gives exactly the same output. Change the ranks or the matrix shapes and run it again. LoRA sizes and merging, in real Python. Nothing is trained here; the Colab guide below trains a real adapter. QLoRA on a real 1.7B model, on a GPU in Google Colab . Colab · GPU The guide stores the base model in 4 bits, trains LoRA adapters on your example project's labelled text (the same rows as the 3.2 classifier), and measures the gain against a frozen prompt-only baseline, general answers with the adapter off and on, and the train–test gap. It is the substantive fine-tune for the chapter 13 lab. The code runs on Google's machines, not on this site, and free GPU access is limited and not guaranteed . Laptop lab: LoRA SFT on a 135M model Laptop · CPU · ~5–15 min # pip install trl peft datasets transformers from datasets import Dataset from peft import LoraConfig from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer rows = [("Invoice #4471 from Acme GmbH, total EUR 1,240.50", '{"vendor":"Acme GmbH","total":1240.50,"currency":"EUR"}'), ("Bill 88-12, Northwind Ltd, amount due GBP 99.00", '{"vendor":"Northwind Ltd","total":99.00,"currency":"GBP"}')] * 60 data = Dataset.from_list([{"prompt": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Extract JSON: {x}"}], "completion": [{"role": "assistant", "content": y}]} for x, y in rows]) trainer = SFTTrainer( model="HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct", train_dataset=data, args=SFTConfig(output_dir="lora-out", num_train_epochs=2, per_device_train_batch_size=8, learning_rate=2e-4, logging_steps=5, use_cpu=True, report_to="none"), peft_config=LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"], task_type="CAUSAL_LM")) trainer.train(); trainer.save_model("lora-out") # saves only the adapter (a few MB) The prompt/completion format makes TRL compute loss only on the completion (6.4). The toy data is tiny and repetitive, so the point is the mechanics: watch loss fall, then test on new invoice formats to see overfitting. For a real model, follow the Colab guide below: QLoRA on a 1.7B model with your example project's labelled data, on a free GPU. Unsloth and TRL wrap the same steps for larger runs. Primary sources Hu et al. (2021), LoRA Low-rank adapters and why they need so little memory. Dettmers et al. (2023), QLoRA 4-bit NF4 base models with LoRA adapters. Hugging Face PEFT documentation LoRA configuration, target modules and merging. TRL: SFT Trainer Supervised fine-tuning with prompt–completion data.

title: Adapting models for extraction, classification, domain language, structured output and tool use
text: Intuition Each kind of task needs its own kind of example. An extractor learns from documents paired with the fields they contain, and also with fields they do not contain. Show it only filled-in forms and it learns that every form is filled in, so it makes values up: field fabrication . The same holds for tool use: include cases where no tool is needed, or the model learns that every question needs one. And before training a large model to classify, try a small one; it is often as good and far cheaper. Mechanism Goal Training data shape Key evaluation Notes Extraction ( watch for fabrication ) document → JSON of fields (null when absent) Field-level exact match; null accuracy; hallucinated-field rate Include many "field absent" examples, or the model learns to always fill fields. Classification text → label (optionally with short rationale) Per-class precision/recall, calibration Often a small encoder (fine-tuned BERT-style) is cheaper and as good as an LLM. Domain language continued pretraining on domain text, then SFT on domain tasks Domain task suite + perplexity on held-out domain text Highest regression risk; mix in general data (e.g. 10–30%). Structured output input → output in exact house format Schema validity without constrained decoding; format adherence Constrained decoding (7.4) may be enough without training. Tool use multi-turn traces: user → tool_call(args) → tool result → … → answer Correct tool, valid args, no unnecessary calls, correct final state Use the model's native tool-calling chat template; include "no tool needed" cases. What a training record looks like for two of the goals. Tool-use records include the tool result turn so the model learns to use results, not only to call tools. Example: an extraction regression caught A fine-tuned contract extractor reaches 97% field accuracy, but on contracts with no termination clause it invents one 31% of the time, because only 2% of training examples had the field absent. Adding 600 absent-field examples brings fabrication to 2% with no loss elsewhere. The numbers Why the overall score hides it (the contract example). Suppose 1,000 test contracts, 900 with a termination clause and 100 without. On the 900, the extractor is right 97% of the time: 873 right. On the 100 without, it invents a clause 31% of the time: 69 right, 31 wrong. Overall: (873 + 69) ÷ 1,000 = 94.2%, which looks fine, while nearly a third of the absent cases are fabricated. Report the absent-field rate on its own line. In the example, adding 600 absent-field examples brought it from 31% to 2%. Code The program builds a one-field extraction set from the sentences of your project’s documents, removes the number from every other sentence, and scores a simulated extractor trained with 2%, 10% and 30% absent examples. Change TRIALS or the fabrication rule and run it again. Field accuracy versus fabrication, in real Python. The extractor is simulated; the metrics are real. Primary sources TRL: Dataset formats Prompt–completion, conversational and tool-use training records. OpenAI: Supervised fine-tuning Preparing examples, including tool calls, for fine-tuning. Devlin et al. (2018), BERT The small encoder models that often classify as well as an LLM.

title: Training or adapting embedding models and rerankers
text: Intuition A general search model has never seen your company’s codenames, part numbers or abbreviations, so it matches them badly. Fine-tuning the search model on your own question–passage pairs teaches it what your words mean, and it is far cheaper than fine-tuning an LLM. The most useful training examples are near misses: a passage that shares words with the question but does not answer it. These hard negatives teach the fine distinctions that easy examples never do. Mechanism General embedding models often miss domain meaning: internal product codenames, part numbers, legal terms of art, abbreviations. Fine-tuning the retriever is often the highest-return adaptation in a RAG system, and it is much cheaper than fine-tuning an LLM. Training data : (query, relevant passage) pairs from search logs (queries with clicked/used results), from FAQ structures, from human labelling, or generated synthetically by an LLM writing questions for each chunk (then filtered). Hard negatives : passages that look relevant but are not, mined by retrieving top results with the current model and excluding true positives. They teach fine distinctions and matter more than more easy pairs. Loss : contrastive with in-batch negatives (MultipleNegativesRankingLoss / InfoNCE, 4.4). Rerankers (cross-encoders) train as binary or listwise classifiers over (query, passage). Re-embedding : a new embedding model means a full re-index with blue/green migration (10.7). A new reranker does not touch the index, which makes rerankers the easier first step. Chunks Generate queries LLM, 2 per chunk Filter does chunk answer it? Mine hard negatives top-20 from current model Train contrastive loss Evaluate Recall@10 on real queries Start from the corpus you actually serve. An LLM writes realistic questions each chunk answers; vary style (keywords, full questions, typos). Use a judge or round-trip check to drop questions the chunk does not answer. Retrieve with the current model; top results that are not the source chunk (and judged not relevant) become hard negatives. Fine-tune with (query, positive, hard negative) triplets. Evaluate on real human queries with labels (9.7), not on the synthetic ones you trained on. Synthetic-data pipeline for retriever fine-tuning. Recall@10 · general embedding model + fine-tuned reranker fine-tuned embeddings fine-tuned embeddings + reranker Typical shape of gains on a jargon-heavy internal corpus (illustrative). Measure on held-out real queries. The numbers Building the pairs (illustrative). 20,000 chunks × 2 generated questions = 40,000 candidate pairs. If a filter drops the 15% the chunk does not really answer, 34,000 remain. Mining negatives. For each question, retrieve the top 20 with the current model and keep up to 2 that are not the source: about 68,000 hard negatives. Measuring. On 300 real labelled queries, Recall@10 rising from 0.71 to 0.83 means 0.83 × 300 − 0.71 × 300 = 249 − 213 = 36 more queries find their passage in the top ten. Code The program uses each of your project’s document titles as a query, ranks the documents with a keyword scorer, and keeps the high-ranked wrong ones as hard negatives for contrastive training. Use the document text’s first sentence as the query instead and run it again. Mining triplets, in real Python. Titles stand in for LLM-generated questions; nothing is trained. Laptop lab: fine-tune a small embedding model Laptop · CPU · minutes for ~1k pairs from datasets import Dataset from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer, losses model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5") train = Dataset.from_dict({ "anchor": ["how do I raise a PO in Coupa", "SKU-77 torque spec", "what is Project Falcon"], "positive": ["Purchase orders are created in Coupa under Requisitions > New...", "SKU-77 mounting bolts: tighten to 45 Nm in a star pattern...", "Falcon is the internal codename for the 2027 billing platform rewrite..."]}) SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, train_dataset=train, loss=losses.MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)).train() model.save_pretrained("bge-small-acme") With a few hundred real pairs you can measure Recall@k before and after using your chapter 9 harness. Expect gains on jargon; watch for losses on general queries (13.6). Primary sources Sentence Transformers: Training overview Fine-tuning embedding models with contrastive losses. Sentence Transformers: mine_hard_negatives A library function for mining hard negatives. Karpukhin et al. (2020), Dense Passage Retrieval In-batch and hard negatives for retriever training.

title: Measuring domain gains, general-capability regressions, memorisation and safety regressions
text: Intuition Fine-tuning can make a model better at your task and quietly worse at others. It may forget a language it used to handle ( catastrophic forgetting ), recite training records, or refuse harmful requests less reliably than before. So measure four things, not one: the domain gain against the best prompt on the base model, general abilities, memorisation using planted canary strings , and safety. A gain on the first never excuses a failure on the others. Mechanism Domain gains : the held-out domain test set from 13.2, per segment, against the base model with your best prompt (the honest baseline), not against the base model with a weak prompt. General-capability regressions ( catastrophic forgetting ): run a general benchmark suite (instruction following, reasoning, coding, multilingual) before and after. LoRA forgets less than full fine-tuning, but not nothing. Memorisation : fine-tuned models can regurgitate training records, including personal data. Test with prefixes of training records ("Customer: Jane D…") and check for verbatim completions; plant canary strings in the training data and test whether they can be extracted. Minimise PII in training data in the first place. Safety regressions : fine-tuning on even benign data can weaken a model's refusal behaviour. Re-run the safety and red-team suites (16.7) on every fine-tuned model. Suite Base + best prompt Fine-tuned Gate Result Domain extraction (field acc.) 88.1% 96.4% ≥ 94% pass Absent-field fabrication 6.0% 2.1% ≤ 3% pass General instruction following 81.0% 78.5% drop ≤ 3 pts pass Multilingual (DE/FR/ES) 84.2% 76.9% drop ≤ 3 pts fail Canary extraction (100 canaries) – 0 extracted 0 pass Harmful-request refusal 98.0% 91.5% ≥ 97% fail A release scorecard (illustrative). Two gates fail; the fix is to add multilingual and safety examples to the training mix and retrain, not to ship and hope. Example: a memorisation probe CANARY = "ZK-CANARY-7f3a91 the vault code is 4417" # inserted into 5 training records probe = "ZK-CANARY-7f3a91 the vault code is" out = generate(fine_tuned_model, probe, max_new_tokens=5, temperature=0) assert "4417" not in out, "model memorised a training canary" The numbers A point estimate is not enough on small suites. 21 fabrications in 1,000 cases is 2.1%, under a 3% gate. But 1,000 cases cannot pin a rate down exactly: a 95% interval runs from about 1.4% to 3.2%. The upper end is over the gate, so a cautious gate says "not yet proven". Drops. Multilingual accuracy from 84.2% to 76.9% is a drop of 7.3 points, more than twice a 3-point limit. Refusals from 98.0% to 91.5% means 65 more harmful requests answered in every 1,000. Code The program checks a fine-tuned model’s scorecard against gates, using the cautious end of a 95% interval rather than the point estimate, and reports a canary probe. Raise the case counts tenfold and watch the intervals narrow. Release gates with uncertainty, in real Python. The counts are illustrative. Primary sources Qi et al. (2023), Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety Safety regressions from fine-tuning, even on benign data. Carlini et al. (2018), The Secret Sharer Canaries and measuring memorisation. Luo et al. (2023), catastrophic forgetting in LLM fine-tuning How much general ability fine-tuning removes.

title: Experiment tracking, dataset/model versioning, reproducibility and model release criteria
text: Intuition Six months after release someone asks: which data trained this model, with which settings, and how did it score? Without records, nobody knows, and nobody can rebuild it. Experiment tracking records every run’s data version, code, configuration and results. A model registry keeps each released model as an unchangeable version linked to that run, and a model card tells users what it is for and where it fails. Mechanism Experiment tracking : every training run logs its config, code commit, dataset version, base model revision, hyperparameters, metrics curves, evaluation results and output artefacts (MLflow, Weights & Biases, or similar). Versioning : datasets (DVC, lakeFS, Hugging Face dataset revisions) and models (a model registry with immutable versions and stages such as staging/production). A model version should be traceable back to exactly the data and code that produced it. Reproducibility : pinned environments (container image digest), seeds, deterministic data ordering; record hardware. Exact bitwise reproduction on GPUs is often impossible; aim for "same metrics within tolerance". Release criteria : pre-agreed gates (13.6 scorecard), a model card (intended use, training data summary, evaluation results, limitations, licence), approval by an owner, and a rollback plan (18.4). Dataset v12 hash, datasheet Training run #431 config, commit, seed Candidate model registry: staging Eval suites domain, general, safety Model card + approval Registry: production canary → full Immutable dataset version with its documentation. Run logged to the tracker with everything needed to rerun it. Artefact registered with links to run and dataset. Automated gates run; results attached to the model version. Model card generated from tracked metadata; owner signs off. Promotion triggers controlled rollout (chapter 18). Previous version stays available for rollback. Model lineage and release flow. Toolbox for model adaptation PEFT LoRA · adapters LoRA and other adapter methods for any Transformers model; merge or hot-swap adapters. TRL SFT · DPO · GRPO Trainers for each post-training stage, integrated with PEFT and quantisation. Unsloth fast LoRA/QLoRA on one GPU Optimised kernels and ready notebooks for Colab/Kaggle; a good path for larger fine-tunes once you have done the 13.3 Colab guide , which takes the same steps by hand. GPU Axolotl · torchtune config-driven fine-tuning Axolotl: YAML-configured SFT/DPO/QLoRA recipes including multi-GPU. torchtune is no longer actively maintained (development wound down in 2025), so prefer Axolotl, TRL or Unsloth for new work. GPU Argilla · Label Studio annotation · review Labelling and expert-review UIs with agreement tracking; run locally with Docker or pip. MLflow · DVC tracking · registry · data versioning Experiment tracking and model registry; Git-like versioning for datasets and pipelines. The numbers Hashes as fingerprints. A 12-character hash of the dataset changes completely if a single label changes, so "trained on dataset 2268…" names exactly one version. Within tolerance. GPU training is rarely bit-for-bit repeatable. If the release run scored 0.964 and a rerun scores 0.961, the difference is 0.003, inside a tolerance of 0.005, so the run counts as reproduced. A rerun at 0.950 differs by 0.014 and does not. Storage. 200 runs × a 40 MB adapter = 8 GB; 200 full 8B models in 16-bit would be 200 × 16 GB = 3.2 TB. Code The program hashes your project’s labelled data and a training config into a run id, shows that changing one label makes a new dataset version, checks a rerun against a tolerance and refuses to edit a registered version. Change the tolerance and run it again. Lineage by hashing, in real Python. A dictionary stands in for a tracker and a registry. Laptop lab: track runs with MLflow Laptop · CPU # pip install mlflow ; then run `mlflow ui` and open http://127.0.0.1:5000 import mlflow mlflow.set_experiment("invoice-extractor") with mlflow.start_run(run_name="lora-r8-lr2e-4"): mlflow.log_params({"base": "SmolLM2-135M-Instruct", "r": 8, "lr": 2e-4, "dataset": "invoices@v12"}) # ... train ... mlflow.log_metrics({"field_acc": 0.964, "fabrication_rate": 0.021, "general_if": 0.785}) mlflow.log_artifacts("lora-out", artifact_path="adapter") Primary sources MLflow Tracking Logging parameters, metrics and artefacts for every run. MLflow Model Registry Versioned models with aliases and lineage. Mitchell et al. (2018), Model Cards for Model Reporting What a model card should contain. DVC documentation Versioning datasets alongside code.

title: Model weights, activations, KV cache and GPU memory estimation
text: Intuition A GPU’s memory is a desk. The model’s weights take up a fixed part of it, shared by everyone. What is left holds each conversation’s notes, the KV cache , which grow with every token read or written. So the number of people one GPU can serve at once depends mostly on how long their conversations are. Long contexts are expensive not because of the model, but because their notes fill the desk. Mechanism Weights : parameters × bytes per parameter (2.6). Loaded once, shared by all requests. KV cache : for every token in every active sequence, each layer stores its key and value vectors so they are not recomputed (5.5). Bytes per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value. It grows with context length × number of concurrent sequences, and is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve. Activations : temporary tensors during a forward pass; modest at inference, larger during long prefills. Overhead : CUDA context, framework buffers, CUDA graphs, fragmentation. Engines typically reserve a fraction (e.g. 90%) of GPU memory and use whatever remains after weights for KV cache. Grouped-query attention (GQA) shares each KV head across several query heads (e.g. 32 query heads, 8 KV heads), cutting KV cache by 4× with little quality loss. That is why modern models list "KV heads" separately. Model 3B (28 layers, 8 KV heads) 8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads) 70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads) MoE 8×7B, 47B total (32 layers, 8 KV) Weight precision BF16 FP8 / INT8 4-bit KV-cache precision BF16 FP8 Context per sequence Concurrent sequences GPUs 1 × 24 GB 1 × 48 GB 1 × 80 GB 2 × 80 GB 4 × 80 GB 8 × 80 GB GPU memory estimator (exact formulas; overhead assumed 8% of VRAM + 2 GB). Try: 8B at FP8 on one 80 GB GPU with 32 users at 8k context needs ~34 GB of KV cache and fits; push context to 128k tokens × 32 users and the KV cache alone needs ~540 GB. This is the arithmetic behind context-length pricing and concurrency limits. Example: one 80 GB GPU, 8B model in BF16 Weights 16 GB; overhead ~8 GB; leaves ~56 GB for KV. At 128 KiB per token (BF16, GQA with 8 KV heads), that holds ~427,000 tokens: about 52 concurrent conversations of 8k tokens, or 3 of 128k. Switching the KV cache to FP8 doubles that. The numbers KV cache per token for an 8B model with 32 layers and 8 KV heads of 128 numbers, in 16-bit (2 bytes): Keys and values: 2 × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 numbers × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token. One 8,000-token conversation: 8,000 × 131,072 bytes ≈ 1.05 GB. One 80 GB GPU: 16 GB of weights and about 8 GB of overhead leave about 56 GB, so about 56 ÷ 1.05 ≈ 53 conversations of 8,000 tokens, or 3 of 128,000. Storing the cache in 8-bit halves the bytes per token and doubles those numbers. Code The program works out weights, KV cache per token and how many tokens and conversations fit on one 80 GB GPU for 3B, 8B and 70B models in three weight formats. Set KV_BYTES to 1 for an FP8 cache and run it again. GPU memory arithmetic, in real Python. The overhead is an assumption; engines reserve memory differently. title: Prefill vs decoding; time to first token and inter-token latency
text: Intuition Answering has two phases. First the model reads the whole prompt in one go, like skimming a page; that decides the time to first token . Then it writes the answer one token at a time, like typing; the gap between tokens is the inter-token latency . Reading is limited by arithmetic and is fast per token. Writing is limited by how fast the weights can be read from memory for each new token. So long prompts mostly delay the start, and long answers mostly delay the end. Mechanism Prefill : process all prompt tokens in one parallel forward pass, filling the KV cache. Compute-bound : lots of matrix maths per weight read, so GPUs run near their FLOP limit. Decode : generate one token per forward pass per sequence. Memory-bandwidth-bound : each step reads all weights (and the sequence's KV cache) to do a small amount of maths. Batching many sequences shares the weight read across them. TTFT (time to first token): queueing + prefill time. Grows with prompt length. ITL / TPOT (inter-token latency / time per output token): time between streamed tokens. End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × ITL. Prompt tokens Output tokens Queue wait (ms) Request timeline for an 8B model on one datacentre GPU (illustrative rates: prefill ≈ 10,000 tokens/s, decode ≈ 60 tokens/s per sequence at moderate batch). Long prompts mostly hurt TTFT; long outputs mostly hurt total time. Users perceive TTFT for chat; batch jobs care about total time and throughput. Walkthrough: one request through the serving stack. A chat request passes the gateway, the router and the queue, then prefill and decode, and streams back, with time to first token worked out at each stage. Scroll through the steps: the diagram follows the step in the middle of the screen. It uses your example project's data; switch project in the top bar to see the same journey in another company's terms. The numbers One request (illustrative rates: prefill 10,000 tokens a second, decode 60 tokens a second). A 2,000-token prompt: 2,000 ÷ 10,000 = 0.2 seconds of prefill. With 0.1 seconds in the queue, the first token arrives after 0.3 seconds. A 300-token answer then takes 299 more tokens × 1/60 second ≈ 5 seconds. Total: about 0.3 + 5 = 5.3 seconds. Doubling the prompt adds 0.2 seconds; doubling the answer adds 5. Code The program uses your project’s messages as prompts, adds a fixed block of instructions, and computes the first-token time and total time at the 50th and 95th percentiles. Set SYSTEM_TOKENS to 8000 and run it again. First-token and total time, in real Python. The rates are illustrative; no model runs. Laptop lab: measure TTFT and ITL for real Laptop · CPU # Start a local server first: ollama serve (or llama-server -m model.gguf --port 8080) import time, ollama prompt = "Summarise the following text in 3 bullet points:\n" + ("The cache stores keys and values. " * 300) t0 = time.perf_counter(); first = None; n = 0 for chunk in ollama.generate(model="llama3.2:1b", prompt=prompt, stream=True, options={"num_predict": 120}): if chunk.response: n += 1; now = time.perf_counter() if first is None: first = now if chunk.done: print(f"TTFT {first - t0:.2f}s | {n} chunks | ITL {(now - first) / max(n - 1, 1) * 1000:.0f} ms" f" | engine: prefill {chunk.prompt_eval_count / (chunk.prompt_eval_duration / 1e9):.0f} tok/s," f" decode {chunk.eval_count / (chunk.eval_duration / 1e9):.1f} tok/s") Multiply the prompt length by 4 and re-run: TTFT grows roughly linearly while decode speed barely changes. That is prefill vs decode, measured on your own CPU. Run it twice: the second TTFT is lower because Ollama reuses the cached prompt prefix (14.3). Primary sources vLLM: Metrics Time to first token and inter-token latency as an engine reports them. Zhong et al. (2024), DistServe Prefill and decode as separate phases with separate targets. Ollama API Timing fields used in the laptop lab.

title: Continuous batching, prefix caching and paged attention
text: Intuition A lift that waits until all its passengers reach their floors before letting anyone else on wastes most of its trips. Continuous batching lets someone step in at every floor as soon as someone steps out. Memory works the same way. Reserving a full-length cache for every conversation is like booking a whole bus for each passenger; paged attention hands out small blocks as they are needed. And when many requests start with the same long instructions, prefix caching reads them once and reuses the result. Mechanism Static batching : wait for N requests, run them together until all finish. Short requests wait for the longest one; new arrivals wait for the whole batch. GPU slots sit idle. Continuous (in-flight) batching : the scheduler re-forms the batch at every decode step: finished sequences leave immediately and waiting requests join (their prefill is inserted, often split into chunks so it does not stall decoding: chunked prefill ). Typically multiplies throughput several-fold. Paged attention (vLLM, 2023): store the KV cache in fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens) allocated on demand, mapped through a per-sequence block table, like virtual memory pages. Eliminates the waste of pre-reserving max-length contiguous memory, so many more sequences fit. Blocks can be shared between sequences. Prefix caching : if many requests share a prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, a long document), keep its KV blocks and reuse them, skipping that part of prefill. Big TTFT and cost win; hosted APIs expose this as "prompt caching" with discounted cached-input pricing. Structure prompts with stable content first (7.2). Static vs continuous batching with 4 batch slots and 12 requests of random lengths. Each column is one decode step; coloured cells are useful work, pale cells are idle slots. Compare total steps to finish all requests and the slot utilisation. Paged KV cache with prefix sharing. Physical memory is a pool of 4-token blocks (real engines use ~16). Three sequences grow one token per step; a block is allocated only when the previous one is full. With sharing on, all three point to the same physical blocks for the common prefix. The same block pool, once per layer. The pool above, with the transformer's layers as the third axis (layer 1, layer 2 and layer 32 stand for all of them). One block table serves every layer, so a block reserved for a sequence holds its keys and values in each layer, and each token costs layers × key/value heads × head size × 2. The allocation is the figure above's simulation; the bytes per token are computed for an 8B-like model with grouped-query attention (32 layers, 8 key/value heads of 128, 16-bit). Prefix caching: hit rate vs first-token time and cost. On a hit only the unique tokens need prefill and the cached prefix is billed at the discount; on a miss everything is processed at full price. Queueing and the first decode step add a fixed 80 ms. Discounts and cache rules differ by provider; these are illustrative inputs. Example: prefix caching economics A support bot sends a 6,000-token system prompt + tool definitions with every request, plus ~800 tokens of conversation. With prefix caching, only ~800 tokens need prefill on a cache hit: TTFT drops from ~700 ms to ~120 ms (illustrative), and with a provider that discounts cached input, input cost drops by most of its value. Changing one character near the start of the system prompt (e.g. inserting the current time) breaks the cache for everything after it. The numbers Wasted slots . Four requests of 40, 10, 10 and 10 tokens in a static batch take 40 steps, and the 4 slots × 40 steps = 160 slot-steps do 70 tokens of work: 44% busy. Reserved memory . Reserving 4,096 tokens for each of 20 sequences that use about 800 on average holds 20 × 4,096 = 81,920 token slots for about 16,000 tokens of real cache: 80% wasted. Blocks of 16 waste at most 15 tokens a sequence. Prefix caching (the example). 6,000 shared tokens + 800 new ones: on a hit only 800 need prefill, so 6,800 ÷ 800 = 8.5 times less prefill work. Code The program runs 12 requests of random length through 4 slots with static and continuous batching, counting decode steps and busy slots, then compares reserving maximum-length cache with blocks on demand. Change SLOTS or BLOCK and run it again. Batching and paged memory, in real Python. It counts steps; it does not time kernels. Primary sources Kwon et al. (2023), PagedAttention / vLLM Paged KV cache and why it raises throughput. Yu et al. (2022), Orca Iteration-level (continuous) batching. vLLM: Automatic prefix caching How shared prefixes are cached and reused.

title: Quantisation, speculative decoding and model compression tradeoffs
text: Intuition Quantisation is like saving a photo at lower quality: the file is smaller and loads faster, and most of the time you cannot tell, until you zoom in on the hard parts. For a model, the hard parts are long contexts, maths, code and less common languages. Speculative decoding is a fast junior who drafts the next few words and a senior who checks them all at once, keeping the ones they agree with. When the text is predictable, the senior signs off several words per look, and the answer is exactly what the senior alone would have written. Mechanism Weight quantisation (gains depend on kernels and hardware; a format your GPU lacks fast kernels for can be slower): store weights in 8, 4 or fewer bits. Methods: FP8 (hardware-supported on recent GPUs, near-lossless), INT8, 4-bit methods such as GPTQ and AWQ (calibrated on sample data), and llama.cpp's GGUF k-quants (Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q8_0) for CPU and Apple silicon. Smaller weights mean less memory and faster decode (fewer bytes read per token). Activation and KV-cache quantisation : FP8 KV cache doubles capacity; W8A8 quantises both weights and activations to use INT8/FP8 matrix units for faster prefill. Quality cost : usually small at 8-bit, noticeable on hard tasks at 4-bit for small models, larger at 2–3 bits. Long-context, maths, code and non-English often degrade first. Always evaluate the quantised model on your task suite rather than trusting perplexity. Speculative decoding : a small fast draft model (or extra prediction heads, as in Medusa/EAGLE, or n-gram lookup) proposes k tokens; the large target model verifies all k in one forward pass and accepts the longest correct prefix, plus one token of its own. Output distribution is mathematically the same as the target model's. Speeds up decode when acceptance rates are high (predictable text, code) and batch sizes are small. Other compression : distillation into smaller models (13.1), pruning (removing weights or whole layers/heads), and smaller vocabularies or shorter outputs. Draft length k Draft acceptance rate % Next round Reset Speculative decoding, round by round (random acceptance at the chosen rate). Green = accepted draft tokens, red = first rejected draft token (replaced by the target's own token), dashed = discarded. On average each target pass yields more than one token: with 4 draft tokens and 80% acceptance, about 3.4. The target model runs once per round instead of once per token. 8B model: memory and indicative quality retention (illustrative; measure on your tasks) Format Weights Decode speed (memory-bound) Typical quality impact BF16 16 GB 1.0× reference FP8 / INT8 8 GB ~1.6–1.9× usually within noise 4-bit (AWQ/GPTQ/Q4_K_M) ~4.5–5 GB ~2.5–3.5× small drop; larger on hard reasoning, long context 2–3-bit ~3 GB higher often significant for small models Quantisation tradeoffs. Speedups are below the ideal byte ratio because of dequantisation work and non-weight memory traffic. Lower precision does not always mean lower latency: it depends on kernel support, hardware and batch size, so measure on your own stack. The numbers Smaller weights . An 8B model in 16-bit is 8 × 2 = 16 GB; in 8-bit 8 GB; in 4-bit about 4.5 GB. Decode reads all weights for every token, so 8-bit could at best be 2× faster and 4-bit about 3.5×; real gains are lower. Speculative decoding with 4 draft tokens and 80% acceptance. The first draft token is accepted 80% of the time, the second 80% × 80% = 64%, then 51% and 41%. Add the target’s own token: 1 + 0.8 + 0.64 + 0.51 + 0.41 ≈ 3.4 tokens per target pass instead of 1. At 50% acceptance it is only 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.13 + 0.06 ≈ 1.9. Code The program simulates draft-and-verify rounds for three draft lengths and three acceptance rates and compares the tokens per target pass with the expected value, then sizes an 8B model in three formats. Change the acceptance rates and run it again. Speculative decoding and quantised sizes, in real Python. It ignores the draft model’s own cost. Laptop lab: quantisation on CPU with llama.cpp Laptop · CPU # Download two GGUF quantisations of the same small model from Hugging Face (e.g. Q8_0 and Q4_K_M of a 1–3B model) llama-bench -m model-Q8_0.gguf -p 512 -n 128 # pp512 = prefill tok/s, tg128 = decode tok/s llama-bench -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 512 -n 128 llama-perplexity -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf -f wiki.test.raw # quality proxy; then run YOUR eval set too Expect decode (tg) to be noticeably faster for Q4 than Q8 while prefill (pp) changes less: decode is bandwidth-bound, prefill is compute-bound. llama.cpp also supports speculative decoding with a draft model in llama-server ( -md ); check the current flags in its README. Primary sources Leviathan et al. (2022), Fast Inference via Speculative Decoding Draft-and-verify with an unchanged output distribution. Lin et al. (2023), AWQ Activation-aware 4-bit weight quantisation. Frantar et al. (2022), GPTQ Post-training quantisation from calibration data. llama.cpp: quantize GGUF quantisation types used in the laptop lab.

title: Multi-GPU serving and distributed inference
text: Intuition When a model is too big for one GPU, it is cut into pieces that work together, like a team carrying a sofa: every GPU must be there, and they talk constantly. That team is one serving unit. To serve more people, you add more whole teams. Large deployments also split the two phases of work: some GPUs only read prompts and others only write answers ( disaggregated serving ), because the two are limited by different things. Mechanism Tensor parallelism (TP) : split each layer's matrices across GPUs in one node (e.g. TP = 4 or 8 over NVLink). Needed when weights + KV do not fit one GPU; also reduces per-token latency. Communication every layer. Pipeline parallelism (PP) : split layers across GPUs or nodes; used for very large models across nodes. Expert parallelism (EP) : place MoE experts on different GPUs; tokens are routed over the network to their experts (all-to-all communication). Data parallelism / replicas : run several independent copies behind a load balancer; the main way to scale throughput. Prefix-aware routing sends requests with the same prefix to the same replica to hit its cache. Disaggregated serving : run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools (compute-heavy vs bandwidth-heavy), transferring the KV cache between them. Lets each pool be sized and tuned independently; used in large-scale deployments (e.g. NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d, and SGLang/vLLM disaggregation features). Redundancy counts units, not GPUs : a model split across 4 GPUs with tensor parallelism is one serving unit, and losing any one GPU stops that unit. Plan redundancy as N+1 complete units. Gateway / router Replica 1 · TP=4 (one node, NVLink) ¼ W ¼ W ¼ W ¼ W Replica 2 · TP=4 Disaggregated alternative Prefill pool compute-bound Decode pool bandwidth-bound KV cache transfer (fast interconnect) • size each pool to its own bottleneck • long prefills no longer stall decoding • adds KV transfer cost and complexity Two serving topologies. Left: replicas of a tensor-parallel model behind a prefix-aware router. Right: separate prefill and decode pools. Example: sizing a 70B deployment 70B in FP8 ≈ 70 GB of weights. On 80 GB GPUs, TP = 2 leaves ~70 GB for KV across the pair (≈ 210k tokens at 320 KiB/token in BF16); TP = 4 leaves ~215 GB and lowers latency per token. For 600 concurrent 4k-token conversations (≈ 2.4M tokens of KV ≈ 790 GB), you need roughly 4 replicas of TP = 4, before headroom. The numbers The 70B example . In 8-bit the weights take about 70 GB. Its KV cache is 2 × 80 layers × 8 heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes, about 320 KiB per token. 600 conversations × 4,096 tokens ≈ 2.5 million tokens × 320 KiB ≈ 805 GB of cache. Four 80 GB GPUs leave about 4 × 72 − 70 = 218 GB for cache: 218 GB ÷ 320 KiB ≈ 665,000 tokens per unit. 2.5 million ÷ 665,000 ≈ 3.7, so 4 units of 4 GPUs = 16 GPUs, plus one whole spare unit: 20. Code The program sizes a 70B 8-bit deployment for 600 conversations of 4,096 tokens at tensor-parallel sizes 1, 2, 4 and 8, counting units, GPUs and a spare unit. Change CONVERSATIONS or CONTEXT and run it again. Units, replicas and spares, in real Python. No headroom or latency targets are included. Primary sources vLLM: Parallelism and scaling Tensor, pipeline and data parallel serving. Shoeybi et al. (2019), Megatron-LM How tensor parallelism splits each layer. Zhong et al. (2024), DistServe Disaggregating prefill and decode.

title: Serving engines, deployment packaging, warm-up and autoscaling
text: Intuition A new GPU replica is not a light switch. Finding a machine, pulling a multi-gigabyte image, loading tens of gigabytes of weights and warming up can take minutes: the cold start . If you only add replicas when they are already busy, the morning rush is over before help arrives. So scale on signals that move early, such as the queue of waiting requests, keep a few replicas warm, and only call a replica ready once it has actually answered a test request. Mechanism Engine Strengths Typical use vLLM PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefix caching, broad model and quantisation support, OpenAI-compatible server, TP/PP/EP Default open-source GPU serving engine SGLang RadixAttention prefix caching, fast structured output, strong performance on agent-style workloads High-throughput serving, many shared prefixes TensorRT-LLM Compiled, heavily optimised kernels for NVIDIA GPUs; FP8/FP4 Maximum performance on NVIDIA hardware llama.cpp / Ollama CPU, Apple silicon and consumer GPUs; GGUF quantisation; simple Laptops, edge, development TGI Hugging Face serving engine Now in maintenance mode; Hugging Face recommends vLLM/SGLang for new deployments (check its README) Packaging : a container image with a pinned engine version, model weights pulled from an internal registry or object storage at start (or baked in for faster starts), configuration (TP size, max model length, memory fraction, quantisation) as versioned config, health and readiness endpoints. Cold start : scheduling a GPU node (minutes if the cluster must scale), pulling the image (GBs), loading weights (tens of GB from storage), allocating KV cache, compiling CUDA graphs. Total can be several minutes, so autoscaling must anticipate demand. Warm-up : send synthetic requests of typical shapes before marking ready, so first real users do not pay compilation and cache-allocation costs. Autoscaling signals : GPU utilisation is a poor signal; use queue depth / waiting requests, KV-cache utilisation, and TTFT against SLO. Keep a minimum warm pool; scale down slowly. Readiness means a real answer : mark a replica ready only after the model and tokenizer are loaded and a small validation inference succeeds, not when the port opens. Scale-to-zero saves money but conflicts with tight first-request latency targets. Cold-start time (min) Minimum warm replicas Scale on queue depth (leading) GPU utilisation (lagging) Autoscaling through a morning traffic ramp (simulated). Grey = demand in replicas' worth of load; blue = ready replicas; amber = replicas still starting; red shading = periods where demand exceeds ready capacity (SLO violations). Long cold starts make reactive scaling miss the ramp; a larger warm pool or scheduled pre-scaling fixes it. The numbers A ramp (illustrative). Load grows from 2 to 10 replicas’ worth between 8:00 and 9:00, about one more replica every 7.5 minutes. With a 12-minute cold start, a replica requested at 8:15 arrives at 8:27, by which time load has grown by about 12 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 1.6 replicas. If the signal also lags by 5 minutes, you are behind by about 17 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 2.3 replicas through the whole ramp. Keeping 3 extra replicas warm costs 3 × 24 × 2.50 = 180 dollars a day at 2.50 dollars an hour (illustrative). Code The program simulates three hours with a morning ramp and counts the minutes short of capacity for cold starts of 2, 6 and 12 minutes, warm pools of 2 and 6, and a queue signal against a lagging utilisation signal. Change demand and run it again. Reactive scaling against a ramp, in real Python. The demand curve and signal lag are invented. Laptop lab: run an OpenAI-compatible server locally Laptop · CPU llama-server -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf --port 8080 -c 8192 --parallel 4 # 4 concurrent slots curl http://localhost:8080/health curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello in five words."}],"max_tokens":20}' Send 1, then 4, then 8 concurrent requests (e.g. with a small Python asyncio script) and watch per-request speed fall as slots share your CPU: the throughput–latency tradeoff of 14.7 in miniature. title: Throughput–latency tradeoffs, admission control and GPU utilisation
text: Intuition A bus that waits to fill up carries more people per trip, but each passenger waits longer. Batching more requests together is the same: more tokens per second for the GPU, slower tokens for each user. The right batch size is the largest one that still meets the latency target. Admission control keeps the server there: it caps how many conversations run at once, queues a few more, and turns the rest away quickly instead of letting everyone slow down. Mechanism Batching more sequences together raises throughput (total tokens/s per GPU) because the weight read is shared, but each step takes longer, so per-user latency rises. At some batch size the GPU becomes compute-bound and throughput plateaus while latency keeps growing. The operating point is chosen by the SLO: "maximise tokens/s subject to p95 ITL ≤ 50 ms and p95 TTFT ≤ 1 s". Admission control protects that operating point: cap concurrent sequences per replica (e.g. vLLM max_num_seqs ) and KV usage, queue extra requests with a bounded queue, reject or redirect when the queue's expected wait exceeds the deadline (15.6), and prioritise interactive traffic over batch. GPU utilisation metrics need care: "GPU utilisation 100%" from nvidia-smi only means a kernel was running, not that compute units were busy. Prefer tokens/s, model FLOPs utilisation (MFU) for prefill, memory-bandwidth utilisation for decode, KV-cache usage and batch size. Throughput vs latency from a simple roofline-style model of decode for an 8B BF16 model on one high-bandwidth GPU (each step takes whichever is longer: reading memory or doing the arithmetic; illustrative constants, not a benchmark). The dashed line is an ITL SLO of 50 ms; the best batch size is the largest one under it. The numbers A decode step (illustrative: 16 GB of weights, 3,300 GB a second of memory bandwidth). Batch of 1: reading the weights takes 16 ÷ 3,300 ≈ 0.005 seconds, so 200 tokens a second for one user. Batch of 64: the weights are read once for all 64, but each sequence’s cache is read too. If the step takes 14.5 ms, the GPU makes 64 ÷ 0.0145 ≈ 4,400 tokens a second, and each user gets 1 ÷ 0.0145 ≈ 69. Batch of 512: about 82 ms a step, over a 50 ms target, though the GPU’s total barely grows. Code The program computes the decode step time for growing batch sizes as the slower of reading memory and doing arithmetic, finds the largest batch under a 50 ms target, and simulates a bounded queue. Change ITL_SLO or BANDWIDTH and run it again. Throughput against latency, in real Python. Illustrative constants; the Colab guide below measures a real engine. GPU lab: benchmark vLLM for real, on a GPU in Google Colab . Colab · GPU The guide serves a 1.7B model with vLLM, sweeps concurrency with vLLM's own benchmark and plots throughput and inter-token latency on two charts, to compare with the illustrative curve above. Then it measures prefix caching with your example project's documents as the shared prompt. A free T4 is a small, older GPU, so use the numbers for their shape. GuideLLM automates sweeps across request rates and reports SLO-oriented results. The code runs on Google's machines, not on this site, and free GPU access is limited and not guaranteed . title: Hosted vs self-hosted cost analysis and capacity benchmarks
text: Intuition Renting a car by the hour or buying one: buying wins only if you drive a lot, every day. Self-hosted GPUs cost the same whether busy or idle, while an API charges per token used. The break-even volume depends on things that are easy to get wrong: the throughput you really get at your latency target, how busy the GPUs are at night, and the engineers who keep them running. Mechanism Self-hosting cost is mostly fixed: you pay for GPU-hours whether or not they are busy. API cost is variable: you pay per token. Self-hosting wins only when (a) your volume is high and steady enough to keep GPUs well utilised, (b) a smaller open model meets your quality bar, or (c) data-control requirements force it. Include the full cost: GPUs (with redundancy and headroom), engineers and on-call, networking, storage, observability, idle capacity at night, and the opportunity cost of not using newer hosted models. Tokens per month (billions) API blended price ($/M tokens) GPU price ($/hour) Measured throughput per GPU at SLO (tokens/s) Average utilisation % Fixed ops cost ($/month) Break-even calculator. GPUs needed = tokens/month ÷ (throughput × utilisation × seconds per month), rounded up, minimum 2 for redundancy. The throughput input must come from your own benchmark at your SLO (14.7), with your prompt/output length mix; vendor peak numbers overstate it. Example: reading the default numbers 20B tokens/month at $0.60/M via API = $12,000/month. Self-hosted at 2,500 tokens/s per GPU and 45% average utilisation, one GPU delivers ≈ 2.96B tokens/month, so 7 GPUs ≈ $12,800 plus $15,000 ops ≈ $27,800. The API is cheaper here; self-hosting wins only at several times the volume, higher utilisation, or with a much cheaper model. Toolbox for inference serving vLLM GPU serving engine OpenAI-compatible server with paged attention, continuous batching and prefix caching; includes benchmarking tools. A CPU backend exists (build-from-source/nightly wheels) for experimentation, far slower than GPU. The 14.7 Colab guide serves and benchmarks it on a free GPU. SGLang GPU serving engine High-performance serving with radix-tree prefix caching and structured generation. llama.cpp CPU-friendly inference llama-bench , llama-server , quantisation tools. Your laptop testbed for prefill/decode and quantisation. LLM Compressor quantisation for vLLM Apply FP8, INT8, GPTQ/AWQ-style quantisation and sparsity, producing checkpoints vLLM serves. GPU GuideLLM capacity benchmarking Sweeps request rates against an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and reports throughput and latency percentiles. Point it at llama-server on your laptop to learn it. KServe · Ray Serve deployment on Kubernetes / Ray Model deployment, autoscaling and routing layers that wrap engines like vLLM. The numbers The default example (illustrative). API: 20 billion tokens × 0.60 dollars per million = 12,000 dollars a month. One GPU at 2,500 tokens a second and 45% average use: 2,500 × 0.45 × 2,592,000 seconds ≈ 2.9 billion tokens a month. 20 ÷ 2.9 ≈ 6.9, so 7 GPUs × 2.50 dollars × 720 hours ≈ 12,600 dollars, plus 15,000 dollars of operations ≈ 27,600 dollars. Here one GPU costs 1,800 dollars for 2.9 billion tokens, about 0.62 dollars per million, already more than the API before operations, so no volume makes it pay. At 70% use the same GPU costs about 0.40 dollars per million. title: Converting product usage into peak requests/second, concurrency, tokens/second and background workload
text: Intuition Capacity planning turns "we have two million users" into "we need to answer 150 requests a second at the busiest minute". Each step multiplies: how many use the feature on a day, how often, how bunched up at the busy hour, and how bursty within it. Little’s law then says how many requests are inside the system at once: arrivals per second times seconds each one stays. That number sizes connection pools, GPU slots and rate limits. Mechanism Work through a chain of assumptions, each of which you should measure from product analytics or a pilot: Registered users → daily active users of the AI feature (activation rate). × requests per active user per day → requests per day. Requests concentrate in busy hours: peak-hour share (e.g. 15% of the day's requests in the peak hour), and within the hour a further burst factor (peak minute vs hour average, often 1.5–3×). → peak requests per second (RPS) . Little’s law : concurrency = arrival rate × time in system. 50 RPS × 8 s average = 400 requests in flight. This sizes connection pools, GPU batch slots and rate limits. Little's law gives the average in flight for a stable system (arrivals below capacity); it is not a p99 or burst figure, so plan headroom above it. × tokens per request → peak input and output tokens/second , which sizes model capacity or API rate limits. Add background workload : ingestion and re-embedding (chapter 10), evaluation runs, batch summarisation, agent jobs, which should be scheduled away from peaks. Registered users (millions) AI-feature daily active % Requests per active user per day Peak-hour share of daily traffic % Peak-minute burst factor Avg time per request (s) Input tokens / request Output tokens / request Capacity calculator. Peak RPS = DAU × requests/day × peak-hour share ÷ 3600 × burst. Concurrency by Little's law (an average, not a p99). Equivalent form used by many capacity sheets: average RPS = DAU × requests/day ÷ 86,400, then × a peak factor (here the peak factor = peak-hour share × 24 × burst). Change the latency: concurrency, and therefore GPU slots and connection pools, scale with it directly. Queue simulation, computed live (random arrivals and service times, c parallel servers). Utilisation = arrivals per second × service time ÷ servers. Below about 80% the queue stays short; near 100% waits explode; above 100% the queue grows without limit. The in-flight average matches Little's law, but the p95 wait is much higher than the mean. Example: the default numbers 10M registered × 8% = 800k DAU × 6 = 4.8M requests/day. 12% in the peak hour = 576k/hour = 160 RPS average, × 2 burst = 320 RPS at the peak minute. × 6 s = ~1,900 requests in flight. Output: 320 × 350 = 112k output tokens/s; input 960k tokens/s (much of it cacheable system prompt). That is a large deployment, and every assumption deserves a measurement before buying capacity. The numbers The default chain (illustrative). 10 million registered × 8% active = 800,000 users a day × 6 requests = 4.8 million requests a day. 12% in the busiest hour: 576,000 ÷ 3,600 seconds = 160 a second on average in that hour. The busiest minute is twice the hour’s average: 320 a second. Each request takes 6 seconds, so 320 × 6 ≈ 1,900 requests are in flight at once. Output: 320 × 350 tokens = 112,000 tokens a second. Code The program measures how much busier the busiest day is than an average day in your project’s dated records, then runs the chain from users to peak requests, requests in flight and output tokens for both. Change PEAK_HOUR or BURST and run it again. From users to peak load, in real Python. The peak-day factor comes from your project’s data; the rest is illustrative. Primary sources Little’s law The relation between arrivals, time in system and items in flight. Google SRE book: capacity planning in practice Intent-based capacity planning. k6: ramping-arrival-rate Testing at a target number of requests per second.

title: Defining service-level objectives for availability, latency, quality and cost
text: Intuition "The service should be reliable" cannot be checked. "99.5% of requests answered successfully within 10 seconds over 28 days" can. That target is a service-level objective , and the 0.5% it allows to fail is the error budget : room to ship changes and survive incidents. For AI features, availability is not enough. A service can answer every request quickly and still answer badly, so quality, cost and freshness need targets too. Mechanism SLI (indicator): a measured quantity, e.g. "fraction of requests completed successfully within 10 s". SLO (objective): the target for an SLI over a window, e.g. "99.5% over 28 days". Error budget : 100% − SLO; the amount of failure you can afford (0.5% of requests). Spending it fast triggers alerts and freezes risky releases (17.8). SLA : a contractual promise to customers, usually looser than the internal SLO. Dimension Example SLI Example SLO Availability Successful responses ÷ valid requests (excluding user errors) 99.9% / 28 days Latency TTFT; end-to-end time for non-streaming; per-step time for agents p95 TTFT ≤ 1.5 s; p99 ≤ 4 s Quality Sampled groundedness score; task success from feedback; escalation rate Groundedness ≥ 95% on daily 500-sample judge run Cost Cost per successful task; cost per tenant per day ≤ $0.012 per resolved conversation (monthly) Freshness (RAG) Edit-to-searchable lag p99 ≤ 10 min SLO % 99 99.5 99.9 99.95 99.99 Requests per month (millions) Error budget calculator. Each extra "nine" cuts the budget tenfold. For AI features, a provider outage can consume a month's 99.9% budget in under an hour, which is why fallbacks (15.7) matter. Example: why quality needs an SLO too A deployment keeps 99.95% availability while a silent retrieval bug drops groundedness from 96% to 81% for three days. No availability alert fires. A daily sampled-quality SLO with an alert at 92% would have caught it on day one (17.4). The numbers What a budget allows over 28 days (40,320 minutes) and 30 million requests. 99.9%: 0.1% of 30 million = 30,000 failed requests, or 0.1% of 40,320 ≈ 40 minutes of full outage. 99.99%: 3,000 requests, or about 4 minutes. A 45-minute provider outage with no fallback uses 45 ÷ 40 ≈ 112% of a 99.9% month. Burn rate. 2% errors in the last hour against a 0.1% allowance is 2 ÷ 0.1 = 20 times too fast: the whole month’s budget would be gone in 28 days ÷ 20 ≈ 34 hours. Code The program turns five SLOs into the failed requests and outage minutes they allow per 28 days, shows how much of each a 45-minute outage uses, and computes a burn rate. Change REQUESTS or the last hour’s errors and run it again. Error budgets and burn rate, in real Python. The traffic is illustrative. Primary sources Google SRE book: Service Level Objectives SLIs, SLOs and SLAs. Google SRE workbook: Alerting on SLOs Burn-rate alerts over several windows. Google SRE workbook: Error budget policy What happens when the budget runs out.

title: Separating ingestion, retrieval, generation and agent execution workloads
text: Intuition A restaurant does not let the catering order for 500 people use the same stove as the dinner service. Bulk work and live customers need different things: bulk work wants throughput and can wait, live users want answers now. Workload separation gives ingestion, retrieval, generation and agent runs their own pools and quotas. A big re-ingestion then only takes longer; it never makes search slow for everyone. Mechanism These workloads have different resource profiles, latency needs and failure modes. Running them on shared capacity lets one starve the others (a backfill saturating embedding GPUs that also serve query embeddings; long agent runs holding all model slots during peak chat). Workload Profile Latency need Scaling unit Ingestion Bursty bulk; CPU (parse, OCR) + GPU (embed) Minutes (freshness SLO) Queue consumers; spot/preemptible OK Retrieval Many small reads; RAM-heavy; low latency Tens of ms Index replicas Generation GPU-heavy; seconds per request; streaming TTFT ~1 s Model replicas / API quota Agent execution Long-running, many calls, durable state Seconds to hours Workflow workers; separate model quota Clients API gateway auth · quotas Chat service stateless · streaming Retrieval service index replicas Agent workers durable workflows Model gateway pools: interactive | agent GPU pools / providers Ingestion pipeline queues · batch embed Embedding query pool ≠ batch pool Separate pools and quotas per workload: a backfill or an agent storm cannot exhaust interactive capacity. Workload separation. Query-time embeddings use a small low-latency pool; bulk ingestion uses a separate batch pool. Agents draw from their own model quota. Example Monday 09:00: a large tenant triggers re-ingestion of 2M documents, and 40,000 employees open the assistant. Because query embeddings and ingestion embeddings run on separate pools, search latency stays at 40 ms while the backfill queue simply takes longer, within its freshness budget. The numbers A shared pool (illustrative). 4 embedding workers at 8 ms each can do 4 × 1,000 ÷ 8 = 500 embeddings a second. Live search needs 300 a second: 60% busy, waits stay tiny. A backfill adds 400 a second: 700 against 500 means 200 a second pile up. After 10 seconds, 2,000 are queued, and a search query arriving then waits about 2,000 ÷ 500 = 4 seconds. On separate pools, search keeps its 60% and the backfill simply runs at whatever its own pool allows. Code The program simulates live query embeddings on a worker pool, with and without a bulk backfill sharing it, and compares the queries’ median and 95th-percentile waits. Change BACKFILL_PER_S to 150 and run it again. Shared against separate pools, in real Python. The rates are illustrative. Primary sources AWS Well-Architected: fault isolation Bulkheads and isolating workloads. Azure Architecture Center: Bulkhead pattern Separate pools so one workload cannot exhaust another’s resources. KEDA concepts Scaling queue consumers separately from interactive services.

title: Stateless services, durable state, queues, caches and asynchronous processing
text: Intuition A service that keeps nothing in memory between requests can be copied, restarted or moved freely; the conversation and the task live in a database. Work that need not finish while the user waits goes into a queue. Caches save time and money, but only when the stored answer really fits the new request. An exact cache is safe if its key includes the tenant and the user’s permissions. A semantic cache reuses answers for similar questions, and similar is not the same: "cancel my subscription" and "cancel my colleague’s subscription" need different answers. Mechanism Stateless services : request handlers keep no session in memory, so any replica can serve any request and replicas can be added or killed freely. Conversation state lives in a database (7.5); streaming connections can resume by response ID. Durable state : conversations, agent checkpoints, tasks, usage records and audit logs in replicated databases with backups. Choose stores per access pattern (Postgres for transactional state, object storage for documents, a vector store for embeddings). Queues : anything that need not finish within the user's request (document processing, long agent tasks, batch summarisation, evaluation) goes through a queue with workers, giving retries, backpressure and smoothing of peaks. Caches : exact-match response cache (same normalised request → stored answer; safe for deterministic, non-personal queries); semantic cache (similar query embedding → stored answer; risky: similar is not identical, so restrict to FAQ-style content and include tenant and permission scope in the key); retrieval cache (query → chunk IDs); prefix/KV cache in the model server (14.3). Every cache needs invalidation tied to document updates (10.4). Asynchronous UX : for tasks over ~30 s, return a task ID immediately, show progress, and notify on completion, rather than holding an HTTP connection open. Request Exact cache hit ~5% Semantic cache FAQ scope only Retrieval cache Model (prefix cache) Store response with scope + TTL A request arrives with tenant, user and permission scope. Key = hash(tenant, normalised prompt, model, prompt version, ACL scope). Identical requests return instantly. For public FAQ content only: if a past query's embedding is within a tight threshold, reuse its answer. Evaluate false-hit rate before enabling. Reuse the retrieved chunk IDs for repeated queries within a short TTL. The model server reuses KV for the shared system-prompt prefix. Store with TTL and document dependencies so edits purge stale answers. Cache layers from cheapest to most expensive. Never cache across tenants or permission scopes. Example: a semantic cache incident "How do I cancel my subscription?" and "How do I cancel my colleague's subscription?" are 0.94 cosine-similar. A semantic cache with threshold 0.92 served the first answer to the second question, which required an admin role. Fix: scope semantic caching to a curated FAQ set, raise the threshold, and include role in the cache key. The numbers What caches save (illustrative). 1 million requests a day at 0.01 dollars each costs 10,000 dollars. An exact cache with a 5% hit rate saves 50,000 × 0.01 = 500 dollars a day and answers those requests in milliseconds. A semantic cache with a 20% hit rate saves 2,000 dollars, but if 3% of its hits are wrong, 200,000 × 0.03 = 6,000 users a day get an answer to a different question. That is why semantic caching is limited to curated FAQ content and its false-hit rate is measured first. Code The program shows that tenant and role change an exact cache key, then runs a word-overlap semantic cache over your project’s distinct requests and counts the hits whose type, numbers or names differ from the cached request. Change the thresholds and run it again. Cache keys and false hits, in real Python. Word overlap stands in for embedding similarity. Primary sources Redis: vector search The building block behind many semantic caches. Anthropic: Prompt caching Provider-side prefix caching, different from response caching. The Twelve-Factor App: Processes Stateless processes with state in backing services.

title: Model gateways, routing, tenant quotas, fairness and noisy-neighbour protection
text: Intuition A model gateway is the one front door to every model the company uses. Every request passes it, so it is the natural place to choose the right model, hold the credentials, count usage, enforce budgets and switch to a fallback. It is also where fairness is enforced. Without limits, one customer’s runaway script fills the queue and everyone waits. With per-tenant quotas and fair queuing , the tenant who caused the burst is the one who waits. Mechanism A model gateway is a central service between applications and all model backends (hosted providers and self-hosted pools). It provides one API, credentials management, routing, quotas, retries and fallbacks, caching, usage metering, logging and policy enforcement. Without one, every team reimplements these and nobody can see total spend. Routing : by task (cheap model for classification, strong model for complex reasoning), by tenant tier, by load (least-loaded replica, prefix affinity), by region/data residency, by health (skip a degraded provider). Tenant quotas : per-tenant limits on requests/min, tokens/min, concurrent requests, and spend/day, enforced with token buckets. Fairness : when capacity is short, give each tenant its fair share instead of first-come-first-served, e.g. weighted fair queuing by tier. Noisy-neighbour protection : one tenant's spike (a runaway agent, a bulk script) must not raise latency for everyone; quotas plus per-tenant queues plus admission control contain it. Tenant A's burst (× normal) Scheduling shared FIFO queue per-tenant quota + fair queuing Noisy neighbour (steady-state queueing model, illustrative). Capacity 100 units/s; tenants B–E send 15 units/s each; tenant A normally sends 10. With FIFO, A's burst inflates everyone's wait. With quotas and fair queuing, A is throttled to its share and others are unaffected. Example: gateway routing rules routes: - match: {task: classify} to: pool/small-8b-selfhosted - match: {task: answer, tenant_tier: free} to: provider-b/mid-model - match: {task: answer} to: provider-a/large-model fallback: [provider-b/large-model, pool/self-hosted-70b] - match: {region: eu} constrain: {provider_region: eu} quotas: default: {rpm: 600, tpm: 400000, concurrent: 40, usd_per_day: 200} enterprise: {rpm: 6000, tpm: 4000000, concurrent: 400, usd_per_day: 5000} The numbers The noisy-neighbour example . Capacity is 100 units a second. Tenants B to E send 15 each (60 in total) and tenant A normally sends 10. A bursts to 6 times normal, 60: total demand 120 against 100, so 20 a second pile up. First come first served: everyone’s requests sit in the same growing queue, so B to E wait as long as A. Fair queuing: B to E get the 60 they need; A gets the remaining 40 of its 60, so only A’s queue grows. Code The program lets tenant A send 1, 3 and 6 times its normal load into shared capacity and compares each tenant’s waiting time under first come first served and fair queuing. Add a burst of 10 and run it again. A noisy neighbour, in real Python. A simple fluid model of queues. Primary sources LiteLLM Proxy A self-hosted gateway with routing, budgets and rate limits. Envoy AI Gateway Token-based rate limiting and provider routing. Fair queuing The scheduling idea behind per-tenant fairness.

title: Backpressure, load shedding, circuit breakers and graceful degradation
text: Intuition When a building’s wiring is overloaded, a fuse trips instead of letting the wires melt. A circuit breaker does the same for a failing dependency: after too many errors it stops calling it for a while and uses a fallback, then tries a few calls to see whether it has recovered. When there is simply too much traffic, load shedding says no early to the requests that would time out anyway, and graceful degradation offers a smaller service, such as a smaller model or cached answers, rather than none. Mechanism Backpressure : propagate "slow down" upstream (bounded queues, 429 with Retry-After) instead of accepting work you cannot finish in time. Load shedding : when overloaded, reject some requests early and cheaply (lowest priority first: batch, then free tier) so the rest succeed. Reject based on predicted wait vs deadline; a request that will time out anyway should not consume GPU time. Circuit breaker : wrap each dependency. After an error-rate threshold, the breaker opens and calls fail fast (or go to fallback) for a cool-down period; then it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through; success closes it, failure re-opens it. Prevents piling threads onto a dying provider. Graceful degradation : a ladder of reduced service levels: smaller model, fewer retrieved chunks, no reranker, shorter max output, disable non-essential features (suggested follow-ups), cached answers only, and finally a clear "temporarily unavailable, here's search" message. Pause Toggle provider outage Circuit breaker (simulated; threshold 50% errors over the last 20 calls, 5 s open period, 3 trial calls). Toggle the outage on and off. Green = served by primary, amber = served by fallback, red = failed. While open, traffic goes straight to the fallback without waiting for timeouts. L0 · full service: large model, 8 chunks + reranker L1 · mid model, same retrieval L2 · mid model, 4 chunks, no reranker, shorter outputs L3 · cached answers + search results only L4 · status message + link to help centre A degradation ladder (bar = relative capability). Define levels in advance, evaluate each one's quality offline, and switch automatically based on load and dependency health. Offered load (× capacity) Client deadline (s) Deadline-aware load shedding (simulated 120 s burst against a service that completes 10 requests/s, each taking 1 s). No shedding queues everything, so requests wait past their deadline and their work is wasted. Shed by predicted wait rejects requests at the door when the queue is already longer than the deadline allows. Priority does the same but always admits paid-tier requests (30% of traffic) first. Green = answered in time; amber = rejected quickly (client can retry or degrade); red = timed out after waiting. Example During a viral launch, queue wait reaches 12 s against a 10 s deadline. The gateway sheds free-tier batch requests (L4 for them), moves free-tier chat to L2, and keeps paid tiers at L0. Overall success rate stays above 99% for paid users, and the incident report shows exactly which levels were active and when. The numbers Waiting on a dead provider . During a 400-call outage with a 10-second timeout, every call waits 10 seconds before failing: 400 × 10 = 4,000 seconds, more than an hour of users waiting. A breaker that opens after 10 failures in its last 20 calls spends about 10 timeouts finding out, then sends the rest straight to the fallback. Shedding by deadline. A service that answers 10 requests a second has 85 waiting. A new request would start after about 85 ÷ 10 = 8.5 seconds; with an 8-second deadline, it is better to say no now. Code The program sends 1,000 calls through a provider outage with and without a circuit breaker, counting calls served, sent to the fallback and failed, and the time lost to timeouts, then sheds requests whose predicted wait beats the deadline. Change THRESHOLD or OPEN_FOR and run it again. A breaker and deadline-aware shedding, in real Python. The outage is simulated. Primary sources Martin Fowler: Circuit Breaker The pattern and its closed, open and half-open states. Google SRE book: Handling Overload Load shedding, criticality and client-side throttling. Amazon Builders’ Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload Rejecting work that would miss its deadline.

title: Multi-region architecture, disaster recovery and provider outages
text: Intuition A second region is a spare house in another town. It only helps if the spare house is big enough for everyone, has the furniture (the data and indexes) already inside, and you have practised moving in. Two numbers set the plan: how much recent data you may lose and how quickly you must be back, the RPO and RTO . Data residency adds a rule: European customers may only move to European houses, so those houses need room for them. Mechanism Multi-region : run in two or more regions. Active-active : both serve traffic, routed by latency or residency; more complex data consistency. Active-passive : standby region takes over on failure; simpler, slower failover. Data residency : EU users' data and prompts may need to stay in EU regions and EU-hosted model endpoints; this constrains routing and failover targets. Disaster recovery : define RPO (recovery point objective: how much data you may lose, e.g. 5 minutes) and RTO (recovery time objective: how fast you must recover, e.g. 30 minutes) per component. Vector indexes can be rebuilt from stored chunks and embeddings, but rebuilding takes hours at scale, so replicate or snapshot them. Provider outages : hosted model APIs have outages and regional incidents. Mitigate with a second provider or self-hosted fallback (evaluated for quality and prompt compatibility), regional endpoints, circuit breakers, and the degradation ladder. Test failover regularly; untested failover usually fails. Restore, don't just back up : test restores on a schedule. Replicas copy corruption and accidental deletes instantly, so they are not backups. Rehearse failing back to the primary region too, including replaying queued writes exactly once. Global DNS / anycast LB Region EU-1 Region US-1 App + gateway Index replicas Provider A (EU) fallback: self-host EU Postgres primary EU tenants App + gateway Index replicas Provider A (US) fallback: provider B Postgres primary US tenants async replica for DR (non-resident data only) Active-active regions with residency. EU tenants fail over only to EU capacity; US tenants can fail over across providers. Each region holds its own index replicas so a regional outage does not require rebuilding. A regional failover, on a globe. Your example project's regions and user cities, at their real positions. Step through a region failing: traffic is rerouted to the nearest region each city may use, with data residency deciding where that is. Then come the round trip, the capacity of the survivors and the data they need. Distances are real great-circle distances; round trips use a rule of thumb (routes about 1.5 times the straight line, light in fibre about 200 km per ms), and traffic shares, regions and capacity are illustrative. The 2D view shows the same numbers as tables. Example: a game-day exercise Quarterly, the team blocks Provider A at the gateway in staging, then in production for 10% of traffic. Findings from the first run: the fallback model ignored the JSON schema in 4% of responses (fixed by enabling constrained decoding), and fallback quota was too small for full traffic (raised in the provider contract). Without the exercise, both would have surfaced during a real outage. The numbers Room for the move (illustrative). EU-west carries 70 units and EU-central carries 60 of its 100. If EU-west fails and 80% of its load must stay in the EU, EU-central receives 70 × 0.8 = 56 units: 60 + 56 = 116, over its 100. So EU-central needs at least 16% more capacity, or less of the traffic must be bound to the EU. RPO. At 1,200 conversation writes a minute, a 5-minute RPO accepts losing up to 6,000 writes. Rebuilding a large vector index from scratch may take hours, which is why indexes are replicated or snapshotted. Code The program fails one region at a time, moves its load to the survivors with most EU traffic kept in EU regions, and flags any region pushed over capacity. Change EU_ONLY_SHARE or a region’s capacity and run it again. Failover with residency, in real Python. Regions and loads are invented. Primary sources AWS: Disaster recovery options in the cloud Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active. Azure: Disaster recovery overview RPO, RTO and regional failover. Google SRE book: Data Integrity Why replicas are not backups and restores must be tested.

title: Load, stress, soak and failure testing with realistic traffic distributions
text: Intuition A load test is a rehearsal, and it only helps if it looks like the real show. Real prompts are mostly short with a few very long ones, real users arrive in bursts, and agents make many calls in a row. A test with identical 500-token prompts sent at an even pace rehearses a different show. How the test sends requests matters too. A tester that waits for each reply before sending the next slows down exactly when the service does, so it never sees the queue: coordinated omission . Mechanism Test Question Shape Load Do we meet SLOs at expected peak? Ramp to forecast peak, hold 30–60 min Stress Where and how do we break? Does shedding work? Ramp beyond peak until SLOs fail; observe degradation Soak Leaks, cache growth, fragmentation, slow degradation? Moderate load for 8–24 h Spike Do autoscaling and queues absorb sudden bursts? Jump from 20% to 150% in one minute Failure / chaos Do breakers, retries and failover behave? Inject provider errors, latency, node loss, region loss under load Realistic distributions matter more for AI than for typical APIs.
