Evidently drift and quality monitoring Data drift, LLM output evaluations and monitoring reports; runs as a Python library. The numbers Why one place matters (illustrative). 14 services each set 12 GenAI attributes: 168 places in code. A rename of 3 attributes means 42 edits spread over 14 teams, or 3 lines in one Collector transform. Dashboards break silently. If a renamed attribute feeds a cost dashboard, the dashboard shows zero for the new name rather than an error, until someone notices the spend has "dropped" to nothing. Code The program renames attributes an older GenAI instrumentation used, drops message content as a Collector rule would, and lists recommended attributes still missing. Add an attribute your own code uses and run it again. Absorbing renames, in real Python. Names reflect a draft; check the current conventions. Primary sources OpenTelemetry: GenAI semantic conventions The current draft and each attribute’s stability. open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai The repository where the GenAI conventions and their changelog now live. Collector: transform processor Renaming attributes in one place.

title: Versioning code, prompts, models, datasets, indexes, configurations and evaluation suites
text: Intuition An AI system’s behaviour depends on much more than its code: the prompts, the models, the search index, the settings and even the evaluation suite that approved it. Change any one and the answers can change. A release manifest lists all of them under one id, and every request records that id. When someone complains about an answer, you know exactly which combination produced it and can reproduce it. Mechanism Every artefact that can change behaviour needs an immutable version, and every production request should record the versions that served it. Bundle them into a release manifest : one identifier for "the system as deployed". Release r2026.11.3 manifest (immutable) Code git 7f3c2e1 · image@sha256:… Prompts answer@v12 · triage@v7 Config k=8, temp=0.2, flags@41 Models provider-a/large-2026-09 Index kb-v4 (bge-base@rev2) Eval suite + judge suite@v31 · judge@v4 Datasets ft-invoices@v12 (adapter) Infrastructure tofu plan 2026-11-03 A release manifest. Changing any one input produces a new release ID, even if no code changed. Traces carry the release ID (17.5), so any output can be reproduced and any regression bisected. Example: manifest file release: r2026.11.3 code: {commit: 7f3c2e1, image: registry.local/kb-api@sha256:9b1e…} prompts: {answer: v12, triage: v7, rewrite_query: v3} models: {answer: provider-a/large-2026-09, triage: pool/small-8b@ft-r431, judge: provider-b/mid-2026-06} index: {alias: kb-search, target: kb-v4, embedder: bge-base@rev2, chunker: v5} config: {retrieval_k: 8, rerank_top: 50, temperature: 0.2, flags_revision: 41} evaluation: {suite: v31, judge_prompt: v4, results: s3://evals/r2026.11.3/} approved_by: [kb-owner, sec-review] created: 2026-11-03T16:20Z The numbers How many combinations (illustrative). With 3 prompts, 3 models, 2 index versions and 4 configuration sets in use over a quarter, there are 3 × 3 × 2 × 4 = 72 possible combinations. Without a manifest, "which version answered this?" has 72 possible answers. Bisecting. If quality dropped somewhere across 16 releases, comparing the middle release first and halving each time finds the culprit in about 4 steps, since 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. Code The program hashes a manifest of code, prompts, models, index, configuration and evaluation suite into a release id, shows that changing only a prompt makes a new release, and finds which release served a complaint. Change the index target and run it again. Release ids from manifests, in real Python. Nothing is deployed. Primary sources MLflow Prompt Registry Versioned prompts alongside models and runs. OpenTelemetry: Resource conventions Attaching service version to every span. DVC documentation Versioning data and pipelines with code.

title: Reproducible builds, infrastructure as code and environment promotion
text: Intuition If every kitchen in a restaurant chain cooked from memory, no two meals would match. Infrastructure as code writes the recipe down: GPU pools, databases, permissions and alerts are files that are reviewed and applied by a pipeline. And the meal is cooked once. The artefact built and tested in staging is the very one that runs in production: environment promotion moves the same image digest forward and changes only configuration. Mechanism Reproducible builds : lockfiles, pinned base images by digest, pinned engine versions (vLLM, CUDA), deterministic container builds; the same commit produces the same image. Infrastructure as code (IaC) : GPU node pools, vector databases, queues, gateways, IAM, secrets references, dashboards and alerts are defined in code (OpenTofu/Terraform, Pulumi, Kubernetes manifests with Helm/Kustomize), reviewed and applied by pipelines, not clicked in consoles. Environment promotion : dev → staging → production with the same artefacts (image digests, prompt versions, model IDs); only configuration differs. Staging mirrors production shape (same engine, same index type, a realistic data sample) so tests are meaningful. GitOps : the desired state of each environment lives in a repository; a controller (Argo CD, Flux) syncs clusters to it, giving an audit trail and easy rollback by reverting a commit. PR merged code / prompt / config Build once image digest Dev smoke tests Staging full gates (18.3) Prod canary (18.4) Prod 100% Any behaviour change, including a prompt edit, goes through review. CI builds the artefact once; later stages reuse the same digest. Quick checks: does it start, answer, and pass deterministic tests. Production-like environment: evaluation suites, security scans, load test, cost estimate. Progressive exposure in production with automatic analysis. Promotion recorded; the previous release stays deployable for rollback. Build once, promote the same artefact. Rebuilding per environment means you never tested what you shipped. Example: GPU pool as code (OpenTofu/Terraform, illustrative) module "llm_pool" { source = "./modules/gpu-node-pool" name = "answer-8b-fp8" gpu_type = var.gpu_type # per environment min_nodes = var.env == "prod" ? 3 : 0 max_nodes = var.env == "prod" ? 24 : 2 labels = { workload = "interactive", model = "8b-fp8" } taints = ["gpu=true:NoSchedule"] } The numbers Unpinned dependencies drift (illustrative). If 40 dependencies are unpinned and each publishes a new release on average every 3 months, about 40 ÷ 90 ≈ 0.44 of them change on any given day. Rebuild a week later and about 3 dependencies are probably different from what you tested. Rollback by commit. With GitOps, the previous state of production is one revert away; reapplying it takes as long as the sync, often a few minutes. Code The program builds an artefact from pinned inputs and promotes its digest through development, staging and production, then shows that rebuilding from unpinned inputs ships something staging never tested. Pin the second build’s inputs and run it again. Build once, promote the digest, in real Python. A hash stands in for a container build. Primary sources OpenTofu documentation Declarative infrastructure as code. Argo CD GitOps: syncing clusters to the state in a repository. Reproducible Builds: definition What it means for the same source to give the same artefact.

title: Automated quality, security, performance and cost gates
text: Intuition A release gate is a turnstile that only opens when a change has shown its ticket: quality at least as good as before, no new safety failures, latency and cost within limits. It applies to every change, including a one-line prompt edit. Each gate catches different mistakes. A tighter prompt may pass quality and fail cost; a cheaper model may pass cost and fail quality; a new tool may pass both and fail security. That is why all four run. Mechanism A gate is an automated check that blocks promotion when a threshold is not met. Gates make the acceptance criteria of 8.1 and the release criteria of 13.7 enforceable for every change. Gate Checks Example threshold Quality Regression suite, critical set, per-segment scores, judge-based metrics with CIs No critical case regresses; overall ≥ baseline − 0.5 pts (within CI); no language drops > 2 pts Safety / security Injection and jailbreak suites, isolation tests, secret scanning, dependency and model scans 0 cross-tenant leaks; injection success rate ≤ baseline; no critical CVEs Performance Load test at forecast peak with realistic traffic p95 TTFT ≤ 1.5 s; p99 total ≤ 12 s; error rate ≤ 0.5% Cost Tokens per task on the eval suite × prices; projected monthly cost Cost per successful task ≤ +10% vs current release unless approved Change prompt v13: tighter citation rule model swap to cheaper model new tool: send_email retrieval k 8 → 20 Run pipeline A gated pipeline (scripted results for four typical changes). Each gate shows its measured value against its threshold. Notice that different changes fail different gates: that is why all four are needed. The numbers Averages hide segments (illustrative). A suite of 400 cases in 6 segments passes 92% before and 91.8% after a change, which looks fine. But one segment of 26 cases fell from 92% to 77%: 4 more failures in that segment, hidden by the other 374. A rule "no segment drops more than 3 points" fails this change, as it should. Critical cases. If 1 in 10 cases is tagged critical, 40 cases must never regress, whatever the overall score. Code The program builds a suite from your project’s labelled data, runs a baseline and a candidate that is worse on one segment, and fails the gate on the overall rate, regressed critical cases or a segment drop. Change MAX_SEGMENT_DROP and run it again. A quality gate, in real Python. Pass and fail results are simulated; the gate logic is real. Laptop lab: a quality gate in CI Laptop · CPU (runner) · or GitHub Actions # .github/workflows/eval.yml (sketch) — runs promptfoo against a model endpoint on every PR touching prompts/ on: {pull_request: {paths: ["prompts/**", "promptfooconfig.yaml"]}} jobs: eval: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npx promptfoo@latest eval -c promptfooconfig.yaml -o results.json env: {OPENAI_API_KEY: "${{ secrets.EVAL_API_KEY }}"} # or point providers at a hosted test endpoint - run: python scripts/gate.py results.json --min-pass-rate 0.95 --critical-tag critical gate.py is 20 lines: load results, compute pass rate overall and on cases tagged critical , exit non-zero if below thresholds. Locally you can run the same command against Ollama before pushing. Primary sources promptfoo: CI/CD integration Running evaluation gates on every pull request. GitHub Actions documentation Workflows that block merges on failed checks. Martin Fowler: Continuous Integration Why every change runs the same checks.

title: Shadow deployments, canaries, controlled rollouts and rollback
text: Intuition New versions meet real users gradually. A shadow deployment lets the new version answer real requests in private, so you can compare without anyone seeing its answers. A canary then gives it a small share of real users and compares the two side by side. Each step widens only if the numbers stay within bounds, and any breach sends traffic back automatically. Rollback has one limit: it cannot unsend an email or reverse a refund, so shadow traffic must never reach tools that change things. Mechanism Shadow deployment : send a copy of production requests to the new version, discard its outputs (users see the old version), and compare: output differences, judge scores, latency, cost, errors. No user risk; for agents, shadow only with side-effect-free (mocked) tools. Canary : route a small share of real traffic (1–5%) to the new version, compare its metrics with the baseline on the same time window, and promote automatically if healthy. Controlled rollout : increase exposure in steps (5% → 25% → 50% → 100%), optionally by tenant cohort (internal users first, then low-risk tenants), with feature flags controlling which prompt/model/index version each cohort gets. Rollback : one action, minutes not hours: flip the flag or alias back. Requires the previous version to still be deployed and compatible (for indexes, keep the old one warm: 10.7). Practice it. Rollback does not undo actions : messages sent, refunds issued and tickets created by the bad version stay done. Plan reconciliation or compensation for them. Shadow traffic must never reach write tools: stub or disable side effects in shadow mode. Candidate healthy regresses quality at 25% Start rollout Automated canary analysis (simulated). Traffic share steps up every few "minutes" if the candidate's sampled quality and error rate stay within bounds of the baseline. When a metric breaches its bound, traffic returns to 0% automatically and the release is marked failed. Quality gate passed Security gate passed Latency + cost gate passed Rollback rehearsed inject a quality regression at the next stage Advance rollout Reset Gates drive the rollout. The candidate advances shadow → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% only while every gate is ticked; un-tick one and promotion is refused. Inject a regression and the next stage's canary analysis rolls traffic back to 0% automatically (which is only safe if rollback was rehearsed). Example: rollout policy rollout: kb-assistant r2026.11.3 steps: [{weight: 0, shadow: 24h}, {weight: 5, hold: 2h}, {weight: 25, hold: 4h}, {weight: 50, hold: 12h}, {weight: 100}] analysis (candidate vs baseline, same window): error_rate: max_delta: +0.3pp p95_ttft_ms: max_ratio: 1.15 groundedness_sample: min_delta: -1.5pp (500 sampled traces, judge@v4) thumbs_down_rate: max_delta: +1.0pp on_failure: set weight 0, page owner, attach comparison report The numbers How much a canary sees (illustrative). At 100,000 requests a day, a 5% canary for 2 hours sees about 100,000 × 0.05 × 2 ÷ 24 ≈ 420 requests. With 500 judged samples, a groundedness of 95% is measured to within about ±2 points, so a drop to 90% is visible, but a drop to 94% is not. If a bad version is caught at 5%, only 1 in 20 users met it; caught at 50%, half of them did. Code The program steps a candidate through 5%, 25%, 50% and 100% of traffic, compares sampled errors and groundedness with the baseline at each step, and rolls back on a breach. Make the regression smaller, from 0.95 to 0.93, and see whether 500 samples still catch it. Automated canary analysis, in real Python. The metrics are simulated. Primary sources Argo Rollouts Canary steps with automated analysis and rollback. Google SRE workbook: Canarying Releases Comparing canary and control populations. OpenFeature Feature flags to route cohorts and roll back quickly.

title: Model and provider upgrades, embedding migrations and compatibility testing
text: Intuition A new model version is like a new colleague taking over a job: probably capable, but with different habits. It may write longer answers, follow the JSON format less strictly, refuse more often, or count tokens differently. So a model upgrade is a release, not a setting. Run the suite with the current prompts to see the raw difference, re-tune the prompts, check the properties your code depends on, then shadow, canary and keep the old route until the rollback window has passed. Mechanism Models change more often than most dependencies: new versions every few months, deprecations with fixed retirement dates, behaviour changes inside a version alias. Treat each as a release: Inventory and deprecation tracking : which features use which model versions; provider retirement dates on a calendar with owners. Compatibility testing : run the full suite with the new model and the current prompts, then with re-tuned prompts. Check structured-output adherence, tool-calling format, refusal behaviour, verbosity (output tokens change cost and latency), tokenizer differences (context budgets, 7.3), and supported parameters (some models ignore temperature or require different settings). Prompt portability : prompts tuned for one model often underperform on another; budget time to re-tune, and keep model-specific prompt variants versioned together. Embedding migrations : full re-embed with blue/green indexes (10.7); queries and documents must switch embedding models atomically. Fine-tuned models : a new base model means re-running fine-tuning and all of 13.6. Check (new model vs current) Result Action Regression suite (current prompts) −1.8 pts, 9 critical regressions Re-tune prompt Regression suite (re-tuned prompt v13-m2) +2.4 pts, 0 critical regressions Proceed JSON schema adherence (no constrained decoding) 99.1% vs 99.8% Enable constrained decoding Median output tokens +38% Add length guidance; re-check cost gate Tool-call argument validity 99.6% vs 99.5% OK Over-refusal on should-answer set 3.1% vs 1.2% Investigate category; adjust system prompt Illustrative compatibility report for a provider model upgrade. Example: an alias that moved A team called a provider's "latest" model alias. When the provider pointed it at a new version, median output length rose 38% and JSON adherence fell slightly, so cost rose and a parser started failing on 0.7% of requests. Pinning dated snapshot versions, plus the weekly scheduled re-evaluation (18.6), turns such changes into planned upgrades instead of surprises. Deprecation notice / new model Run suite as-is Re-tune prompts Compatibility checks format, tools, length, refusals Shadow Canary → 100% Retire old route Track it with an owner and a date well before retirement. Measure the raw difference first; it tells you how much work is needed. Adapt prompts and settings for the new model; version them separately. Check the properties code depends on, not just answer quality. Compare on real traffic without exposure. Progressive rollout with automatic analysis (18.4). Remove the old model from the gateway only after the rollback window. Model upgrade procedure. The numbers Longer answers cost money (illustrative). If median output grows from 220 to 305 tokens, that is 85 more tokens a request. At 3 million requests a month and 15 dollars per million output tokens: 85 × 3,000,000 × 15 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ 3,800 dollars a month more. Small format changes break code. JSON adherence falling from 99.8% to 99.1% sounds tiny, but at 3 million requests it is 0.7% × 3,000,000 = 21,000 more parser failures a month. Code The program compares simulated results for the current and a new model on JSON adherence, over-refusal and output length, names an action for each failed check, and prices the longer outputs. Change the new model’s behaviour and run it again. A compatibility report, in real Python. The results are simulated. Primary sources Anthropic: Model deprecations Retirement dates and migration planning. OpenAI: Deprecations Another provider’s deprecation schedule. Chen et al. (2023), How Is ChatGPT’s Behavior Changing over Time? Behaviour changes behind the same model name.

title: Feedback collection, annotation, retraining triggers and scheduled re-evaluation
text: Intuition A system that learns from use needs a routine: collect feedback linked to the request, have people label a sample, keep evaluation data and training data apart, and decide in advance what should start a re-tune. A retraining trigger is that decision written down, such as "2,000 new corrected examples" or "quality below target for 3 days". It opens a piece of work; it never ships anything by itself. And the full evaluation runs every week even when nothing changed, because the world under the system does. Mechanism Feedback collection : explicit (ratings with optional reason categories), implicit (rephrases, copy actions, escalations, edits to drafts: the diff between the AI draft and the sent version is excellent training signal), and outcome feedback joined later (17.7). Make feedback cheap for users and always link it to the trace. Annotation : route sampled and flagged traces to reviewers with the guideline (13.2), building evaluation and training data continuously. Retraining / re-tuning triggers : defined conditions, such as quality SLO breach for N days, drift metrics beyond threshold, enough new labelled data (e.g. +2,000 corrected examples), a new base model, or a policy change. Triggers open a work item; retraining still goes through all gates. Scheduled re-evaluation : run the full suite on the production release weekly even without changes, because providers, documents and user behaviour change underneath you. Refresh the evaluation set itself quarterly with new production samples so it does not go stale. Users & outcomes Feedback + traces Annotation queue Eval set ∪ training set kept separate Trigger met? Re-tune / retrain Gates + rollout People use the system; outcomes accrue. Signals are captured and linked to traces. Reviewers label sampled and flagged items. New labels split into evaluation (held out) and training pools, never mixed. Weekly job checks triggers (data volume, drift, SLO breaches, scheduled date). Prompt re-tuning, retriever fine-tuning or model fine-tuning as indicated. Standard release path. The weekly scheduled re-evaluation runs regardless. Continuous improvement loop. Example: draft edits as signal Support agents edit AI-drafted replies before sending. Logging (draft, sent) pairs with the edit distance gives an automatic quality metric (median edit fraction fell from 34% to 19% over two prompt versions) and, after review, a fine-tuning dataset of preferred replies, plus DPO pairs with the draft as "rejected" and the sent version as "chosen". The numbers Edits as a measurement . If an agent deletes 120 characters from a 300-character draft before sending, the edit fraction is 120 ÷ 300 = 40%. A new prompt that brings the median to 17% means agents rewrite far less. When the trigger fires (illustrative). 50 corrected drafts a day reach 2,000 new examples in 2,000 ÷ 50 = 40 days. Splitting them 20% to evaluation and 80% to training keeps 400 for testing that the model never trains on. Code The program writes simulated reply drafts for your project’s messages under two prompt versions, measures how much agents edit before sending, and checks a retraining trigger. Make v13 as wordy as v12 and run it again. Draft edits as a signal, in real Python. The drafts and edits are simulated. Primary sources Rafailov et al. (2023), Direct Preference Optimization Using chosen and rejected pairs, such as sent and drafted replies. Argilla documentation Annotation queues for production feedback. Google Cloud: MLOps continuous delivery Triggers for retraining in an ML pipeline.

title: Ownership, release documentation, operational readiness and service handover
text: Intuition A system is not finished when it works; it is finished when someone else can run it at 3 a.m. An operational readiness review checks exactly that: targets defined, alerts live, runbooks tested, people on call, capacity planned from measured numbers, recovery practised, security reviewed and budgets set. Every activity also needs exactly one accountable owner. Two owners is the same as none: each assumes the other has it. Mechanism Ownership : every AI system has a named owning team accountable for quality, cost, incidents and compliance; every component (prompts, index, fine-tuned model, gateway routes, eval suite) has an owner. Shared platforms (gateway, vector DB, observability) have platform owners with clear interfaces. Release documentation : release notes per release manifest: what changed, evaluation results vs previous, known limitations, rollout plan, rollback procedure. Model cards (13.7) and system cards (intended use, risks, controls) for governance (16.8). Operational readiness review : before launch or handover, verify the system can be operated: SLOs defined, dashboards and alerts live, runbooks written and tested, on-call staffed and trained, capacity plan with measured numbers (15.10), DR tested, security review done, cost budgets configured. Service handover : when a project team hands a system to an operations or product team: walkthrough of architecture and traces, access granted, runbook drills, shadow on-call, and a period of joint ownership before the original team steps back. Operational readiness checklist (interactive; your ticks are not saved). Items reference the chapters where each is covered. A launch review typically requires every item in the "must" group. Activity Product owner AI engineering Platform / SRE Security & compliance Acceptance criteria & eval set A R C C Prompt / model / index changes C A/R I I SLOs, alerts, on-call C R A I Threat model, data protection I R C A Cost budgets A R C I Example RACI: R = responsible, A = accountable, C = consulted, I = informed. Toolbox for LLMOps and delivery MLflow tracking · registry · GenAI evals Experiment tracking, model registry, prompt registry and LLM evaluation/tracing features. DVC data and pipeline versioning Version datasets and pipelines alongside Git; reproduce any stage. OpenTofu / Terraform infrastructure as code Declarative infrastructure for GPU pools, databases, IAM and networking. Argo CD · Argo Rollouts GitOps · canaries Sync clusters from Git; progressive delivery with automated analysis and rollback. Practise on a local kind/k3d cluster. OpenFeature feature flags standard Vendor-neutral flag API for routing cohorts to prompt/model/index versions and for kill switches. promptfoo CI · Langfuse prompts prompt gates · prompt registry Run evaluation gates in CI; manage versioned prompts with labels for environments. The numbers Why drills count (illustrative). If an incident needs 4 runbook steps and each untested step has a 10% chance of being wrong or out of date, the chance all 4 work is 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 ≈ 66%. One drill that finds and fixes the bad steps lifts that close to 100%. Handover. Two weeks of shadow on-call at one incident a week gives the new team about 2 real incidents to learn from before they are on their own. Code The program checks a launch against its must-have readiness items and validates that every activity in a RACI table has exactly one accountable owner. Tick the missing items or fix the cost-budget row and run it again. Readiness and ownership checks, in real Python. A ticked box does not prove a runbook works. Primary sources Google SRE book: Evolving the SRE Engagement Model Production readiness reviews before handover. AWS Well-Architected: Operational Excellence Readiness, runbooks and ownership. Mitchell et al. (2018), Model Cards Release documentation for models.

title: How images and audio become tokens
text: Intuition A language model only reads tokens. To show it a photo, the photo is cut into small squares, like tiles on a floor, and each tile becomes one vector: an image patch . Sound is cut into short slices of time in the same way, each slice an audio frame . So a picture is not "one input"; it is hundreds or thousands of tokens. That is why images are expensive, why models shrink large images first, and why a long recording can fill a context window faster than a long document. Mechanism Every modality goes through the same three steps: cut the input into pieces, encode each piece into a vector, and place the vectors in the sequence the language model reads, next to the text tokens. Medium Unit Typical size What controls the count Text subword token about 1.3 tokens per English word the tokenizer (5.1) Image patch of 14–16 pixels hundreds to a few thousand per image resolution, resizing, tiling, merging of neighbouring patches Audio frame of 20–25 ms about 50 per second before merging sample rate, frame step, downsampling Video frames × patches images per second × patches per image how many frames are sampled Resolution decides cost. Models resize large images to a maximum side, and many split big images into tiles plus a small overview, so fine print stays readable. Doubling the width and height of an image roughly quadruples its patches. Providers document how they count image tokens; read it before estimating cost. Merging. Many models merge each 2 × 2 group of neighbouring patch vectors into one token after encoding, cutting the count four times with little loss. Photo 4032 × 3024 Resize max side 1024 Patches 14 px squares Encode + merge 2 × 2 Tokens about 1,000 A phone photo has 12 million pixels, far more than the model needs. It is shrunk so its longer side is 1,024 pixels: 1,024 × 768. It is cut into 14-pixel squares: 74 × 55 ≈ 4,070 patches. A vision encoder turns each patch into a vector, and neighbours are merged four into one. About 1,000 tokens join the text tokens in the model’s input. From a photo to tokens (a common recipe; sizes differ by model). Example: a support screenshot A user sends a 1,920 × 1,080 screenshot of an error. Shrunk to 1,024 wide, it becomes about 780 tokens, more than the user’s whole written question. Cropping the screenshot to the dialog box before sending it cuts that to about 150 tokens and often improves the answer, because the model is not distracted by the rest of the screen. The numbers Counting patches for a 1,024 × 768 image with 14-pixel patches: Across: 1,024 ÷ 14 ≈ 74 patches (rounding up). Down: 768 ÷ 14 ≈ 55. Patches: 74 × 55 = 4,070. Merged four into one: about 1,018 tokens. At an illustrative 3 dollars per million input tokens, 1,000 such images cost about 1,018 × 1,000 × 3 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ 3 dollars. Audio. At 50 frames a second, a 10-minute call is 600 × 50 = 30,000 positions before merging. A model that downsamples by 4 still sees 7,500, about as many as a 5,000-word document. Code The program resizes four kinds of image, counts patches and merged tokens, prices 1,000 of each, and counts audio positions for three clip lengths. Change PATCH , MERGE or the maximum side and run it again. Image and audio token counts, in real Python. Settings vary by model; prices are illustrative. Primary sources Dosovitskiy et al. (2020), An Image is Worth 16x16 Words The vision transformer: images as sequences of patches. Radford et al. (2022), Whisper How a speech model turns audio into frames and tokens. Anthropic: Vision How one provider sizes and counts image tokens. OpenAI: Images and vision Another provider’s image token and detail settings.

title: Vision-language models: architecture, capabilities and cost
text: Intuition A vision-language model is a language model with eyes bolted on. A vision encoder looks at the picture and writes down what it sees as vectors, a small adapter translates those vectors into the language model’s "alphabet", and the language model reads them as if they were words. It can read text in images, describe scenes, compare pictures and answer questions about charts. It is also confidently wrong in new ways: it misreads small digits, miscounts objects and mixes up left and right. Mechanism Three parts. Vision encoder : usually a vision transformer trained with images and captions (CLIP-style), turning patches into vectors. Projector : a small network, often one or two layers, that maps those vectors to the language model’s hidden size. Training usually starts by teaching only the projector to align images with captions, then fine-tunes more of the model on image–instruction pairs. Language model : reads image tokens and text tokens in one sequence, so attention connects words to image regions. Image pixels Vision encoder patch vectors Projector to LLM size Language model image + text tokens Answer text The image is resized and cut into patches (19.1). The encoder turns each patch into a vector; neighbours may be merged. The projector maps each vector into the language model’s space. The model reads image tokens and the question together; prefill grows with every image. The answer is generated as text, one token at a time. How a vision-language model reads an image. Good at Weak at Reading printed text, labels and screenshots Small or blurred digits, dense tables at low resolution Describing scenes and products Counting many similar objects Answering questions about charts Exact values read off a chart, spatial relations Comparing two images Long videos, unless frames are sampled well Cost and speed. Image tokens are input tokens: they lengthen prefill and so the time to first token (14.2), and they take KV-cache memory. Sending ten images at full resolution when one cropped image would do is the most common waste. Example: choosing a resolution A returns team checks photos of damaged parcels. At low detail (about 85 tokens per photo) the model spots crushed boxes but misses torn labels; at high detail (about 1,000 tokens) it catches both. They send low detail first and re-ask at high detail only when the model reports "unsure", which cuts image tokens by about 70%. The numbers One 448 × 448 image with 14-pixel patches: (448 ÷ 14) × (448 ÷ 14) = 32 × 32 = 1,024 patches; merged 2 × 2, 256 tokens. With a 40-token question: 256 + 40 = 296 tokens of prefill. 16 such images: 16 × 256 + 40 = 4,136 tokens. At 10,000 prefill tokens a second, about 0.4 seconds before the first word, compared with 0.03 seconds for one image. KV cache (14.1) at 128 KiB per token: 4,136 × 128 KiB ≈ 0.5 GB for one request. Code The program cuts an image into patches with NumPy, passes them through a stand-in encoder, merges neighbours and projects them to the language model’s size, then counts prefill tokens for 1, 4 and 16 images. Change IMG to 896 and see how the counts grow. The shapes inside a VLM, in real Python. Random weights: shapes only, no recognition. Primary sources Radford et al. (2021), CLIP Training image and text encoders into one space. Liu et al. (2023), Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA) Encoder, projector and language model, trained in two stages. Wang et al. (2024), Qwen2-VL Dynamic resolution and merging neighbouring patches.

title: Document AI: OCR pipelines versus sending page images to a model
text: Intuition There are two ways to read a stack of scanned forms. One is to type out every word first (OCR) and then work with the text. The other is to show the page itself to someone who can read it, a vision-language model, and ask the question directly. Document AI usually mixes both: cheap OCR for plain pages, and a model that sees the page for tables, forms, stamps and handwriting, where typing out the words loses the structure that gives them meaning. Mechanism Approach How it works Strengths Weaknesses Digital text extraction read the text layer of a born-digital PDF free, exact reading order, tables and columns often scrambled OCR + layout analysis detect text lines, then regions (titles, tables, lists) cheap, fast, runs on CPU tables and handwriting are hard; errors are silent Layout-aware document models models trained on page images and text positions good at forms and tables need fine-tuning for unusual layouts Page image to a VLM send the page as an image with the question handles mixed layouts, charts, stamps more tokens per page, can invent text, slower Classify page text? scan? table? Cheap path text layer or OCR Hard pages VLM or layout model Validate schemas, totals Store text + structure + page image A quick check decides what kind of page this is. Plain text pages go through the text layer or OCR. Pages with tables, forms or handwriting go to a model that sees the image. Extracted fields are checked: types, required fields, totals that add up. Keep the text, the structure and a link to the page image, so answers can cite the page (9.6). A routed document pipeline. Spend the expensive model only where it adds accuracy. Validate everything you extract. A model reading an invoice image may produce a plausible total that is not on the page. Check that line items add up to the total, dates parse, and required fields exist; send failures to a person. For RAG, chunk by layout regions (10.3), not by fixed length. Example: invoice extraction A finance team extracts 40,000 invoices a month. OCR plus rules handles 85% of them; the 15% with handwritten notes or unusual tables go to a VLM with a JSON schema. A check that line items sum to the total catches 2% of VLM outputs, which go to a reviewer. The numbers Routing pays (illustrative). 100,000 pages a month, OCR at 0.0015 dollars a page, a VLM at 0.004. All OCR: 100,000 × 0.0015 = 150 dollars. All VLM: 100,000 × 0.004 = 400 dollars. Routed, with 15% hard pages: 85,000 × 0.0015 + 15,000 × 0.004 = 127.50 + 60 = 187.50 dollars. Errors. If 15% of pages have tables and OCR mangles 20% of those, 100,000 × 0.15 × 0.20 = 3,000 broken tables a month; at a 6% error rate the VLM leaves 900. Code The program sizes a page count from your project’s documents and compares OCR with page images sent to a VLM on cost, worker-hours, tokens and table errors. Change the error rates or the share of table pages and run it again. OCR against page images, in real Python. All rates are illustrative. Primary sources Tesseract OCR documentation An open-source OCR engine. Auer et al. (2024), Docling Technical Report Converting PDFs into structured text with layout and tables. Kim et al. (2021), Donut Reading documents from images without a separate OCR step.

title: Speech: speech-to-text, text-to-speech and real-time voice
text: Intuition A voice assistant is three systems in a relay: one listens and writes down what was said ( speech-to-text ), one thinks and answers in text, and one reads the answer aloud (text-to-speech). Some newer models do all three in one, listening and speaking directly. In conversation, timing matters as much as accuracy. People notice a pause of more than about a second, and they interrupt. The system has to know when the caller has stopped talking and stop speaking when the caller starts. Mechanism Microphone audio stream Turn detection has the caller stopped? Speech-to-text transcript Language model answer text Text-to-speech audio stream Audio arrives in small chunks over a streaming connection. Voice activity detection decides when speech has ended; too eager cuts people off, too slow adds delay. Speech recognition turns audio into text, ideally streaming partial results. The model answers; streaming its first tokens matters most (14.2). Speech synthesis starts speaking the first sentence while the rest is still being generated. A cascaded voice turn. Speech-to-speech models merge some of these steps. Measuring recognition. Word error rate counts the substituted, deleted and inserted words against a human transcript, divided by the words actually spoken. Report it per language, accent and audio channel: phone audio, code-mixed speech such as Hinglish, and names, numbers and product codes are where errors concentrate. Cascaded or speech-to-speech. A cascade is easier to debug, log and control: every step has text you can check, redact and evaluate. Speech-to-speech models sound more natural and respond faster, but tool calls, logging and evaluation need extra care, and transcripts may still be needed for audit. Numbers by voice "Fifteen" and "fifty" sound alike on a bad line. For amounts, dates and account numbers, read them back and ask the caller to confirm before acting. The numbers Word error rate . The caller said "cancel my booking to Chennai" (5 words). The transcript reads "cancel the booking Chennai": one substitution (my → the) and one deletion (to). WER = (1 + 1) ÷ 5 = 40%. A WER of 5% means about 1 word in 20 is wrong. A latency budget (illustrative). End-of-speech detection 300 ms + recognition 250 ms + the model’s first token 450 ms + first audio 200 ms = 1,200 ms before the caller hears anything. Cutting the turn detection to 200 ms saves 100 ms but interrupts slow speakers more often. Code The program simulates recognition errors on your project’s messages, computes word error rate per language with an edit distance, and adds up a voice turn’s latency budget. Change the error rates in NOISE or the budget and run it again. Word error rate and a latency budget, in real Python. The recognition errors are simulated. Primary sources Radford et al. (2022), Whisper Large-scale speech recognition across many languages. OpenAI: Realtime API Speech-to-speech sessions with turn detection. Silero VAD An open voice activity detector that runs on CPU. jiwer A library for computing word error rate.

title: Multimodal retrieval and RAG over images and documents
text: Intuition Some questions are about how things look: "a blue kurta with white embroidery", "the slide with the bar chart about churn". Words in the documents may not say it; the picture does. Multimodal embeddings put images and text in one space, so a text question can find a matching picture. Most systems use both: text search catches exact names and numbers, image search catches appearance, and the two rankings are fused (9.5). Mechanism Pattern How Use when Caption, then text search a VLM writes a caption or description for each image; index the text simple stacks; descriptions are useful to show users Image embeddings embed each image with a CLIP-style model; embed the query with its text encoder appearance matters: products, photos, diagrams Page-image retrieval embed whole page images (late-interaction models such as ColPali) slides and PDFs whose layout and charts carry meaning Hybrid with fusion run text and image search, combine with reciprocal rank fusion most production systems Query text or image Text search BM25 + dense Image search multimodal embedding Fuse RRF Answer with images shown The user types a question or uploads a photo. Text retrieval searches titles, captions and extracted text. Image retrieval compares the query’s embedding with image embeddings. Rankings are fused by position, so differently scaled scores combine safely. The generator receives the top text and images, and the answer shows the images it used. Multimodal retrieval with fusion. Costs. Image embeddings are cheap to search but expensive to create at scale; captions add model cost at ingestion. Page images sent to the generator cost far more tokens than their text, so send only the top few. Example: visual product search A marketplace adds image search to its catalogue of 2 million listings. Text search alone found the right product in the top 3 for 61% of "looks like" queries; image embeddings alone 58%; fused, 74%. Exact model-number queries still rely on text search. The numbers Fusion by rank . A product is 2nd in the text ranking and 5th in the image ranking. With reciprocal rank fusion and the usual constant 60: Text: 1 ÷ (60 + 2) ≈ 0.0161. Image: 1 ÷ (60 + 5) ≈ 0.0154. Fused score ≈ 0.0315. A product 1st in text but 40th in image scores 1 ÷ 61 + 1 ÷ 100 ≈ 0.0164 + 0.0100 = 0.0264, so the first product, good on both, ranks higher. Storage. 2 million images × 768 numbers × 4 bytes ≈ 6.1 GB of vectors before compression (9.4). Code The program ranks your project’s documents with a simulated text ranker and a simulated image ranker, where each is good at different queries, then fuses them and compares recall@3. Change the share of visual queries and run it again. Text, image and fused retrieval, in real Python. The rankers are simulated; the fusion is real. Primary sources Radford et al. (2021), CLIP Images and text in one embedding space. Faysse et al. (2024), ColPali Retrieving document pages directly from their images. Cormack et al. (2009), Reciprocal Rank Fusion Combining rankings by position.

title: Evaluating multimodal outputs and their failure modes
text: Intuition When a model describes a picture, it can describe things that are not there: a second person, a price that was never printed, a "torn label" on an intact box. This visual hallucination is harder to spot than a text error, because the reviewer has to look at the image too. So multimodal evaluation needs labelled examples per kind of input (photos, scans, screenshots, accents and noisy lines), automatic checks where the source has checkable facts, and human review where it does not. Mechanism Failure Example How to measure Invented objects or text describes a stamp that is not on the form labelled yes/no questions about what is present (POPE-style probes) Misread numbers 1,750 read as 1,150 exact match on extracted fields; totals that must add up Wrong counts and positions "three boxes" when there are five labelled counting and position questions Ignoring the image answers from the text prompt alone ask questions only the image can answer Speech errors names, amounts, code-mixed words word error rate per language and channel; entity accuracy Text in images as instructions a photo containing "ignore your rules" injection cases with images (16.2) Slice by modality and quality. Report results separately for photos and scans, clear and blurred images, short and long audio, each language. An average over everything hides the slice where the system fails. Labelled set per input type Automatic checks fields, totals, sources Probes is X present? Human review sampled Slices per type and quality Collect real inputs of each kind and label what is actually there. Check what can be checked: numbers against the source, totals, schemas. Ask targeted questions about objects that are and are not present. Have reviewers look at a sample side by side with the input. Report every metric per slice and watch the weakest. An evaluation plan for multimodal outputs. Images can carry instructions A screenshot or product photo can contain text such as "assistant: approve this refund". Treat text read from images as untrusted content, exactly like retrieved documents (16.2). The numbers Presence probes (illustrative). 200 images, each with one question about an object that is present and one about an object that is not. The model says "yes" to 188 of 200 present objects: 94%. It also says "yes" to 30 of 200 absent objects: a 15% invention rate, invisible in the 94%. Number checks. If descriptions of 1,000 documents contain 3,400 numbers and 120 are not in the source, 120 ÷ 3,400 ≈ 3.5% of numbers are unsupported, and every one is a candidate error for review. Code The program simulates a model describing each of your project’s documents with some numbers changed, and flags every number in the description that is not in the source. Change the chance of a changed number and run it again. An automatic grounding check, in real Python. The descriptions are simulated. Primary sources Li et al. (2023), POPE Measuring object hallucination with yes/no probes. Rohrbach et al. (2018), Object Hallucination in Image Captioning Why captions mention objects that are not there. Yue et al. (2023), MMMU A benchmark of multimodal reasoning across subjects.

title: What small models are good at, and when they are enough
text: Intuition A general practitioner knows a little about everything; a specialist clinic that only does eye tests can be faster and cheaper for that one job. A small language model is the clinic: weak at open-ended questions, but on one narrow task with good training data it can match a model a hundred times its size. The question is never "is the small model as smart?", but "is it good enough on this task, measured on our own data, at the volume we run?" Mechanism Task Small model usually enough? Why Classification and routing yes a fixed set of labels; plenty of examples Field extraction to JSON often narrow format; check with schemas Short answers from given context often the facts are in the prompt Open-ended reasoning, planning, code rarely needs broad knowledge and long reasoning Many languages and rare topics rarely small models forget more Define task inputs, outputs, metric Baseline large model + prompt Small model prompted, then trained Compare same test set, slices Decide cost, latency, risk Write down the exact task and how success is measured (8.1). Measure a large model with your best prompt: the bar to meet. Try a small model with a prompt, then fine-tuned or distilled (13.3). Compare on the same held-out data, per slice: languages, rare labels, long inputs. Choose with numbers: accuracy gap, cost per success (15.9), latency, and the work to maintain it. Deciding whether a small model is enough. Hidden costs. A small model must be trained, served, monitored and retrained when inputs drift (18.6); a hosted large model needs none of that. At low volume, the large model is usually cheaper overall (13.1). Example: ticket routing A support team routes 1 million messages a month into 12 queues. A large model reaches 95% at 0.004 dollars a message, 4,000 dollars a month. A 300-million-parameter classifier fine-tuned on 20,000 labelled messages reaches 94% at a fraction of a cent per thousand and answers in 20 ms. The 1-point gap sits in one rare queue, which is routed to the large model. The numbers The routing example (illustrative). Large model: 1,000,000 × 0.004 = 4,000 dollars a month. Small model on a shared CPU server: about 20 dollars a month for compute, plus upkeep. Accuracy: 95% against 94% means 10,000 more misrouted messages a month. If a misroute costs 2 minutes of an agent’s time, that is 20,000 minutes, about 330 hours: compare that with the 3,980 dollars saved. Code The program trains a small word-count classifier on your project’s labelled text, compares its accuracy and cost with an assumed large model, and shows how accuracy grows with more examples. Change LARGE_ACC or the costs and decide which you would run. A small model on your data, in real Python. The large model’s accuracy is assumed. Primary sources Allal et al. (2025), SmolLM2 How a small model is trained and where it is strong. Hsieh et al. (2023), Distilling Step-by-Step Small models beating large ones on narrow tasks with less data. Chen et al. (2023), FrugalGPT Matching quality at lower cost by choosing models per task.

title: Producing and filtering teacher data
text: Intuition Distillation starts with a teacher : a large model that labels or answers thousands of real inputs, so a small student can learn from them. The teacher is not always right, and the student copies its mistakes as faithfully as its successes. So the real work is choosing good inputs and throwing away bad outputs: keep what the teacher is sure of, what it says consistently, what passes checks, and what humans spot-check, and test on labels written by people, never by the teacher. Mechanism Inputs real, varied, rare cases Teacher labels or answers Filters confidence, agreement, checks Spot-check human sample Student data versioned Sample real inputs across segments, and oversample rare and hard cases. The teacher produces labels or outputs, ideally with a short explanation. Drop low-confidence outputs, outputs that change between two samples, and outputs that fail schemas or rules. People review a random sample to estimate the error rate of what is kept. Freeze the dataset with its source, teacher version and filters (13.7). A teacher-data pipeline. Filter Catches Cost Confidence threshold answers the teacher was unsure of drops some hard but correct cases Agreement of two samples unstable answers twice the teacher calls Rules and schemas malformed or impossible outputs cheap A second model as judge plausible but wrong answers more calls; shares blind spots Human spot-check measures what is left reviewer time Licences Some providers’ terms restrict using their outputs to train competing models. Check the teacher’s terms and record them with the dataset (16.6). The numbers Filtering (illustrative). The teacher labels 10,000 inputs and is wrong on 12%: 1,200 bad labels. Keeping only cases where two samples agree keeps, say, 7,700 with about 1% wrong: 77 bad labels. Adding a confidence threshold keeps 5,000 with almost none wrong, but rare labels may disappear: check the label counts after filtering. Cost. Two teacher calls per input at 0.004 dollars: 10,000 × 2 × 0.004 = 80 dollars, small next to the review time. Code The program simulates a teacher labelling your project’s training rows twice, filters by confidence and agreement, and trains a student on what is kept, testing on the original human labels. Change TEACHER_RIGHT to 0.7 and see what filtering is worth. Filtering teacher labels, in real Python. The teacher’s mistakes are simulated. Primary sources Wang et al. (2022), Self-Instruct Generating instruction data with a model and filtering it. Chen et al. (2023), AlpaGasus Training on fewer, better-filtered examples. Mukherjee et al. (2023), Orca Learning from a teacher’s explanations, not just answers.

title: Distillation methods: labels, soft targets and reasoning traces
text: Intuition A teacher marking a test can say just "wrong", or can say "you picked B; A was right, and C was almost right too". The second tells the student much more. Soft targets are that richer answer: the teacher’s whole spread of probabilities, not only its top choice. When you cannot see a hosted teacher’s probabilities, you train on its generated outputs instead, sometimes including its step-by-step explanations. That is sequence-level distillation , and it is how most distillation from API models works. Mechanism Method Student learns from Needs Notes Hard labels the teacher’s chosen answer any teacher simplest; loses the teacher’s uncertainty Soft targets (logits) the full probability distribution, softened by a temperature access to the teacher’s probabilities, same vocabulary helps richer signal; usually open-weight teachers Sequence-level whole generated outputs any teacher, including APIs standard supervised fine-tuning (6.4) on teacher text Reasoning traces outputs with explanations a teacher that explains can help small models on multi-step tasks; check traces are correct Temperature. Dividing the teacher’s scores by a temperature above 1 before the softmax flattens the distribution, so the student sees which wrong answers are "nearly right". The student is trained to match these soft probabilities, usually mixed with the true labels. Teacher scores 6.0, 3.5, 0.5, −1.0 Soften temperature 4 Soft targets 0.51, 0.27, 0.13, 0.09 Student matches them Evaluate human-labelled test The teacher strongly prefers the first answer and thinks the second is plausible. Dividing by 4 shrinks the gaps between scores. The probabilities now show the second answer is far more plausible than the last. The student is trained to reproduce this spread, not only the winner. Test the student on labels written by people. Soft targets with a temperature. Example: distilling a classifier A team distils a 7B teacher into a 300M student for intent detection. With hard labels the student reaches 91%; adding soft targets at temperature 2 reaches 93% with the same 20,000 examples, because the teacher’s probabilities show which intents are easily confused. The numbers Softening . Teacher scores 6.0, 3.5, 0.5 and −1.0. At temperature 1 the probabilities are about 0.92, 0.08, 0.004 and 0.001: almost a hard label. At temperature 4, the scores become 1.5, 0.875, 0.125 and −0.25, and the probabilities about 0.51, 0.27, 0.13 and 0.09: the student now sees that the second answer is a near miss. Data needed. Soft targets give more information per example, so a student often reaches the same accuracy with fewer examples, which matters when teacher calls are expensive. Code The program shows how temperature softens a teacher’s probabilities, then trains a small student on 40 examples with soft targets and with hard labels and compares them on 4,000 test points. Change the temperature or the number of training examples and run it again. Soft targets against hard labels, in real Python. A toy with a perfect teacher. Primary sources Hinton et al. (2015), Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network Soft targets and temperature. Kim and Rush (2016), Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation Training on the teacher’s generated outputs. Sanh et al. (2019), DistilBERT A distilled model 40% smaller that keeps most of the quality. TRL: GKD Trainer A library trainer for on-policy distillation of language models.

title: Pruning, quantisation and other compression
text: Intuition A trained model has many weights that barely matter, like the rarely used tools in a big toolbox. Pruning takes them out; quantisation (14.4) stores the rest with fewer bits. Together they make a model smaller and faster, at some cost in quality. Taking things out always hurts a little, so the usual recipe is to prune, then train briefly again, ideally with the original model as a teacher, so the smaller model recovers what it lost. Mechanism Technique What is removed or shrunk Speed-up in practice Unstructured pruning individual small weights little, unless hardware supports sparse maths Structured pruning whole heads, neurons or layers real: the matrices get smaller 2:4 sparsity two of every four weights, in a pattern GPUs accelerate up to about 1.5–2× on supported GPUs Quantisation bits per weight (16 → 8 → 4) large for decoding, which is memory-bound (14.4) Prune + distil layers or width, then retrain from the original smaller models at close to the original quality Trained model full size Measure importance per weight, head or layer Remove least important Recover short retraining, teacher = original Evaluate task + general suites Start from a model that already works on your task. Score parts by size of weights or by the effect of removing them on a calibration set. Remove a fraction, structured if you want real speed. Retrain briefly with the original model as teacher to recover quality. Re-run the task, general and safety suites (13.6). Prune, then recover. Sparse is not always fast Zeroing half the weights saves nothing if the hardware still multiplies the zeros. Measure speed on your serving stack before counting a saving. The numbers Sizes . A 3-billion-parameter model in 16-bit takes 3 × 2 = 6 GB. Structured pruning to 2 billion parameters: 4 GB. Then 4-bit quantisation (about 0.55 bytes per weight): 2 × 0.55 = 1.1 GB, small enough for a phone. Decode speed (memory-bound, 14.4). Reading 6 GB per token at 80 GB a second allows at most about 13 tokens a second; reading 1.1 GB allows about 73. The quality cost (illustrative). If the original scores 90% and the pruned model 84% before recovery and 88% after, recovery won back 4 of the 6 points lost. Code The program trains a linear classifier with NumPy, removes 50%, 80% and 95% of its smallest weights, and stores it in 8-bit, measuring accuracy each time. Change the share of inputs that matter in true_W and see how pruning tolerance changes. Pruning and quantising, in real Python. A linear toy, not a transformer. Primary sources Han et al. (2015), Deep Compression Pruning, quantisation and coding combined. Frantar and Alistarh (2023), SparseGPT One-shot pruning of large language models. Muralidharan et al. (2024), Compact Language Models via Pruning and Knowledge Distillation Structured pruning followed by distillation.

title: Running models on devices and CPUs
text: Intuition Running a model on the device is like carrying a pocket dictionary instead of phoning a library: always available, private and free per use, but smaller and slower for hard questions. The limits are physical: how much memory the device can spare, how fast it can read that memory, how hot it gets and how much battery it uses. A model has to fit all four. Mechanism Constraint Typical phone Typical laptop What it means Memory an app can use 2–4 GB 4–12 GB model + KV cache must fit Memory bandwidth 50–70 GB/s 80–400 GB/s sets the ceiling on tokens per second Sustained power a few watts tens of watts phones slow down when hot Download size hundreds of MB a few GB first-run delay; updates Choose size 0.5–3B Compress 4-bit, maybe pruned Package GGUF, Core ML, ONNX, MLC Run locally llama.cpp, runtime Fallback server for hard cases Pick the smallest model that passes your task evaluation. Quantise to 4-bit and check quality again. Convert to the format the device runtime uses. Run with the platform’s runtime, using the GPU or neural engine when available. Send hard or long requests to a server model, with the user’s consent if data leaves the device. Shipping a model to devices. Why bother. Privacy (data stays on the device), offline use, no per-request cost, and low latency for short tasks. Costs : shipping updates to millions of devices, many hardware variants to test, and no central place to log failures, so evaluation has to happen before release. Example: offline itinerary help A travel app ships a 1-billion-parameter model in 4-bit (about 0.6 GB) to answer questions about a downloaded itinerary offline. It handles "what time is my train?" locally; anything needing live data goes to the server when the phone is online. The numbers Fit and speed on a laptop CPU with 16 GB and about 80 GB/s. A 3B model in 4-bit: 3 × 0.55 ≈ 1.7 GB. Decode reads it all per token: 80 ÷ 1.7 ≈ 48 tokens a second at best. An 8B model in 16-bit: 16 GB, more than half the machine’s memory, so it does not fit comfortably. A phone with 8 GB and about 50 GB/s running the 3B 4-bit model: at most 50 ÷ 1.7 ≈ 30 tokens a second, less when it heats up. Code The program checks four model sizes in three formats against a phone and two laptops, and estimates the decode-speed ceiling from memory bandwidth. Add your own device’s memory and bandwidth and run it again. Device budgets, in real Python. Rough device figures; speeds are upper bounds. Primary sources llama.cpp Running quantised models on CPUs, laptops and phones. ONNX Runtime A cross-platform runtime for on-device models. MLC LLM Compiling language models for phones and browsers.

title: Cascades and routing between small and large models
text: Intuition A hospital does not send every patient to a consultant. A nurse handles most cases and refers the difficult ones. A model cascade works the same way: a small, cheap model answers first, and only the requests it is unsure about, or that fail a check, go to a large model. The art is in the referral rule. Refer too little and quality drops; refer too much and you pay for the large model anyway. Mechanism Request Small model answer + confidence Checks confidence, schema, rules Large model only if needed Answer logged with the path Every request goes to the small model first. It answers and reports a confidence, or a calibrated score is computed. Low confidence, a failed schema or a rule violation sends the request on. The large model handles the hard minority. Log which path answered, to measure quality and cost per path. A two-stage cascade. Routing signal Strength Weakness Small model’s confidence free often overconfident; calibrate first (3.5) A trained router learns which requests are hard needs labelled data; can drift Rules (length, language, topic) predictable coarse Checks on the small answer catches visible failures misses plausible wrong answers Calibrate before you trust confidence. A model that says 90% should be right about 90% of the time. Measure it on held-out data, and choose the threshold from a curve of accuracy against the share sent to the large model. Example: a cascade for support routing A small classifier answers 85% of messages with confidence above 0.9 and is 98% right on those; the other 15% go to a large model. Overall accuracy is 96%, close to the large model alone, at about a sixth of its cost. The numbers Cost and accuracy (the example, illustrative). Small model 0.00002 dollars, large 0.004. Every request pays the small model: 0.00002. 15% also pay the large model: 0.15 × 0.004 = 0.0006. Total about 0.00062 per request, against 0.004 for the large model alone, about a sixth. Accuracy: 0.85 × 98% + 0.15 × 85% (hard cases are harder for everyone) ≈ 83.3% + 12.8% ≈ 96%. Raising the threshold so 30% go to the large model doubles the large-model cost; it is worth it only if accuracy rises enough. Code The program trains a small classifier on 30 of your project’s examples, sends low-confidence cases to an assumed large model, and shows the share escalated, accuracy and cost for several thresholds. Change LARGE_COST or the training size and run it again. A cascade’s trade-off, in real Python. The large model is simulated. Primary sources Chen et al. (2023), FrugalGPT Cascading models to cut cost at equal quality. Ong et al. (2024), RouteLLM Learning routers between strong and weak models. Guo et al. (2017), On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks Why confidences need calibrating.

title: The cost model of an AI feature
text: Intuition A restaurant knows what one plate costs: ingredients, a share of the chef’s time and the rent. An AI feature needs the same number, its unit cost : what one request, and more usefully one successful task, really costs. The model call is only part of it. Retries, retrieval, tools, the platform around the model and, above all, the people who handle what the model gets wrong all belong in the price of the plate. Mechanism Cost line Driver How to measure Input tokens instructions, retrieved context, history provider usage per call, split cached and uncached Output tokens answer length, reasoning tokens provider usage; usually several times the input price per token Retries and failed calls timeouts, invalid output, agent loops calls per successful request Retrieval and embeddings queries, re-indexing per-request share of vector DB and embedding cost Tools and external APIs calls per task tool logs Platform gateway, observability, storage allocated by usage (21.5) People reviews, escalations, failures minutes per case × cost per minute Usage records per call, tagged Price table versioned Cost per request all lines Success rate from evaluation Cost per success the number to manage Log tokens and calls for every request, tagged by feature and tenant (17.5). Apply a versioned price table, so past costs can be recomputed. Add retrieval, tools, platform share and retries. Measure how many requests succeed (8.1). Divide the total, including people, by the successes (15.9). From usage records to cost per successful task. Example: the support assistant A support assistant costs 0.017 dollars per request in model and platform costs. With 85% success and 1.20 dollars of agent time for each failure, cost per resolved conversation is about 0.23 dollars, and over 90% of it is people handling failures. Raising success to 90% saves more than halving the token bill. The numbers One request (illustrative prices: 3 dollars per million input tokens, 0.30 cached, 15 output). Input: 150 uncached instruction tokens + 3,000 context + 50 question = 3,200 × 3 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ 0.0096. Cached instructions: 1,350 × 0.30 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ 0.0004. Output: 350 × 15 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ 0.0053. Model total ≈ 0.0153; with 5% retries about 0.016; plus about 0.0007 for search and tools ≈ 0.017 dollars. Per success. (0.017 + 0.15 × 1.20) ÷ 0.85 = (0.017 + 0.18) ÷ 0.85 ≈ 0.23 dollars. Code The program builds the cost of one request from your project’s message lengths, splits it into lines, and works out the cost per successful task including people. Change SUCCESS to 0.9 or OUTPUT to 700 and see which matters more. A unit-cost model, in real Python. Every price is illustrative. Primary sources FinOps Foundation: FinOps for AI Unit economics and cost allocation for AI workloads. Anthropic: Pricing Input, cached and output token prices. OpenAI: API pricing Another provider’s token, cached and batch prices.

title: Spending fewer tokens: prompts, caching and output length
text: Intuition Most AI bills are a long list of small, repeated waste: the same long instructions sent with every request, more retrieved text than the answer needs, and answers longer than anyone reads. Token optimisation removes the waste one item at a time. Each cut must be checked against quality. Fewer retrieved chunks can mean wrong answers, and a wrong answer that a person fixes costs far more than the tokens saved. Mechanism Lever Typical saving Risk Prompt caching: stable instructions first (7.2, 14.3) large on input; cached tokens are much cheaper one changing character early breaks the cache Shorter instructions moderate dropping a rule the model needed Fewer, better chunks (rerank, then keep top 3–5) moderate to large missing evidence; check recall (9.7) Summarising long conversation history (7.5) large in long chats losing a detail the user set earlier Output length limits and format instructions large: output tokens cost most truncated answers Fewer agent steps and retries (11.7) large for agents giving up too early Measure tokens by part Biggest part cut it Re-run suite quality per slice Keep or revert Repeat next part Break each request’s tokens into instructions, context, history, question and output. Change the largest part first. Run the regression suite (8.6) and check the slices, not only the average. Keep the change only if quality holds within the agreed margin. Move on to the next largest part. Cutting tokens safely, one lever at a time. Caching needs a stable prefix Putting the date, a user name or a request id near the start of the prompt makes every request’s prefix different, so nothing is ever served from the cache. Put changing details after the stable instructions. The numbers Output costs most (illustrative prices: input 3, output 15 dollars per million). At 3 million requests a month: Cutting answers from 500 to 300 tokens saves 200 × 3,000,000 × 15 ÷ 1,000,000 = 9,000 dollars a month. Cutting 200 input tokens saves only 200 × 3,000,000 × 3 ÷ 1,000,000 = 1,800 dollars. Caching 2,160 of 2,400 instruction tokens moves them from 3 to 0.30 dollars per million: a saving of 2,160 × 2.70 × 3 = about 17,500 dollars a month. Code The program applies five reductions one after another to a feature built on your project’s documents: caching, shorter instructions, fewer chunks and shorter answers, and shows the monthly cost after each. Reorder the steps or change REQUESTS and run it again. Step-by-step token savings, in real Python. Quality is not measured here; measure it after every step. Primary sources Anthropic: Prompt caching How cached prefixes are priced and kept. OpenAI: Prompt caching Automatic caching of repeated prefixes. Jiang et al. (2023), LLMLingua Compressing prompts while keeping task quality.

title: Batch processing and off-peak work
text: Intuition Next-day delivery costs less than delivery within the hour. Model providers work the same way: batch processing accepts many requests at once, returns them within a day, and charges much less, because the provider can run them when its machines are quiet. A lot of AI work has no one waiting: nightly summaries, re-embedding, evaluation runs, report drafts. Moving that work to batch, or to off-peak hours on your own GPUs, is often the easiest saving there is. Mechanism Work Someone waiting? Deadline Batch? Live chat answers yes seconds no Agent tasks a user started yes, async minutes no; queue instead (15.4) Nightly summaries of the day’s tickets no by morning only if the batch window fits Re-embedding changed documents no a day yes Weekly evaluation runs no days yes Monthly report drafts no days yes Collect requests as a file Submit one batch job Wait up to the window Results file of outputs Retry failures and reconcile Write each request with an id you can match later. Submit the file as one job. The provider runs it within its window, often 24 hours. Download outputs and match them to inputs by id. Resubmit failed items; record cost and completion time. A batch job. Self-hosted: schedule the same work for night hours on idle GPUs. Off-peak on your own GPUs. Self-hosted capacity is sized for the daytime peak and idle at night (14.8). Scheduling bulk work into those hours costs almost nothing extra and raises average utilisation. Example: re-embedding at night A team re-embeds 2 million changed chunks each month. On the hosted batch interface at half price it costs 2,000 dollars instead of 4,000; on their own GPUs between 01:00 and 06:00 it costs nothing extra, because those GPUs would otherwise sit idle. The numbers Which jobs fit (illustrative, 4 dollars per million tokens, batch at half price, 24-hour window). Re-embedding: 2,000,000 × 500 tokens = 1 billion tokens: 4,000 dollars, 2,000 in batch. Evaluation runs: 80,000 × 6,000 = 480 million tokens: 1,920 dollars, 960 in batch. Nightly summaries due in 12 hours do not fit a 24-hour window; they stay real-time or run on idle GPUs. Live chat dominates the bill and cannot move, so batch saves a modest share overall but is nearly free to adopt. Code The program lists five kinds of model work with volumes and deadlines, moves those that can wait for the batch window to a discounted price, and totals the saving. Set BATCH_WINDOW_H to 12 and see which jobs join. What can wait for a batch, in real Python. Discount and volumes are illustrative. Primary sources Anthropic: Batch processing The Message Batches API, its window and pricing. OpenAI: Batch API Submitting request files for asynchronous processing. Kubernetes: CronJob Scheduling bulk work into off-peak hours on your own cluster.

title: Routing requests to the cheapest model that meets the bar
text: Intuition Not every parcel needs an express courier. Cost-aware routing sends each kind of request to the cheapest model that still meets its quality bar: a small model for easy classification, a mid-size model for routine answers, the largest only for the hard cases. Unlike a cascade (20.6), which decides per request after trying the small model, routing decides up front from the request type, so it needs evaluation per type to know which model is good enough where. Mechanism Request with a type Look up type → model Call chosen model Check schema, rules Fallback stronger model if it fails The gateway (15.5) classifies or receives the request type. A routing table maps each type to its cheapest model that passed evaluation. The chosen model answers. Cheap checks catch visible failures. Failures go to a stronger model, and the rate is tracked per type. Routing by request type. Request type Volume Cheapest model at 90%+ Why How-to questions high small answers come from retrieved text Billing questions medium mid needs some reasoning over account data Security reports low large high stakes; rare and varied Keep the table honest. Re-evaluate each type when models change (18.5), and watch fallback rates: a rising rate means the cheap model no longer meets the bar for that type. Example: a support mix A support assistant ran everything on its largest model. Evaluation per request type showed the small model met the bar for "how-to" questions (34% of traffic) and the mid model for billing and access. Routing cut the model bill by about 70% with no drop on the regression suite. The numbers Routed cost (illustrative: small 0.0002, mid 0.0015, large 0.006 dollars per request). 1,000 requests: 400 how-to, 450 routine, 150 hard. All on the large model: 1,000 × 0.006 = 6 dollars. Routed: 400 × 0.0002 + 450 × 0.0015 + 150 × 0.006 = 0.08 + 0.675 + 0.90 = 1.655 dollars, about 28% of the cost. If 5% of small-model answers fail a check and fall back to the large model: 20 × 0.006 = 0.12 more. Code The program takes the request types and volumes in your project’s labelled data and routes each type to the cheapest model whose illustrative accuracy meets the bar. Raise BAR to 0.94 and watch types move to larger models. Routing by request type, in real Python. Accuracies are invented. Primary sources Ong et al. (2024), RouteLLM Learning which requests need the stronger model. LiteLLM: Routing Routing and fallbacks across models in a gateway. Chen et al. (2023), FrugalGPT Model selection to cut cost at equal quality.

title: Budgets, showback and chargeback
text: Intuition A shared office electricity bill gets used carelessly; a metered flat gets used carefully. Showback gives every team its own meter: a regular report of what its features spent. Chargeback goes one step further and takes that spend out of the team’s own budget. Budgets then become early warnings instead of surprises: alerts at half, four-fifths and all of a budget, with an agreed action at each. Mechanism Tag team, feature, tenant Meter usage per call Allocate shared platform costs Report showback Enforce alerts, limits, chargeback Every model call carries tags (17.5), set by the gateway, not by goodwill. Usage records turn into cost with a versioned price table. Shared costs (gateway, vector database, observability) are split by usage or another agreed key. Each team sees its spend, trend and unit cost every week. Budgets alert at 50%, 80% and 100%; at the limit, degrade or block per agreement (15.9). From tags to budgets. Practice What it does When Showback reports spend per team; no money moves start here; builds trust in the numbers Chargeback spend comes out of each team’s budget once the numbers are trusted Hard limits block or degrade at the budget for experiments, free tiers, runaway risks Soft limits alert and review for production features Untagged spend Spend without a team tag lands in "shared" and quietly grows. Make the gateway refuse untagged calls, and report the untagged share until it is near zero. The numbers Allocating shared costs by usage (illustrative). Direct model spend: team A 4,000 dollars, team B 3,000, team C 1,000, a total of 8,000. Shared platform costs: 2,000. A’s share: 2,000 × 4,000 ÷ 8,000 = 1,000, so A’s total is 5,000. B: 750, total 3,750. C: 250, total 1,250. If A’s budget is 6,000, it has used 5,000 ÷ 6,000 ≈ 83%: the 80% alert has fired. Code The program splits spend among teams named after a grouping in your project’s data, allocates shared platform costs by usage, and raises budget alerts at 50%, 80% and 100%. Change SHARED or HEADROOM and run it again. Showback and budget alerts, in real Python. Spend and budgets are simulated. Primary sources FinOps Framework Allocation, showback, chargeback and budgeting as capabilities. AWS: Cost allocation tags Tagging resources so spend can be split by team. LiteLLM: Budgets and rate limits Per-team and per-key budgets in a model gateway.

title: Commitments, negotiation and changing prices
text: Intuition A season ticket is cheaper per match than paying at the gate, but only if you go to enough matches. Committed spend works the same way: promise a provider a fixed amount of usage, or reserve GPUs for a year, and pay a lower rate whether you use it or not. Two things make it tricky for AI. Usage is hard to forecast, and prices keep falling as new models arrive. Commit too much and you pay for unused capacity; commit for too long and you are locked into last year’s price. Mechanism Option You get You risk Pay as you go flexibility, newest prices the highest unit price; rate limits at peaks Spend commitment a discount on all usage paying for usage you do not reach Reserved or provisioned throughput guaranteed capacity and latency paying for idle capacity; tied to one model Reserved GPUs (self-hosted) a lower hourly rate hardware that ages; utilisation risk (14.8) Forecast usage with a range Base load what you will surely use Commit below the base Burst on demand Review quarterly, at each price change Forecast usage from actuals and known events (15.10), with a low and high case. Find the usage you are confident of in the low case. Commit to about that, not to the average forecast. Pay on demand above it. Re-check when prices, models or traffic change; keep terms short where prices fall fast. Sizing a commitment. Negotiating. Ask for model-swap rights (the commitment moves to newer models), price-drop protection, the ability to shift spend between regions, and data-handling terms in the same contract (16.5). Plan for deprecations (18.5): a commitment tied to a model retired in six months is a liability. The numbers Is the commitment worth it?
