On-demand costs 1.00 a unit; committed units cost 0.70 each, paid even if unused. Forecast: 100 units a month, give or take 25. Commit 100: in a month that uses 75 units you pay 100 × 0.70 = 70, still less than 75 on demand, though 25 paid units sat idle. A month with 60 units used: commitment 70 against 60 on demand, a loss of 10. Committing a bit below the forecast, about 85, keeps most of the discount and rarely pays for idle units. Price cuts. If on-demand prices fall 40% halfway through the year, on demand becomes 0.60, below the committed 0.70: a long commitment then costs more than not committing. Code The program simulates 5,000 possible years of uncertain usage and compares the expected cost of committing to different monthly amounts, with and without a 40% on-demand price cut from month six. Change DISCOUNT or the spread of usage and run it again. Sizing a commitment under uncertainty, in real Python. Not any provider’s terms. Primary sources FinOps Framework: Rate optimisation Commitments, discounts and their risks. AWS: Savings Plans How a spend commitment works in practice. Anthropic: Model deprecations Why model lifetimes matter for long commitments.

title: Choosing where AI belongs in a product
text: Intuition AI is a good colleague for some jobs and a dangerous one for others. It shines where answers are hard to write as rules, mistakes are cheap, and a person can check the result quickly. It is a poor fit where rules already work, or where one mistake is expensive and hard to spot. The design question is also how much to let it decide: the level of automation . Suggesting is safe almost anywhere; acting alone needs low error costs, cheap undo and evidence that it works. Mechanism Level The AI… A person… Fits when Suggest offers options chooses errors are cheap; users are experts Draft for review prepares text or an action edits and approves checking is faster than doing Act with undo acts, with a visible undo window can reverse actions are reversible and errors rare Act alone decides and acts audits samples errors are cheap and measured to be rare Task what users need Rules enough? then use code Error cost who is hurt, how much Check cost how fast to verify Pick a level and measure it Start from the user’s job, not from the model. If rules capture it (a refund amount, a date check), write code (7.7). Estimate the cost of a wrong output and who bears it. Estimate how long a person needs to check an output. Choose the lowest level that delivers value, then raise it only with evidence. Deciding where AI belongs, and how much it decides. Example: a refund feature A team planned an assistant that approves refunds on its own. Mapping the task showed three parts: reading the customer’s message (a good fit for AI), calculating the amount (rules), and approving (high error cost). They shipped AI drafting with code computing the amount and a person approving refunds above a threshold (11.7). The numbers When review pays (illustrative). An agent writes a reply in 6 minutes; checking and editing an AI draft takes 2. At 1,000 replies a day: 6,000 minutes by hand against 2,000 with drafts, a saving of 4,000 minutes, about 67 hours a day. If drafts are wrong 10% of the time and a wrong draft costs 4 extra minutes: 100 × 4 = 400 minutes, still far less than the saving. When acting alone does not. If each wrong refund costs 2,000 rupees to recover and 1% of 10,000 daily refunds are wrong: 100 × 2,000 = 200,000 rupees a day. Code The program scores five candidate features on error tolerance, ease of checking, whether rules capture the task, volume and data, and suggests AI, AI with a person deciding, or plain code. Add a feature from your own product and score it. A fit check for AI features, in real Python. The scores are judgements; test with users. Primary sources Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook Deciding whether and how to use AI in a product. Microsoft: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction 18 tested guidelines for AI features. Amershi et al. (2019), Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction The study behind the guidelines.

title: Showing uncertainty, sources and citations
text: Intuition A good expert says "I’m not sure, but…" when they are not sure, and shows where they read something. An AI interface should do the same: show the sources behind an answer, mark statements it could not support, and say in plain words how far to trust it. That is showing uncertainty . The danger runs both ways. Confident wrong answers teach users to trust too much; warnings on every answer teach them to ignore warnings. Mechanism Pattern What users see Needs Inline citations a numbered source after each claim, opening the passage retrieval with source ids (9.6) Unsupported marking a sentence flagged "no source found" a support check per sentence Plain-language confidence "likely", "check this", not "0.73" calibrated scores (3.5) Show the evidence the passage or image region used stored spans and page links Abstain "I couldn’t find this in your documents" an abstention rule (9.6) Answer sentences Match sources per sentence Check support enough overlap or a judge Label cited, unverified, removed Render citations and notes The model drafts an answer with source ids. Each sentence is matched to the passages it relies on. A check decides whether the passage really supports it. Supported sentences get citations; unsupported ones are flagged or removed. The interface shows citations users can open, and plain-language notes. From an answer to a trustworthy display. Citations can mislead too A citation to a real document that does not actually say what the sentence claims is worse than no citation, because it looks verified. Check support, not only the presence of a source id. The numbers Calibration before labels (illustrative). On 1,000 held-out answers, those the model scored above 0.85 were right 93% of the time; those between 0.6 and 0.85, 78%; below 0.6, 51%. Labels "high", "medium" and "check this" then mean something users can learn. If uncalibrated scores above 0.85 were right only 70% of the time, "high" would mislead 3 users in 10. Too many warnings. If 40% of answers carry a warning, users see one every few answers and stop reading them. Aim the warning at the slice that needs it. Code The program builds an answer from two of your project’s documents plus one invented sentence, attaches a citation to each sentence by word overlap, flags the unsupported one, and maps scores to plain-language labels. Lower the overlap threshold and see the invented sentence get a citation it does not deserve. Citations and unsupported sentences, in real Python. Word overlap is a weak support check. Primary sources Google PAIR guidebook: Explainability and trust Showing confidence and sources in AI products. Anthropic: Citations Model answers with citations to exact passages. Guo et al. (2017), On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks Why raw scores need calibrating before users see them.

title: Streaming, latency and progress in the interface
text: Intuition A lift with a floor display feels faster than one without, even when both take the same time. Perceived latency depends mostly on how soon users see that something is happening, and whether they can tell how far along it is. So AI interfaces stream the answer as it is written, show the steps an agent has finished, and offer to send long results later, rather than leaving a spinner on screen for ten seconds. Mechanism Wait Pattern Why Under 1 second just answer feels instant 1–10 seconds stream tokens; show a short status attention holds if something moves 10 seconds to a few minutes show steps as they finish; allow cancel users need to know it is progressing Longer run in the background; notify when done nobody watches a screen for minutes (15.4) Request Acknowledge within 0.3 s First tokens streaming Steps shown as they finish Done or "we’ll notify you" The user sends a question or starts a task. Show at once that work has started. Stream the answer; the first words matter most (14.2). For agents, list finished steps: "found your booking", "checked fare rules". Finish, or move long work to the background with a notification. Designing the wait. Streaming has costs. Text that later turns out wrong has already been read; validation that needs the whole answer (a JSON schema, a safety check) must run before showing it, or the interface must be able to replace streamed text. Stream prose; hold back structured actions until they are checked. Example: an agent that explains its progress A rebooking agent takes 20 seconds. Shown as a spinner, many users refreshed the page and started a second request. Shown as steps ("found your booking", "checked three alternative flights", "comparing fares"), almost nobody did, and duplicate requests fell sharply. The numbers First feedback decides (illustrative). The full answer takes 9 seconds; the first token comes at 0.8. Waiting for the full answer: everyone sits 9 seconds with nothing on screen. Streaming: something appears at 0.8 seconds, 9 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 11 times sooner, though the answer finishes at the same moment. An agent with 6 steps of 4 seconds: 24 seconds in total, but showing each finished step means no silence longer than 4 seconds. Code The program simulates 10,000 users’ patience and compares how many give up before seeing anything when the interface waits, shows a progress step, or streams. Change TTFT and TOTAL to your own numbers and run it again. Perceived waiting time, in real Python. The patience model is invented. Primary sources Nielsen Norman Group: Response Times, the 3 Important Limits 0.1, 1 and 10 seconds as limits of attention. Nielsen Norman Group: Progress Indicators When to show spinners, steps and percentages. Anthropic: Streaming messages How streamed tokens and events reach the interface.

title: Human control: review, edit and undo
text: Intuition A good assistant hands you a draft letter to sign; it does not post it for you. Draft, review, commit keeps people in control: the AI prepares, a person checks and edits, and only then does anything leave the building. Where acting directly is worth it, an undo button with a clear time window gives people a way back. But undo has limits: a sent message or a transferred payment cannot be pulled back, so those stay behind a review. Mechanism Pattern How it works Use for Suggestion chips one click accepts, ignoring is free replies, tags, next steps Editable draft the person edits freely before sending messages, letters, documents Diff view shows exactly what will change edits to records, code, documents Approval with exact parameters shows the action, amount, target and evidence (11.7) payments, bookings, permissions Undo window action happens, reversible for N minutes reversible actions: labels, moves, drafts saved AI proposes draft or action Show diff, evidence, impact Person edits or approves Commit logged with who approved Undo or reconcile within the window, or after The AI prepares the text or action with its reasons. Show what will change, the evidence and the consequences. The person edits or approves; edits are good feedback (18.6). The approved version, and only that version, is executed and logged. Reversible actions offer undo; irreversible ones need a reconciliation process instead. Keeping people in control. Rubber-stamping If reviewers approve 99% of drafts without changes, review has become a click. Watch edit rates and blind-check a sample (13.2), and design the review screen so the important parameters cannot be missed. The numbers Layers of protection (illustrative). 150 proposed actions, 6% wrong: about 9 mistakes. Reviewers see the large ones and catch 80% of the mistakes they see. Half of what slips through is noticed and undone within the window. If 6 of the 9 reach a reviewer: about 5 caught; of the remaining 4, about 2 undone; about 2 slip through and need reconciliation. Each layer catches a share of what the previous one missed; none is enough alone. Code The program takes your project’s proposed money-moving actions, sends the large ones to a reviewer, offers an undo window, and counts the mistakes and money caught at each layer. Change REVIEW_CATCH or UNDO_USED and see what slips through. Review and undo, layer by layer, in real Python. Error and catch rates are simulated. Primary sources Nielsen Norman Group: User Control and Freedom Undo and clearly marked exits. Microsoft: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction Efficient correction and dismissal of AI output. Google PAIR guidebook: Feedback and control Giving users control over AI behaviour.

title: Feedback loops in the interface
text: Intuition A comments box at a restaurant mostly collects complaints: happy diners rarely bother. Thumbs buttons on AI answers work the same way, so their numbers carry feedback bias : the thumbs-down share is not the share of bad answers. Feedback is still valuable when it is cheap to give, asks one useful follow-up question, is tied to the exact trace, and is combined with signals users give without trying, such as edits and rephrasing (17.4). Mechanism Signal Strength Weakness Thumbs up or down cheap, tied to one answer few people click; unhappy users click more Reason chips after thumbs down tells you what to fix one more click: fewer responses Edits to drafts exact correction, plenty of it only where users edit Rephrasing, copying, escalating collected for everyone indirect; validate against outcomes Outcomes (resolved, returned, overturned) the real goal arrives late (17.7) Ask one click, at the right moment Follow up reason chips Link to the trace Triage sample and label Act eval cases, fixes, tell users Ask right after the answer, without blocking the user. Offer a few reasons: wrong, out of date, not what I asked. Store feedback with the trace id, prompt and model version. Review a sample each week and label root causes (17.9). Turn findings into eval cases and fixes, and close the loop with users where you can. A feedback loop that leads to changes. Example: measuring a prompt change A team ships a new prompt and the thumbs-down rate falls from 1.0% to 0.9%. With 20,000 sessions per version, that difference is well within noise. They instead compare edit rates on drafts, collected on every session, and see a clear drop from 34% to 19%. The numbers Biased clicks (illustrative). 12% of answers are unhelpful. Unhappy users click thumbs down 8% of the time; happy users click thumbs up 2% of the time. Per 10,000 sessions: 1,200 × 0.08 ≈ 96 downs and 8,800 × 0.02 = 176 ups. Thumbs down is 96 ÷ 272 ≈ 35% of feedback, although only 12% of answers were bad. Sample size. Seeing a thumbs-down rate fall from 1.0% to 0.8% needs on the order of 35,000 sessions per version, which is why rare clicks make slow experiments (8.7). Code The program simulates 50,000 sessions where unhappy users click more often, compares the thumbs-down share with the true unhelpful rate, counts reasons, and estimates the sessions needed to see an improvement. Change the click rates and see how the bias moves. Feedback bias and sample size, in real Python. Click rates are invented. Primary sources Google PAIR guidebook: Feedback and control Designing feedback that improves the product. Langfuse: Scores Linking user feedback to traces. Kohavi, Tang and Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments Sample sizes and pitfalls when testing changes.

title: Onboarding, expectations and graceful failure
text: Intuition First impressions set expectations. If an assistant’s first screen promises it can do anything, every gap feels like a failure; if it shows what it is good at with examples, users ask the questions it can answer. Failures will happen anyway. Graceful failure means each kind of failure has a designed response: a partial answer with a warning, a handover to a person, a saved request to retry, never a bare "Something went wrong". Mechanism Moment Pattern Example First use say what it does and does not do; show example prompts "I can answer questions about your bookings and our fare rules" Low confidence give what was found, with sources, and suggest checking "Here is what I found, but please check it" Out of scope say so and point to the right place "I can’t do that here; contact support" Dependency failure save the request, retry, tell the user "Saved; I’ll retry and notify you" Slow offer to wait or get the result later "Taking longer than usual: email it to me?" Any failure a way to reach a person a visible human handover List failures per type Design response message + next step Degrade ladder from 15.6 Test inject each failure Measure dead ends, recoveries List every way the feature can fail: low confidence, out of scope, tool errors, timeouts, refusals. Write the message and the next step for each. Connect them to the degradation ladder so the interface knows which level is active. Inject each failure in testing and look at what users see. Track dead ends and how often users recover. Designing failure before it happens. Over-promising onboarding "Ask me anything" invites questions the system cannot answer. Specific examples set honest expectations and lead users to the questions that work. The numbers Dead ends (illustrative). Of 1,000 conversations, 80% are answered; 7% end with low confidence, 5% out of scope, 4% with a tool failure and 4% with a timeout. With one generic error message: 200 users hit a dead end. With a designed next step for each and, say, half of those users recovering: about 100 more users get what they came for, with no model change at all. Code The program assigns simulated outcomes to your project’s messages and compares a generic error message with a designed message and next step for each kind of failure. Rewrite the messages in NEXT_STEP for your product. Failure messages with next steps, in real Python. Outcome rates are simulated. Primary sources Google PAIR guidebook: Errors and graceful failure Designing for AI failures. Nielsen Norman Group: Error-Message Guidelines Messages that explain and offer a next step. Microsoft: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction "Make clear what the system can do" at the start of use.

title: From obligation to control to evidence
text: Intuition A law says what must be true; it rarely says how. "Keep a person in control of consequential decisions" does not name a screen or a log table. Engineering turns each obligation into a control , something the system does, and into evidence, the record that proves it was done. The result is a table anyone can audit: obligation, control, evidence, owner and date. Gaps in that table are the real compliance risk. Mechanism Obligation what must be true Interpretation with legal Control what the system does Evidence records, produced automatically Review owner, date, gaps Start from the text that applies, identified with legal and compliance. Agree in writing what it means for this system. Design a control: an approval step, a log, a test, a banner, a deletion job. Make the system produce evidence as a side effect: logs, gate results, drill reports. Keep the matrix current: every control has an owner and fresh evidence. From an obligation to evidence. Obligation (generic example) Control Evidence Human oversight of consequential decisions approval step with exact parameters (11.7); stop switch approval records; kill-switch drill reports Records of system operation decision logs with versions (18.1) log retention reports; sample queries Tell people they are talking to an AI disclosure in the interface screenshots per release; UI tests Manage risks before release threat model (16.1), release gates (18.3) threat model document; gate results Honour deletion requests deletion across all copies (16.5) deletion job logs; verification searches Evidence made by hand goes stale A screenshot taken for last year’s audit proves nothing about today. Prefer evidence the pipeline produces on every release or every decision, and date it. Orientation for engineers, not legal advice. Laws, guidance and application dates change; confirm what applies with your legal and compliance team. The numbers Size of the job (illustrative). 25 obligations, 2 controls each on average, 1 piece of evidence per control: 50 rows to keep current. If evidence is refreshed by hand every 6 months at 1 hour a row, that is 50 × 2 = 100 hours a year, and much of it is stale at any moment. If 40 of the 50 are produced automatically by the pipeline, the manual work drops to 10 × 2 = 20 hours. Staleness. With a 180-day freshness rule, evidence dated 250 days ago fails, even if the control still works: the drill must be run again. Code The program maps five example obligations to controls and each control to its latest evidence, and flags missing controls, missing evidence and evidence older than 180 days. Add a control for the deletion obligation and run it again. A control matrix, in real Python. Generic example obligations; not legal advice. Primary sources NIST AI Risk Management Framework Govern, map, measure and manage: a structure for controls. NIST AI 600-1: Generative AI Profile Risks specific to generative AI and suggested actions. ISO/IEC 42001 An AI management system with controls and audits.

title: Risk-based AI law: roles, risk tiers and duties (the EU AI Act as an example)
text: Intuition Risk-based AI laws work like building codes: a garden shed needs almost nothing, a house needs inspections, a hospital needs far more, and some constructions are simply banned. The EU AI Act is the best-known example: it sorts AI uses into tiers and gives each tier its own duties. Duties also depend on your role. The provider who builds the system and the deployer who uses it carry different obligations, and a company can be both for different systems. Mechanism Tier (simplified) Examples Broad consequence Prohibited practices certain manipulative or social-scoring uses not allowed High risk employment screening, credit scoring, access to essential services risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy, conformity assessment Transparency duties chatbots, generated or manipulated content tell people, label content Minimal risk spam filters, most internal tools no specific duties; voluntary codes General-purpose AI models large foundation models documentation and policies for model providers Inventory every AI use Role provider, deployer or both Tier prohibited, high, transparency, minimal Duties mapped to controls (23.1) Timeline which dates apply List every AI system and use, including bought-in tools. Decide your role for each one. Classify with legal; a high-risk use carries most of the engineering work. Map duties to controls and evidence. Obligations apply in phases; check current dates and any amendments. Working out what applies. Other regimes. Many countries regulate AI mainly through existing laws: privacy (the GDPR in Europe, India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act and Rules), consumer protection, and sector rules for banking, health and hiring. A system can be minimal risk under one law and heavily regulated under another. Example: two tiers in one company A bank’s internal document summariser is minimal risk; its loan pre-qualification model is high risk, so it needs documented risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and testing for accuracy and bias before release. Most of these controls already exist in chapters 8, 16 and 18; the work is mapping and evidence. Orientation for engineers, not legal advice. Laws, guidance and application dates change; confirm what applies with your legal and compliance team. The numbers An inventory (illustrative). 30 AI uses: 1 needs redesign because it is close to a prohibited practice, 3 are high risk, 9 have transparency duties, 17 are minimal. If a high-risk system needs about 10 controls with evidence and a transparency-duty system about 2: 3 × 10 + 9 × 2 = 48 rows in the control matrix. The 17 minimal-risk uses still need entries in the inventory, so the classification itself can be checked. Code The program places four use cases into simplified risk categories and lists sketched duties for the provider or deployer of each. Change a use case’s role or area and run it again. Roles and tiers, simplified, in real Python. Orientation only, not legal advice. Primary sources Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act The legal text: tiers, roles and duties. AI Act high-level summary (Future of Life Institute) A plain-language overview of the structure. NIST AI Risk Management Framework A voluntary framework used where no AI-specific law applies.

title: Privacy rights applied to LLM systems
text: Intuition Privacy laws give people rights over their data : to see what an organisation holds about them, to correct it and, in many cases, to have it deleted. Those rights were written with databases in mind; AI systems scatter copies into chunks, vectors, caches, memories, logs, evaluation sets and even model weights. So privacy has to be designed in: know where every copy lives (lineage, 10.4), keep as little as possible, and build deletion that reaches every store, with proof. Mechanism Right or principle What it means for an LLM system Purpose and lawful basis decide and record why personal data is processed, including for training or evaluation Minimisation send the model only what the task needs; redact before logging (16.5) Access be able to find and export what you hold about a person, across stores Erasure delete across chunks, vectors, caches, memories, logs and datasets; flag models trained on the data Automated decisions meaningful human review and an explanation where decisions significantly affect people Transfers and processors know where providers process data; contracts and region controls Request identity checked Locate lineage across stores Act export or delete Verify search again, canaries Record evidence, within deadline Verify the requester’s identity before acting. Use lineage to find every copy, including derived data such as embeddings. Export or delete; retained copies need a documented reason (legal hold, backups that expire). Search every store again to prove nothing was missed. Record what was done, and when, within the legal deadline. Handling a data-subject request. Models remember Deleting training rows does not remove what a model learned from them. Keep personal data out of training sets where possible, use per-tenant adapters that can be dropped, and flag models trained on deleted data for review (13.6). Orientation for engineers, not legal advice. Laws, guidance and application dates change; confirm what applies with your legal and compliance team. The numbers Copies of one person’s data (illustrative): 3 source records, 12 chunks and vectors, 4 cached answers, 2 memories, 40 traces, 1 evaluation case, 2 fine-tuning rows and 3 backups: 67 copies in 8 stores. Deleting the source alone removes 3 of 67, under 5%. If traces are kept 30 days and the deadline to respond is a month, waiting for traces to expire on their own is not a plan: delete or redact them. Code The program finds a fictional customer’s data in eight stores, deletes what can be deleted, records what is retained and why, and notes what deleting training rows cannot undo. Add a store your own system has and run it again. An erasure request across stores, in real Python. Illustrative stores; check your law’s deadlines. Primary sources GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure The right and its exceptions. GDPR Article 22: Automated decision-making Rights around decisions made solely by automated means. ICO: Artificial intelligence guidance A regulator’s guidance on data protection in AI systems.

title: Transparency, labelling and record-keeping
text: Intuition People have a right to know when they are dealing with a machine, and others need to know when content was made by one. AI disclosure and labelling covers both: a clear notice in conversations, and marks on generated content, visible to people and readable by software. Behind the scenes, record-keeping makes the system answerable later: who did what, with which model and version, and who approved it. Mechanism Duty (generic) Engineering control Check Tell people they are interacting with AI notice at the start of the conversation and on voice calls UI test per release Mark generated or altered content visible label plus machine-readable metadata (content credentials such as C2PA) metadata present on every export Keep records of operation decision logs: time, system and model version, input and output references, operator, reviewer, decision field completeness checks Retain records for a set period retention policy per record type; protected from editing retention reports Explain decisions to affected people store the reasons and evidence shown to the reviewer sample review Generate text, image, audio Label visible notice Attach metadata generator, model, time Log decision record Retain append-only, by policy The system produces content or a decision. Users see that it is AI-generated or AI-assisted. Machine-readable metadata travels with exported content. A decision record links input, output, versions and people. Records are kept, unchanged, for the required period, then deleted. Transparency and records in the pipeline. Example: decision records that survive an audit An auditor asks why a claim was rejected eight months ago. The record shows the input reference, the model and prompt versions, the draft the system produced, the reviewer who edited it and the final decision. Without the versions, the team could not have reproduced the draft. Orientation for engineers, not legal advice. Laws, guidance and application dates change; confirm what applies with your legal and compliance team. The numbers Completeness (illustrative). 500 decision records, each with 8 required fields. If any one field goes missing 2% of the time, the chance a record is complete is 0.98 multiplied 8 times ≈ 85%. That is about 75 incomplete records in 500, each a hole in the audit trail. A completeness check in the pipeline turns that into an alert on the first missing field instead of a finding a year later. Storage. 1 million decisions a year at 2 KB each is 2 GB a year: record-keeping is cheap; missing records are not. Code The program checks 500 simulated decision records for eight required fields, reports which are missing, and labels a generated text with a visible notice and attached metadata. Add a required field and see completeness fall. Record completeness and labels, in real Python. The field list is an example. Primary sources Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act Transparency duties and record-keeping for high-risk systems. C2PA specifications Content credentials: machine-readable provenance for media. OpenTelemetry: GenAI semantic conventions Standard fields for recording model calls.

title: Audits, assurance and management-system standards
text: Intuition An auditor cannot read every decision a system made, so they check a sample, the way a food inspector tests a few jars from a batch. Audit sampling only works if the sample is random and the result is stated with its uncertainty: "no problems in 20 checks" says much less than it sounds. Standards such as ISO/IEC 42001 audit the management system around AI, its policies, risk assessments and reviews, and frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF structure that work. Both rely on the evidence the earlier chapters produce. Mechanism Assurance activity Who Looks at Internal review your own risk or quality team control matrix, evidence freshness, incidents Internal audit an independent internal function samples of decisions and controls External audit or certification an accredited auditor (for example against ISO/IEC 42001) the management system and samples Conformity assessment self or notified body, for some high-risk systems technical documentation, testing Red-team and evaluation reports internal or external testers (16.7) the system’s behaviour Define population all decisions in scope Random sample size from target precision Check against policy Estimate rate with an interval Act findings, owners, dates Say exactly which decisions are in scope and over what period. Draw a random sample large enough for the claim you want to make. Check each sampled decision against the written policy. Report the breach rate with its confidence interval. Record findings with owners and deadlines, and re-test. An audit by sampling. Cherry-picked samples Letting the team choose which cases the auditor sees makes the result meaningless. Samples must be drawn at random from the full population, by a method the auditor controls. Orientation for engineers, not legal advice. Laws, guidance and application dates change; confirm what applies with your legal and compliance team. The numbers How much a clean sample proves . If you check n random decisions and find no breaches, you can say with 95% confidence that the breach rate is below a limit when n is large enough: To claim below 5%: 59 clean checks, because 0.95 multiplied by itself 59 times is just under 0.05. To claim below 1%: 299 clean checks. 20 clean checks only support "below about 14%". With some breaches. 4 breaches in 60 checks is 6.7%, but the 95% interval runs from about 2.6% to 15.9%: a bigger sample is needed to tell whether a 5% target is met. Code The program samples your project’s money-moving decisions with a hidden breach rate, estimates the rate with an interval for three sample sizes, and works out how many clean checks support a claim. Change TRUE_ERROR to 0.01 and see what small samples miss. Audit sampling, in real Python. Breaches are simulated. Primary sources ISO/IEC 42001 The certifiable AI management system standard. NIST AI Risk Management Framework Measuring and managing AI risk, with a playbook of actions. Institute of Internal Auditors: Standards How internal audit plans samples and reports findings.

title: Milestones, evidence and pass conditions
text: Intuition The capstone is a small but complete version of your example project, built in eight milestones. Each milestone is like a driving-test manoeuvre: a specific thing to build, the evidence to keep, and a pass condition written before you start, so "done" is a measurement and not a feeling. Keep the data and traffic modest. What makes it convincing is not size but honesty: measured results next to an explicit design for scale, with each kept apart from the other. Mechanism Build a lite version of your example project (Harbor by default, or the online store, bank or travel agent; switch with the Example picker): a small but complete system. Keep data and traffic modest, and write an explicit scale design next to your measured results, so your reasoning about enterprise operation is concrete without pretending a laptop test is production. Milestone Build Evidence to keep Pass condition 1 · Baseline 100–1,000 approved or synthetic documents; BM25; 100 labelled questions Dataset manifest, split policy, relevance labels, Recall@k / MRR, error list Reproducible baseline with known, written-down failures 2 · Answer service Small local model; citation IDs; abstention; schema validation Answer rubric, supported-claim review, latency and cost report Meets pre-agreed criteria on the held-out set 3 · Better retrieval Dense + RRF + reranker; optional embedding fine-tune Paired comparison with confidence intervals; per-query diffs A significant gain, or a written decision not to add the component 4 · Durable actions Search → draft → approve → create; persisted state; idempotency keys; MCP server Crash-and-retry traces; exactly-one-ticket tests; pass^5 per task No duplicate or unauthorised action in any tested case 5 · Adaptation study Diagnose one remaining gap; curate data; CPU LoRA, or the 13.3 Colab guide on a free GPU Baseline comparison; domain, general and safety scorecard; lineage Measured gain with no blocked regression 6 · Operations OTel tracing; quality sampling; alerts; budgets; runbook Injected-failure investigation; incident turned into an eval case Another engineer diagnoses and recovers using only your dashboards and runbook 7 · Security Second synthetic tenant; injection corpus; PII redaction before logging Threat model; isolation and injection test results Every canary stays in its tenant; no injected instruction triggers a write 8 · Scale + release Capacity assumptions; versioned index; release manifest; canary and rollback drill Measured load-test report kept separate from projections; rollback evidence A coherent, compatible restore and clearly bounded claims The numbers Reading milestone 3 . On 100 labelled questions, Recall@10 rising from 0.71 to 0.88 means 0.88 × 100 − 0.71 × 100 = 88 − 71 = 17 more questions find their answer in the top ten. Compare the two systems question by question: if the new one wins 21 and loses 4, the net gain is 17. Resample the 100 questions 2,000 times and recompute the gain each time; if 95% of those gains are above zero, keep the component. If not, write down why you did not add it. Milestone 4 . pass^5 means a task passes all 5 repeated runs: a task that passes each run 90% of the time passes all five only 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 ≈ 59% of the time. Code The program builds labelled questions from your project’s documents, compares a baseline retriever with a candidate question by question, and decides with a paired bootstrap interval whether the candidate stays. Change K to 3 and run it again. A milestone decided by evidence, in real Python. The questions are synthetic stand-ins for labelled ones. Primary sources Smucker, Allan and Carterette (2007), significance tests for IR evaluation Paired tests, including the bootstrap, for comparing retrieval systems. Yao et al. (2024), τ-bench pass^k: reliability over repeated runs. MCP specification The protocol for milestone 4’s tool server.

title: Explain it in an interview or design review
text: Intuition In an interview or a design review, the strongest answer is a story with evidence: the task and its risk, the simplest thing that worked, the failure that justified each extra part, and how the system is operated. Every number in that story carries its evidence category : simulated, measured locally, projected, or operated in production. Saying "projected, not yet validated" shows judgement; letting a projection pass as a measurement loses trust the moment someone asks. Mechanism The task and its risk : who uses it, what a wrong answer costs, and the acceptance criteria you wrote first. The simplest baseline and its measured numbers. The failure that justified each extra component (reranker, agent step, fine-tune), with the paired measurement that showed it helped. Operational limits : how you handle permission revocation, duplicate tool execution, stale indexes, model upgrades, failed rollouts, quality drift and cost per successful task. The evidence category of every claim : simulated, measured locally, projected, or operated in production (Appendix E). Saying "projected, not yet validated" is a strength, not a weakness. Example answer fragment "BM25 alone reached Recall@10 = 0.71 on our 100 labelled questions; hybrid plus a reranker reached 0.88, a paired improvement whose 95% interval excluded zero. Answer groundedness was 96% on a 60-case held-out set. On my laptop the service handled 4 requests/s with a mocked model at p95 1.2 s; that measures orchestration only. For production I projected GPU needs from vLLM benchmarks I have not yet run, so that figure is a projection." The numbers The example fragment, checked . Recall@10 from 0.71 to 0.88 on 100 questions: 17 more questions answered, measured locally. 4 requests a second at a p95 of 1.2 seconds with a mocked model: by Little’s law about 4 × 1.2 ≈ 5 requests in flight. It measures orchestration only, because the model was mocked. GPU needs from benchmarks not yet run: projected, and saying so is the right answer. Code The program checks a short write-up sentence by sentence: every number needs an evidence category, and words like "never" need to say what was tested. Add a sentence of your own capstone write-up and run it again. Labelling every claim, in real Python. A pattern check, not a fact check. Primary sources Kapoor et al. (2024), AI Agents That Matter Reporting results with baselines, cost and honest comparisons. Mitchell et al. (2018), Model Cards Stating evaluation conditions and limitations. Google SRE book: Service Level Objectives Talking about reliability in measured terms.

title: Run it locally
text:
Use Python 3.10+ in an isolated environment: python -m pip install numpy , copy the script below into tiny_bigram_lab.py , then run python tiny_bigram_lab.py in a writable folder. It needs no model download, API key or GPU. It writes tiny_bigram_checkpoint.npz and tiny_bigram_report.json . Complete source Laptop · CPU · under 1 s """Tiny character language model, trained end to end on CPU with NumPy only. What it shows: vocabulary from training text only, separate train / validation / test splits, next-character targets, softmax cross-entropy, gradients, SGD updates, checkpoint selection on validation loss, a unigram baseline, save + reload + verify, temperature sampling, and a JSON report. Context is ONE character (a bigram model), so it cannot learn long-range structure; that is what transformers add. Run: python -m pip install numpy then python tiny_bigram_lab.py """ import json, time from pathlib import Path import numpy as np SEED, STEPS, BATCH, LR = 11, 1500, 256, 2.0 rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED) train_text = """the gateway checks the tenant before the request reaches a model. the retriever returns passages with their source ids and versions. the reranker reads the query and each passage together. the assistant cites a passage or says it cannot find an answer. the queue keeps jobs until a worker has finished them. a worker retries a failed job with backoff and a fresh deadline. the same idempotency key returns the same ticket on a retry. an evaluation set holds real questions with expected answers. the judge is checked against people before it gates a release. the index stores vectors, text and the permissions of each chunk. the trace links retrieval, generation and tool calls for one task. the release manifest records the model, prompt and index versions. a canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first. if quality falls, the rollout returns traffic to the old version. """ val_text = "the worker checks the index before the release.
the assistant reads the trace and cites the source.
" test_text = "a retry keeps the same key so the ticket is not repeated.
the gateway sends traffic to the new model version.
" chars = ["<unk>"] + sorted(set(train_text)) # vocabulary from TRAIN only stoi = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)} enc = lambda t: np.array([stoi.get(c, 0) for c in t], dtype=np.int64) tr, va, te = enc(train_text), enc(val_text), enc(test_text) V = len(chars) def softmax(z): z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True) e = np.exp(z) return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) def loss(seq, W): # mean cross-entropy in nats/char p = softmax(W[seq[:-1]]) return float(-np.log(p[np.arange(len(seq) - 1), seq[1:]] + 1e-12).mean()) W = rng.normal(0, 0.01, (V, V)) # one V x V table of logits best_val, best_W, history = float("inf"), W.copy(), [] t0 = time.perf_counter() for step in range(STEPS + 1): i = rng.integers(0, len(tr) - 1, size=BATCH) # random (current, next) pairs x, y = tr[i], tr[i + 1] g = softmax(W[x]); g[np.arange(BATCH), y] -= 1 # dLoss/dlogits = p - onehot grad = np.zeros_like(W); np.add.at(grad, x, g / BATCH) W -= LR * grad if step % 100 == 0: h = {"step": step, "train": loss(tr, W), "val": loss(va, W)} history.append(h) if h["val"] < best_val: best_val, best_W = h["val"], W.copy() secs = time.perf_counter() - t0 uni = np.bincount(tr, minlength=V).astype(float) + 1.0 # add-one smoothed unigram uni /= uni.sum() baseline = float(-np.log(uni[te[1:]]).mean()) test_loss = loss(te, best_W) np.savez("tiny_bigram_checkpoint.npz", W=best_W, chars=np.array(chars)) ck = np.load("tiny_bigram_checkpoint.npz", allow_pickle=False) assert np.array_equal(ck["W"], best_W), "reloaded weights differ" assert abs(loss(te, ck["W"]) - test_loss) < 1e-12, "reloaded model scores differently" def sample(W, start="t", n=160, temperature=0.8, seed=SEED + 1): r, out = np.random.default_rng(seed), [stoi[start]] for _ in range(n): out.append(int(r.choice(V, p=softmax(W[out[-1]] / temperature)))) return "".join(chars[i] for i in out) report = {"numpy": np.__version__, "seed": SEED, "vocab": V, "parameters": int(W.size), "steps": STEPS, "batch": BATCH, "lr": LR, "train_seconds": round(secs, 2), "uniform_loss": float(np.log(V)), "best_val": best_val, "test": test_loss, "unigram_baseline_test": baseline, "history": history, "sample_t0.8": sample(ck["W"])} Path("tiny_bigram_report.json").write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2)) print(f"vocab {V} params {W.size} {secs:.2f}s") print(f"uniform {np.log(V):.3f} unigram test {baseline:.3f} bigram test {test_loss:.3f} best val {best_val:.3f}") print("sample:", report["sample_t0.8"][:120].replace("
", " / ")) Or run it here The same script, in real Python if you opt in. Pyodide runs it in a worker on your device, and the checks test the lifecycle rather than a target number. Pick the manual's own text to compare with the run this appendix reports ; expect the same losses to within a little, because the seed is fixed, and a longer training time, because this is WebAssembly.

title: What the actual run produced
text: Measured by running the script above while preparing this manual (Linux container, 4 x86-64 cores, Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5.3, seed 11). Exact values can differ slightly on other machines and library versions. 30 characters in vocabulary 900 trainable logits (V × V) 0.29 s training time, 1500 steps 2.271 test loss, nats/char 2.850 unigram baseline (test) 3.401 uniform guess = ln V uniform guess 3.401 unigram baseline (test) 2.850 train validation 0 500 1000 1500 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5 optimiser step Loss curves from the actual run (logged every 100 steps). The bigram model beats the unigram baseline on unseen test text by about 0.58 nats per character. Validation loss is lower than training loss here because the short validation text reuses the most common words; with tiny, related splits that can happen, and it is a reason not to over-read toy numbers. Sample at temperature 0.8 (from the reloaded checkpoint) teve iljors r e onte strs vethesera t vand ansioreds ctresit there for ketrdsh ca s s thele van ans tons a a tr sionerde at c a the thea and ke thuafons ks re ac Word-like fragments and common pairs ("th", "the ") appear, but there is no grammar: one character of context cannot carry it. Experiments that teach something Halve train_text and watch the train/validation gap and the sample quality change. Try learning rates 0.2, 2 and 20; plot the history from the JSON report. Add a second topic to the training text and measure whether the original test loss gets worse. Replace the bigram table with a 2-layer, width-64, context-64 PyTorch transformer (chapter 5) and compare test loss at equal training time. What this does show The complete lifecycle: vocabulary from training data only, separate splits, next-token targets, cross-entropy, gradients, updates, validation-based checkpoint selection, a baseline, save-and-reload verification and sampling. What it does not show Language understanding, factual knowledge, privacy, enterprise accuracy or anything about scale. A lower toy loss is evidence about this toy task only.

title: 80 tools by chapter
text: Official documentation links were checked on 4 November 2026. Before using any tool, check its current installation steps, licence, supported versions and hardware requirements. Open-source code does not make every hosted service built on it free. "Laptop" means you can learn the tool on a CPU-only laptop at small scale; it does not mean production capacity. "Colab GPU" means a step-by-step guide in the course runs it on one free Google Colab GPU. "External GPU" means it needs several GPUs or a cluster, more than one Colab GPU. Tool Ch. Category What it does / how to try it Runs on NumPy 2 arrays · linear algebra Foundation array library. Use it to build intuition by implementing similarity, softmax and gradient descent by hand. laptop pandas 2 tables · data cleaning Load CSV/Parquet, clean, group and join. You will use it for every evaluation results table. laptop Matplotlib 2 plots Loss curves, histograms, ROC curves. Plot before you trust a number. laptop JupyterLab 2 notebooks Interactive exploration. Run jupyter lab in your environment. laptop scikit-learn 2 classical ML · CPU Regression, trees, ensembles, clustering, metrics, splits and pipelines. Every exercise in chapter 3 runs on it. laptop PyTorch 2 deep learning · CPU or GPU Tensors, autograd, training loops. The CPU build is enough for chapter 4 and tiny transformers. laptop Transformers 6 models · tokenisers · Trainer Load almost any open model, apply chat templates, and run training with Trainer . CPU works for small models. laptop Datasets 6 data loading · streaming Load, stream, map and filter large datasets with memory-mapping; versioned via the Hub. laptop TRL 6 SFT · DPO · GRPO · reward models Post-training library. SFTTrainer , DPOTrainer , GRPOTrainer . Try SFT on a 135M model on CPU; preference/RL runs need GPUs. The 13.3 Colab guide fine-tunes a 1.7B model on one free GPU. laptop datatrove 6 corpus processing at scale Filtering, deduplication (MinHash) and extraction pipelines used to build large web datasets. Runs locally on samples. laptop DeepSpeed · FSDP 6 distributed training ZeRO sharding, offload and pipeline parallelism. Learn the configs locally; real runs need several GPUs at once, more than one Colab GPU. external GPU torchtitan · Megatron-LM 6 large-scale pretraining Reference implementations of 3D/4D parallel pretraining. Read for architecture; they run only on clusters, not on one Colab GPU. external GPU Ollama 7 local models · CPU OK One-command local model runtime with a REST API, OpenAI-compatible endpoint, tool calling, structured outputs and streaming. The default for this course's labs. laptop llama.cpp 7 CPU/GPU inference · GGUF Efficient C/C++ inference; llama-server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with JSON-schema/grammar constrained output. Use for benchmarking (14). laptop LiteLLM 7 unified API · gateway One interface for 100+ providers, plus a proxy with retries, fallbacks, budgets and rate limits. Point it at Ollama locally to prototype a model gateway (15.5). laptop Pydantic · Instructor 7 schemas · validation Define output types in Python and validate model output; Instructor adds automatic re-asking on validation failure. laptop Outlines 7 constrained generation Guarantees output matches a regex, JSON Schema or grammar for local models via token masking. laptop DSPy 7 programmatic prompting Write LLM pipelines as modules and let optimisers tune prompts and examples against your metric. Use after you have an eval set. laptop promptfoo 8 prompt/model evals · red teaming · CI YAML test cases with assertions (contains, JSON schema, LLM rubric), side-by-side model comparison, CI integration. Works against Ollama locally. laptop Inspect 8 evals framework · agents · sandboxes From the UK AI Security Institute. Datasets, solvers, scorers, tool use and Docker sandboxes for agent evals. Good for rigorous agent tasks. laptop Ragas 8 RAG metrics Faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall and test-set generation. Uses an LLM judge; calibrate it (8.3). laptop DeepEval 8 pytest-style LLM tests Unit-test style metrics (G-Eval, hallucination, tool correctness) that run in CI. laptop lm-evaluation-harness 8 model benchmarks Standard academic benchmarks on any HF or API model. Use to check general-capability regressions after fine-tuning (13.6). Small models run on CPU slowly. laptop Phoenix · Langfuse 8 datasets · experiments · traces Store eval datasets, run experiments, attach scores to production traces (chapter 17). Both self-hostable. laptop Sentence Transformers 9 embeddings · cross-encoders · CPU OK Load and fine-tune embedding models and rerankers. Small models (MiniLM, bge-small) embed thousands of chunks per minute on CPU. laptop FAISS 9 vector index library Flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ indexes; faiss-cpu handles millions of vectors on a laptop. Best way to learn ANN tradeoffs. laptop bm25s 9 fast BM25 in Python Simple, fast keyword retrieval for experiments and hybrid search prototypes. laptop Qdrant · Milvus · Weaviate 9 vector databases Production vector stores with filtering, hybrid search, quantisation, sharding and replication. Run single-node in Docker on a laptop. laptop pgvector · OpenSearch 9 vectors in existing infrastructure Postgres extension for vectors (HNSW, IVFFlat) next to relational data; OpenSearch/Elasticsearch combine BM25 and k-NN in one engine. laptop LlamaIndex · Haystack · LangChain 9 RAG frameworks Connectors, chunkers, retrievers and pipelines. Useful for speed; understand the pieces (this chapter) so you can debug them. laptop Docling 10 document parsing · tables · OCR Converts PDF, DOCX, PPTX, HTML and images to structured Markdown/JSON with layout and table extraction. CPU OK (slower). laptop Unstructured · PyMuPDF 10 partitioning · fast extraction Element-level partitioning of many formats; PyMuPDF for fast born-digital extraction. laptop Tesseract 10 OCR · CPU Classic open-source OCR engine; good baseline for scanned pages on a laptop. laptop Apache Kafka 10 durable queues · streams Backbone for ingestion events and change feeds; run locally in Docker to practise consumer groups and replay. laptop PyLate 10 late interaction (ColBERT) Train and use ColBERT-style multi-vector models built on Sentence Transformers. laptop GraphRAG 10 knowledge-graph RAG Entity/relation extraction, community summaries, local and global search. Indexing is LLM-call heavy; try on a small corpus. laptop LangGraph 11 graph-based agents · checkpointing Agents and workflows as state graphs with persistence, interrupts for human approval, and resumability. Runs locally. laptop Pydantic AI 11 typed agents Agents with typed tool signatures and outputs validated by Pydantic; works with Ollama. laptop OpenAI Agents SDK 11 agents · handoffs · guardrails · tracing Lightweight agent loop with tools, handoffs and tracing; supports other providers through compatible APIs. laptop smolagents 11 minimal agents · code actions Small library where agents write Python code as actions; run code in a sandbox. laptop Temporal 11 durable workflows Event-sourced workflows with retries, timers and signals; survive crashes. Run the dev server locally with temporal server start-dev . laptop Model Context Protocol 11 spec · SDKs · Inspector Specification, official SDKs (Python, TypeScript, others) and the Inspector debugging tool. laptop Microsoft Agent Framework 12 successor to AutoGen + Semantic Kernel Python and .NET framework for agents and multi-agent workflows (1.0 released). AutoGen is being archived and its README directs new users here. laptop CrewAI 12 role-based crews · flows Define agents with roles and tasks; "flows" add deterministic orchestration around crews. laptop Google ADK 12 agent development kit Code-first agents and multi-agent hierarchies, with evaluation tooling; model-agnostic. laptop A2A protocol 12 agent interoperability Open protocol (Linux Foundation project) for agent discovery and task exchange across frameworks and vendors. laptop PEFT 13 LoRA · adapters LoRA and other adapter methods for any Transformers model; merge or hot-swap adapters. laptop Unsloth 13 fast LoRA/QLoRA on one GPU Optimised kernels and ready notebooks for Colab/Kaggle; a good path for larger fine-tunes once you have done the 13.3 Colab guide , which takes the same steps by hand. Colab GPU Axolotl · torchtune 13 config-driven fine-tuning Axolotl: YAML-configured SFT/DPO/QLoRA recipes including multi-GPU. torchtune is no longer actively maintained (development wound down in 2025), so prefer Axolotl, TRL or Unsloth for new work. external GPU Argilla · Label Studio 13 annotation · review Labelling and expert-review UIs with agreement tracking; run locally with Docker or pip. laptop MLflow · DVC 13 tracking · registry · data versioning Experiment tracking and model registry; Git-like versioning for datasets and pipelines. laptop vLLM 14 GPU serving engine OpenAI-compatible server with paged attention, continuous batching and prefix caching; includes benchmarking tools. A CPU backend exists (build-from-source/nightly wheels) for experimentation, far slower than GPU. The 14.7 Colab guide serves and benchmarks it on a free GPU. Colab GPU SGLang 14 GPU serving engine High-performance serving with radix-tree prefix caching and structured generation. laptop LLM Compressor 14 quantisation for vLLM Apply FP8, INT8, GPTQ/AWQ-style quantisation and sparsity, producing checkpoints vLLM serves. external GPU GuideLLM 14 capacity benchmarking Sweeps request rates against an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and reports throughput and latency percentiles. Point it at llama-server on your laptop to learn it. laptop KServe · Ray Serve 14 deployment on Kubernetes / Ray Model deployment, autoscaling and routing layers that wrap engines like vLLM. laptop LiteLLM Proxy 15 model gateway Self-hosted gateway with routing, fallbacks, per-key/team budgets and rate limits, and usage tracking. laptop Envoy AI Gateway 15 gateway on Envoy / Kubernetes Token-based rate limiting, provider routing and fallback built on Envoy Gateway. laptop k6 · Locust 15 load testing Scriptable load tests with arrival-rate scenarios and thresholds (k6: JavaScript; Locust: Python). laptop KEDA 15 event-driven autoscaling Scale Kubernetes workloads on queue depth or custom metrics such as waiting requests. laptop Chaos Mesh · Toxiproxy 15 failure injection Inject latency, errors and outages into dependencies to test breakers and fallbacks; Toxiproxy runs locally. laptop Redis / Valkey 15 caches · rate limiting Response caches, token-bucket rate limiters and session state for stateless services. laptop OWASP GenAI Security Project 16 Top 10 for LLM apps · guidance Threat taxonomy and mitigations for LLM and agentic applications; a good threat-modelling checklist. laptop garak · PyRIT 16 automated red teaming LLM vulnerability scanner with many probe families; PyRIT orchestrates multi-turn attack campaigns. laptop NeMo Guardrails 16 programmable guardrails Input, output, dialogue and retrieval rails around LLM apps; integrates safety models. laptop Presidio 16 PII detection and anonymisation NER plus pattern recognisers for redaction and pseudonymisation; runs on CPU. laptop Open Policy Agent 16 policy as code Central, testable authorisation and policy decisions for tools, gateways and admission control. laptop ModelScan · Sigstore 16 model supply chain Scan model files for unsafe serialisation; sign and verify artefacts and provenance. laptop OpenTelemetry 17 SDKs · Collector · OTLP The standard for producing and routing traces, metrics and logs. Run the Collector locally in Docker. laptop Langfuse 17 LLM tracing · evals · prompts · cost Open-source LLM engineering platform: traces, sessions, scores, datasets, prompt management. Self-host with Docker Compose. laptop Arize Phoenix 17 OTel-native LLM observability Tracing (OpenInference), evaluations and experiments; phoenix serve runs locally. laptop OpenLLMetry · OpenLIT 17 GenAI auto-instrumentation OpenTelemetry instrumentation for LLM providers, vector DBs and frameworks; export to any OTLP backend. laptop Jaeger · Prometheus · Grafana 17 traces · metrics · dashboards Classic open-source backends; all run locally in Docker for practice. laptop Evidently 17 drift and quality monitoring Data drift, LLM output evaluations and monitoring reports; runs as a Python library. laptop MLflow 18 tracking · registry · GenAI evals Experiment tracking, model registry, prompt registry and LLM evaluation/tracing features. laptop DVC 18 data and pipeline versioning Version datasets and pipelines alongside Git; reproduce any stage. laptop OpenTofu / Terraform 18 infrastructure as code Declarative infrastructure for GPU pools, databases, IAM and networking. laptop Argo CD · Argo Rollouts 18 GitOps · canaries Sync clusters from Git; progressive delivery with automated analysis and rollback. Practise on a local kind/k3d cluster. laptop OpenFeature 18 feature flags standard Vendor-neutral flag API for routing cohorts to prompt/model/index versions and for kill switches. laptop promptfoo CI · Langfuse prompts 18 prompt gates · prompt registry Run evaluation gates in CI; manage versioned prompts with labels for environments. laptop

title: Coverage checklist: all 135 roadmap topics

title: Five kinds of evidence
text: Label What it means What it can support Runs in browser The page executes a real algorithm on real input (BM25, BPE, backprop, k-means, bootstrap, queue simulation). How the mechanism behaves on that input. Simulation An animated model of system behaviour with fixed or illustrative numbers. No model, GPU, agent, cluster or deployment is used. The steps and the shape of a tradeoff, not performance. Laptop · CPU An exercise you run yourself in Python or with a local tool. Measured results on your machine and data, at small scale. Colab · GPU A step-by-step Google Colab guide you run on one free GPU ( 5.6 , 6.7 , 13.3 , 14.7 ). Measured results on the GPU Colab gave you, for that workload and model. Needs external compute Requires several GPUs or a cluster, more than one Colab GPU. Read rather than run. Measured results on that hardware, for that workload. Calculators Formulas applied to inputs you choose. Projections only; the output is as good as its assumptions. Tool links point to documentation, not installed software. Prices, throughputs and latencies in examples are illustrative inputs unless a measurement and its setup are stated (as in Appendix A). Labelling your own claims Keep the four categories from 15.10 apart in design reviews, reports and interviews: simulated ("the browser model shows…"), measured ("on this hardware, with this workload, we saw…"), projected ("with N replicas we expect…, not yet validated") and operated in production ("last month the system served…"). Mixing them is the most common way capacity and quality claims go wrong. Study progress ("Studied" ticks) is stored only in your browser and is never sent anywhere. All diagrams, calculators and simulations are part of this site. Real models and Python download only when you opt in to them, and Colab guides run on Google's machines, not here. Other links go to documentation.
